# TASKS

Tracks the phased build-out described in the approved plan (see conversation/plan history). Phases ship in order; do not start a phase's tasks until the prior phase's tasks are all checked off.

## Phase 1 — Foundations (KV wiring, auth skeleton, minimal link CRUD)

- [x] Declare `links`, `users`, `analytics` KV stores and grant them per component — file(s): spin.toml, runtime-config.toml — done when: `[component.redirect]` has `key_value_stores = ["links", "analytics"]` and `[component.api]` has `key_value_stores = ["links", "users", "analytics"]`, and `spin up --build --runtime-config-file runtime-config.toml` starts without KV-related errors — **note:** contrary to the original plan assumption, Spin does NOT auto-provision named (non-`default`) stores; a `runtime-config.toml` mapping each to `type = "spin"` is required even for local dev, added here and referenced from CLAUDE.md's Commands section
- [x] Add bootstrap-admin and session/cookie Spin variables — file(s): spin.toml — done when: `admin_bootstrap_username`, `admin_bootstrap_password` (secret), `cookie_secure` are declared and wired into `[component.api.variables]`
- [x] Implement real slug lookup + redirect in `redirect` (no password/analytics yet) — file(s): redirect/main.go — done when: `GET /r/{slug}` for an existing `slug:<slug>` KV record returns `302` to `target_url`; missing/disabled slug returns `404`
- [x] Implement local password hashing + verification helpers (Python) — file(s): api/auth.py — done when: a function hashes a password into `pbkdf2_sha256$<iter>$<salt>$<hash>` using stdlib `hashlib`/`hmac`/`secrets` only, and a matching verify function round-trips correctly, verified with a quick script/spike — **note:** `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` is not available in componentize-py 0.23.0's WASI CPython; implemented PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 manually from `hmac.new`+`hashlib.sha256` instead (confirmed working under `spin up`)
- [x] Implement bootstrap-admin seeding on first run — file(s): api/auth.py, api/app.py — done when: on a fresh KV store, the first request seeds one `user:<username>` admin record from the bootstrap variables, and subsequent runs do not reseed
- [x] Implement `AuthProvider`/`LocalAuthProvider` + session issuance — file(s): api/auth.py — done when: `authenticate(username, password)` returns a `Principal`/`AuthResult` or `None`, and `create_session(username, auth_provider)` writes a `session:<token>` KV record and returns a token
- [x] Implement `POST /api/auth/login`, `POST /api/auth/logout`, `GET /api/auth/me` — file(s): api/app.py, api/auth.py — done when: login sets the session cookie (`HttpOnly`, `Secure` gated by `cookie_secure`, `SameSite=Lax`) and returns `csrf_token`; `me` returns 401 without a valid session and the user/permissions with one; logout clears the session KV record and cookie
- [x] Implement session-validation middleware/helper used by all authenticated endpoints — file(s): api/app.py, api/auth.py — done when: a shared helper resolves the session cookie to a `Principal` or raises/returns 401, re-reading the user record fresh (not cached) each call
- [x] Implement link CRUD (random slug only, no password/custom slug yet) — file(s): api/links.py, api/app.py — done when: `POST/GET/DELETE /api/links` and `GET /api/links/{slug}` work against the `links` KV store, enforce session auth, and enforce owner-or-admin on get/delete
- [x] Build bare-bones `gui`: login, dashboard list, create-link form — file(s): gui/login.html, gui/dashboard.html, gui/index.html, gui/app.js — done when: a user can log in, see their links, and create a new random-slug link, all via `fetch` against `/api/...`
- [x] End-to-end manual verification of Phase 1 — file(s): (none — verification step) — done when: `spin up --build` runs cleanly; a fresh admin can log in via `gui`, create a link, and clicking `/r/{slug}` redirects correctly — verified via a headless-Chromium (Playwright) drive of the real login→dashboard→create→redirect flow, screenshots confirmed, zero console errors. **Note:** local browser testing over plain HTTP requires `SPIN_VARIABLE_COOKIE_SECURE=false` (the session cookie's `Secure` flag otherwise blocks the browser from storing/sending it over non-HTTPS) — production/HTTPS deployments should leave `cookie_secure` at its default `true`.

## Phase 2 — Custom slugs, permissions, password gate, QR

- [x] Add `permissions` list + `links.create_custom_slug` enforcement — file(s): api/auth.py, api/links.py — done when: creating a link with a custom slug returns `403` for a user lacking the permission and succeeds for one who has it (or is `admin`) — verified the admin-bypass and 400/409 paths via curl; the true non-admin-without-permission 403 path was confirmed for real in Phase 5 once user management shipped (created a restricted user via the admin UI, confirmed a live `403`)
- [x] Add custom-slug validation (charset/length) and collision handling — file(s): api/links.py — done when: invalid custom slugs are rejected with a clear error and slug collisions return a conflict error instead of overwriting an existing link
- [x] Add `password_hash` field to link records + `POST /api/links/{slug}/password` — file(s): api/links.py — done when: an owner/admin can set/change/remove a link's password via this endpoint, stored in the shared `pbkdf2_sha256$...` format — also scrubbed `password_hash` from every API response (`create`/`get`/`list`/`set password` now return a `password_protected` boolean instead)
- [x] Implement password-prompt page in `redirect` (embed + html/template) — file(s): redirect/main.go, redirect/prompt.html, redirect/passwordgate.go — done when: `GET /r/{slug}` for a password-protected link renders the prompt instead of redirecting, with the slug safely escaped
- [x] Implement password verification on `POST /r/{slug}` — file(s): redirect/main.go, redirect/passwordgate.go — done when: correct password redirects (`302`), incorrect password re-renders the prompt with an error (`401`), and every request re-fetches the link fresh from KV (no unlock cookie, per the confirmed re-prompt-every-time decision) — verified cross-language (Python-hashed, Go-verified via stdlib `crypto/pbkdf2`) via curl, including that removing a link's password takes effect on the very next request with zero stale state
- [x] Spike: add `qrcode`/`pypng` deps and confirm componentize-py build still works — file(s): api/pyproject.toml — done when: `uv run componentize-py -w spin:up/http-trigger@4.0.0 componentize app -o app.wasm` succeeds with the new deps and the resulting `.wasm` runs under `spin up` — no Pillow/C-extensions pulled in (confirmed via uv.lock: only `qrcode`, `pypng`, `colorama`, all pure Python)
- [x] Implement `GET /api/links/{slug}/qr` (svg + png, web/print sizes, download) — file(s): api/qr.py, api/app.py, spin.toml — done when: both `format=svg` and `format=png` return valid, scannable QR images at both `size=web` and `size=print`, and `download=1` sets `Content-Disposition` — verified under `spin up`; **note:** added a `public_base_url` Spin variable so the QR encodes the short link (`{public_base_url}/r/{slug}`) rather than the raw `target_url` — encoding the target directly would let a scan bypass the redirect, analytics, and password gate entirely
- [x] End-to-end manual verification of Phase 2 — file(s): (none — verification step) — done when: a permitted user creates a custom-slug, password-protected link; visiting it prompts for a password and only redirects on a correct entry; the QR code for the link scans correctly with a phone camera — verified via curl: created a combined custom-slug + password-protected link, confirmed the password prompt/reject/accept flow and a well-formed QR (visually inspected, encodes the short link per source review — no physical phone/camera available in this environment to scan it)

## Bug fixes

- [x] Add custom-slug input to the create-link form — file(s): gui/dashboard.html — done when: `POST /api/links` already supported `custom_slug` (gated on `links.create_custom_slug`) and was exercised via curl/admin-UI-permission-checks in Phase 2/5, but the create form itself never had a field for it, so admins/permitted users had no GUI way to request a custom slug (only random slugs were reachable through the UI) — added a "Custom short link (optional)" input, shown only when `role === "admin"` or `permissions` includes `links.create_custom_slug` (mirrors the existing "Manage users" nav-link gating pattern), wired into the create POST body. Also found and fixed a real bug surfaced while testing this: the input's `pattern="[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}"` threw a console `SyntaxError` in current Chromium, which validates `pattern` using regex "v-mode" (unicode sets) where a bare `-` in a character class must be escaped — fixed to `[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{3,32}`. Verified via headless-Chromium: field visible/usable for admin, hidden for a real restricted (no-permission) user, successful custom-slug creation redirects correctly, and a duplicate-slug submission surfaces the `slug_taken` error — zero console errors after the pattern fix.
- [x] Fix `GET /api/links` ignoring `links.view_all`/admin — file(s): api/links.py, api/tests/test_links.py, gui/dashboard.html — done when: `handle_list` only ever returned the caller's own `owner_links:<username>` slugs, even for admins/`links.view_all` holders — unlike `handle_get`/`handle_update`/`handle_delete`/analytics/qr, which already did the owner-or-view_all check correctly. There was no global slug index to list from, so admins had no GUI route to discover other users' links at all (not even a broken/degraded one) unless they already knew the exact slug. Added an `all_links` KV index (mirrors `auth.list_usernames`'s pattern) maintained in `handle_create`/`handle_delete`, and `handle_list` now serves from it when `role == "admin"` or `links.view_all` is held, else falls back to the owned-slugs index as before. No backfill for links created before this fix — consistent with this repo's existing convention of not adding migration code preemptively (see `list_usernames`/bootstrap-admin precedent). GUI: added an "Owner" column to the links table and switched the "Your links"/"All links" heading based on the same permission check, so an admin's expanded view is legible rather than looking like they own every link. 3 new tests (own-only default, admin-sees-all, view_all-permission-sees-all) plus an index-cleanup assertion added to the existing delete test — full suite 118 passing. Verified live via `spin up --build`: curl'd `/api/links` as admin (both users' links returned) and as a regular user (only their own), then confirmed the same via a headless-Chromium drive of the actual dashboard — zero console errors.

- [x] Tidy the links-table action buttons — file(s): gui/dashboard.html — done when: the previous bare "View" text link + `&nbsp;`-separated Edit/Delete buttons (inconsistent variants, no grouping) are replaced with a single Pico `role="group"` cluster (View rendered as `role="button"` to match Edit/Delete's height/style) — verified visually via a headless-Chromium screenshot.
- [x] Add a shared persistent header/nav across all authenticated GUI pages — file(s): gui/app.js, gui/dashboard.html, gui/links/detail.html, gui/admin/users.html — done when: the Logout button (and whoami/conditional "Manage users" link) no longer disappears when navigating from the dashboard to a link's detail page or the admin users page — previously only dashboard.html had a nav at all. Added `initHeader({backHref, manageUsersHref})` to app.js as the single source of truth, injected into each page's `<header id="app-header">`, returning the fetched principal so each page can still layer its own permission-gated logic (custom-slug field, "All links" heading, etc.) on top — verified via headless-Chromium: logged in, navigated dashboard → link detail → admin/users, confirmed Logout/whoami present and functional on all three.

## Impeccable critique-and-fix loop

Four rounds of `/impeccable critique` on `gui/` (score trend 20 → 26 → 23 → 26 /40), each followed by a targeted fix pass on the user-selected subset of findings, each verified against a fresh `spin up --build` and both test suites. Snapshots archived under `.impeccable/critique/`. No file(s) column below since each round touched a shifting subset of `gui/dashboard.html`, `gui/admin/users.html`, `gui/links/detail.html`, `gui/login.html`, `gui/app.js`, `gui/theme.css`, and `DESIGN.md` — see the critique snapshots for the authoritative per-round finding list.

- [x] Round 1 fixes (score 20 → 26) — done when: added a delete confirmation to the links table (previously the only destructive action in the app with none), routed link create/edit/delete errors through the existing `friendlyError()`/`ERROR_MESSAGES` pattern instead of leaking raw API codes, and gave link creation a real success payoff (`.form-success` banner: slug chip + Copy button) instead of a silent form-clear.
- [x] Round 2 fixes (score 26 → 23, a real regression this round's own new work introduced) — done when: closed the identical raw-error-code leak on `admin/users.html`'s create-user handler (missed by round 1's narrower scope); added self-serve destination-URL and password set/clear to the dashboard edit row (both already existed server-side, just unreachable from the GUI); surfaced `link.custom`/`link.password_protected` as badges and reformatted timestamps via `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with an "(expiring soon)" cue; standardized delete-confirmation copy between the two destructive flows; added `role="alert"`/`aria-live` to all error/success elements; consolidated two ad-hoc off-ramp font sizes into one documented `caption` DESIGN.md token. The regression: the new `.slug-kind-badge` used Signal Blue as a resting fill (violating DESIGN.md's own hover-only rule) and failed AA contrast, "expiring soon" only covered future dates not already-past ones, and the combined edit-row save could partially succeed with no disclosure.
- [x] Round 3 fixes (score 23 → 26) — done when: recolored the badge off Signal Blue onto neutral slate (fixing both the rule violation and the contrast failure), added a distinct "(expired)" state for already-past `end_at` alongside "(expiring soon)", prefixed the edit-row's partial-save error with "Destination and schedule saved." so a password-only failure is never mistaken for total failure, made the 7 sortable table headers keyboard-operable (`tabindex`/`keydown`/`aria-sort`), and fixed the "Custom slug"/"custom short link" terminology drift on the detail page. This round's own re-critique caught two more issues: the badge recolor fix reused a color pair (Signal Blue text on white, ~4.15:1) that was never fixed at the *button* level, and `role="button"` combined with `aria-sort` on the same `<th>` is an ARIA spec conflict.
- [x] Round 4 fixes — done when: fixed a real correctness bug found only by re-critiquing — the dashboard table's and success banner's slug-chip were live `<a href>` elements, so viewing/copying an existing link fired a real `/r/{slug}` redirect and inflated that link's own click count (the exact metric the product exists to report); converted both to non-navigating `<span>`s and added a dedicated per-row Copy button. Also darkened the app's one accent color (`#2b7fd1` → `#276fb8`, `--pico-primary`/`--ss-signal-500`) so every button and link clears 4.5:1 AA contrast, not just the previously-patched badge; added a neutral "(not yet live)" cue mirroring the expiry treatment for links whose `start_at` is still in the future; made the edit-row's partial-save success actually patch the visible row's cells (not just claim success in text); and dropped the conflicting `role="button"` from the sortable headers, keeping `aria-sort` valid on the default `columnheader` role.

Known remaining drift, not part of any round above: `.impeccable/design.json` (the DESIGN.md sidecar) is now stale across several rounds of token/color changes — worth a `/impeccable document` refresh before it's trusted for anything. *(Resolved by the `/impeccable document` refresh recorded below.)*

## Client-side window validation + styled confirmation dialogs

- [x] Client-side start_at/end_at validation on both link forms — raised and implemented 2026-07-24, direction confirmed with the user first (native validation bubble, not a `.form-error` message) — file(s): gui/dashboard.html — done when: added `wireWindowValidation(startInput, endInput)`, a shared local helper wired to both the create-form's `#start-at`/`#end-at` and each row's dynamically-created `.edit-start-at`/`.edit-end-at` pair. Mirrors the server's own `invalid_window_range` condition exactly (start >= end is invalid, not just start > end) via `setCustomValidity()` on the end field, re-evaluated on every `input` event on either field so a since-fixed combination clears the message instead of staying stuck invalid. `datetime-local` values are fixed-width `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm` strings, so a plain string comparison is already correct chronological ordering — no `Date` parsing needed. Verified live: setting Expires before Starts blocks submission natively (confirmed zero API calls fired and no link/edit was created) with the message "Expires must be after Starts."; fixing the dates clears the message and the submit goes through.
- [x] Replace native `confirm()` with a styled, on-brand confirmation for link/user delete — raised and implemented 2026-07-24, four design decisions confirmed with the user first (native bubble vs. inline error was the window-validation question above; this one covered dialog style, shared-vs-duplicated implementation, and confirming scope was just the two existing `confirm()` call sites) — file(s): gui/app.js, gui/dashboard.html, gui/admin/users.html, DESIGN.md, .impeccable/design.json — done when: added a shared `confirmDialog(message, {confirmLabel, cancelLabel})` helper to `app.js` (Pico's native `<dialog>`/`<article>` component, built dynamically so no markup is duplicated per page; resolves a promise; dismissible via its own Cancel button, the Esc key — which fires `cancel`, not `close`, on a native dialog — or a backdrop click, detected as a click landing on the `<dialog>` element itself rather than its `<article>` content). Both `dashboard.html`'s link-delete handler and `admin/users.html`'s user-delete handler now `await confirmDialog(...)` instead of calling `confirm(...)`. Button styling deliberately inverts the row-level convention: Cancel renders as Pico's plain default (primary) button while Confirm/Delete stays `outline secondary` — the same de-emphasis the row-level Delete button already uses (per DESIGN.md's existing "de-emphasis, not warning color, is how destructive reads here" rule) — so the visually prominent button in the dialog is the safe one, not the destructive one. Documented as a new "Confirmation Dialogs" component in `DESIGN.md` and added a matching entry + `generatedAt` refresh to `.impeccable/design.json`. Verified live for both delete flows: the dialog renders with the correct message and on-brand styling; Cancel closes without deleting; Esc closes without deleting; Confirm actually deletes via the real API and the row disappears from the table.

## Impeccable audit (first since the very first 15→19/20 pass) + P0 fix

- [x] `/impeccable audit gui/` — done when: scored 11/20 (Acceptable), pulled down almost entirely by one severe, previously-undetected finding. While spot-checking the new confirm dialog's button color via `getComputedStyle`, found that `--pico-primary-background` resolved to Pico's raw default `#0172ad`, not the theme's `#276fb8` — traced this to a real CSS specificity bug, not a fluke: `theme.css`'s `:root { --pico-primary-background: #276fb8; ... }` (specificity 0,1,0,0) has always lost the cascade against `vendor/pico.min.css`'s own `:root:not([data-theme="dark"]) { --pico-primary-background: #0172ad; ... }` (specificity 0,2,0,0) — higher specificity wins regardless of load order. Confirmed via `git log -p` that this has been broken since `theme.css`'s very first commit (`e93ac50`), surviving 2 full critique rounds and 1 prior audit undetected, because the coincidental fallback values (`#0172ad` on white still clears ~5.24:1 AA) never triggered a visible failure. Systematically diffed every property in both `:root` blocks via the live CSSOM (not just the one primary-color instance) and found **19 of 30 intended overrides silently dead**: the full `--pico-primary*` family (10 properties), `--pico-background-color`, `--pico-color`, `--pico-h1/h2/h3-color`, `--pico-muted-color`/`-border-color`, and `--pico-card-*-color` (3 properties) — meaning page background, body text, headings, and every primary button have been rendering Pico's stock light-theme colors instead of the documented dark-navy identity this entire time. The `--ss-*`-prefixed tokens (nav, slug chip, status badges) were never affected since Pico has no competing declaration for those names, which is exactly why the nav/chips/badges have always looked correct while the rest silently didn't. Also found 2 real accessibility gaps (confirm dialog has no `aria-labelledby`; row-action buttons still lack `aria-label` disambiguation, carried over from the earlier critique) and 1 forward-looking performance note (full DOM rebuild on every sort/filter — fine at current scale). Responsive and the mechanical scan (`detect.mjs`) came back clean (same 2 known false positives).
- [x] Fix the P0 theming/cascade bug — file(s): gui/theme.css, DESIGN.md — done when: changed `theme.css`'s selector from plain `:root` to `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])`, exactly matching Pico's own selector so specificity ties and `theme.css`'s later load order in every page's `<head>` correctly breaks the tie in the theme's favor — zero HTML changes needed. Verified live via `getComputedStyle`: all 19 previously-broken properties now resolve to their intended values (`--pico-primary-background: #276fb8`, `--pico-background-color: #eef1f6`, `--pico-color: #14243d`, `--pico-h1-color: #0a1628`, etc.), confirmed on login, dashboard, admin/users, and the confirm dialog — a genuinely visible difference (darker headings, a real mist-tinted page background instead of pure white) in side-by-side screenshots, not just a numeric confirmation. Added a `Don't declare theme color-variable overrides at plain :root` entry to `DESIGN.md` so this specific mistake doesn't recur if a future override is added the same way. `detect.mjs --json gui/` unchanged (same 2 known false positives); `uv run pytest` (131) and `go test ./linkgate/...` both still pass.
- [x] Fix the audit's 2 P2 accessibility findings — file(s): gui/app.js, gui/dashboard.html, gui/admin/users.html — done when:
  - **Confirm dialog has no accessible name**: `confirmDialog()` now generates a unique `id` for the message `<p>` (a module-level counter, since the dialog is created fresh per call) and sets `aria-labelledby` on the `<dialog>` pointing to it. Verified live: `document.getElementById(dialog.getAttribute('aria-labelledby')).textContent` correctly returns the actual message text ("Delete the link...") instead of the dialog having no computed accessible name.
  - **Row-action buttons lack disambiguation**: added `aria-label` to every row action on both pages — `dashboard.html`'s View/Copy/Edit/Delete (`"View link {slug}"` etc.) and `admin/users.html`'s Edit/Delete (`"Edit user {username}"` etc.) — preserving the visible short label while giving each control a unique accessible name. Verified live via the accessibility tree: buttons now read as `"View link aria-check"`, `"Delete user admin"`, etc. instead of generic, indistinguishable "Delete, button" entries across multiple rows.
  - Verified end-to-end: `detect.mjs --json gui/` unchanged (same 2 known false positives); `uv run pytest` (131) and `go test ./linkgate/...` both still pass.
- [x] Fix the audit's P3 performance note — file(s): gui/dashboard.html — done when: the actual anti-pattern wasn't the `<tr>` markup rebuild itself (genuinely cheap at this app's realistic scale) but `renderLinksTable()` re-querying every row's Copy/Edit/Delete/Cancel button and the edit-form via `body.querySelectorAll(...).forEach(el => el.addEventListener(...))` and attaching a fresh listener set on *every* render — which fires on every sort click and every (debounced) filter keystroke, so the re-listening cost scaled with row count for zero benefit, since the buttons' behavior never actually depends on which render produced them. Replaced with two delegated listeners on `#links-body` (one `click`, one `submit`), attached once at page init, dispatching to named handler functions (`handleCopyClick`/`handleDeleteClick`/`handleEditToggleClick`/`handleCancelEditClick`/`handleEditFormSubmit`) via `event.target.closest(...)` — `renderLinksTable()` itself now only builds row markup, no listener wiring. `submit` bubbles by default (unlike some other form events), so the delegated submit listener needed no special-casing. Verified live, not just by reading the diff: created 2 links, sorted (the exact path that used to re-attach every listener), then exercised Copy, Edit-toggle, Cancel, a full Edit→Save round-trip (confirmed the API call and the visible row update), Delete-with-confirm-dialog, and the filter box — all worked correctly through the new delegated handlers, zero console errors across the whole sequence. `detect.mjs --json gui/` unchanged (same 2 known false positives); `uv run pytest` (131, unchanged — GUI-only) and `go test ./linkgate/...` both still pass.

## Impeccable critique (8th pass, 27/40 — first drop, from genuinely new findings) + 3 P1s + 2 P2s fixed

- [x] `/impeccable critique gui/` (8th pass) — done when: scored 27/40 (Acceptable), the first drop in this project's critique trend (20→26→23→26→25→26→30→27), driven entirely by fresh, previously-undetected findings rather than any regression in the prior pass's fixes (self-delete/admin-promotion confirmations, sticky action column, user-creation payoff, and progressive disclosure all re-verified working correctly). Headline finding, confirmed independently by both assessments and by source inspection: every `<article>` card on every page has been silently rendering Pico's default drop shadow since `theme.css`'s first commit (`e93ac50`), directly violating DESIGN.md's own "No-Shadow Rule" — `theme.css` overrides every other `--pico-card-*` property but never touched `--pico-card-box-shadow`, which defaults to `var(--pico-box-shadow)`, a real 7-layer shadow. Also found: the links table overflows its own container by 21px at a realistic 1400px width with only 4 seeded rows, clipping the "Expires" header; at 390px, the just-shipped sticky action column occludes other columns' content at rest (not merely requiring a scroll) — confirmed pixel-precise (73.6px full overlap of the Owner column on the links table); Edit on an off-screen row gives no scroll-into-view; and deleting a link leaves a stale "Link created" success banner with a live Copy button pointing at the now-dead link. Full report: `.impeccable/critique/2026-07-25T00-09-22Z__gui.md`.
- [x] Fix the 3 P1s + 2 P2s (user chose "Everything") — file(s): gui/theme.css, gui/dashboard.html, gui/admin/users.html, DESIGN.md, .impeccable/design.json — done when:
  - **No-Shadow Rule violation**: added `--pico-card-box-shadow: none;` and `--pico-dropdown-box-shadow: none;` to `theme.css`'s `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` block. Verified live via `getComputedStyle` on the login card: `boxShadow` now resolves to `"none"` (previously a real multi-layer shadow).
  - **Desktop table overflow at 1400px**: the links table's slug chip dropped the redundant origin prefix (identical on every row, e.g. `http://host`) — table cells now show `/r/{slug}` with the full URL in a `title` attribute; Copy/View still use the full URL internally. Verified live: `table.scrollWidth` now exactly equals `figure.clientWidth` (1176 = 1176, was 1197 vs 1176) with the same realistic seeded data (including a long UTM-tagged destination URL) that previously overflowed.
  - **Mobile sticky-column occlusion (390px)**: added a `@media (max-width: 600px)` block to both tables. Links table hides Owner/Destination/Created/Starts, keeping Short link/Status/Expires/Actions (4 columns, aligning with the cognitive-load "≤4 items" guidance); users table hides Permissions. This alone wasn't sufficient — the sticky action column's own rendered width (208px for 4 unwrapped buttons) still didn't leave room for the kept columns, so the action button group also gets `flex-wrap: wrap; max-width: 100px` (70px on the users table's 2-button group) to shrink its footprint. Even after both fixes, a small residual overlap remained on whichever column sits immediately before the sticky column (confirmed live via `getBoundingClientRect`, e.g. "expiring soon" text and "active"/"Status" text partially covered). **Two attempted fixes measured to have zero real effect and were reverted**: `padding-right` alone (adds space after left-aligned content without moving it) and `padding-right` + `text-align: right` (the padding terms algebraically cancel once the cell's own width is also padding-driven in an auto-layout table) — both confirmed via direct pixel measurement to not move the text's rendered position at all across different padding values. The fix that actually works: an explicit `max-width` on the column itself (75px for links' Expires, 60px for users' Status), forcing wrapped text to physically stay within a zone that can never reach the sticky column's fixed screen position. Verified live via `getBoundingClientRect` comparison (not just screenshots): both columns now report `clear: true` (content's rightmost extent ≤ the sticky column's left edge) with real seeded content (`"Jul 25, 2026, 8:00 AM (expiring soon)"`, a long comma-joined permissions-driven "active" status) — confirmed via before/after screenshots showing full, unclipped, cleanly-wrapped text instead of "expiri[ng soon)]" / "Statu[s]" / "Activ[e]" mid-word clipping.
  - **Edit scroll-into-view**: `handleEditToggleClick` (dashboard.html) and the `.edit-btn` handler (admin/users.html) now call `editRow.scrollIntoView({ block: "center" })` when opening (not closing) a row. Verified live at a short viewport (500px): a row measured at `top: 711` (off-screen) scrolled its revealed edit form to `top: 135` (centered in view) after the click.
  - **Stale success banner after delete**: `handleDeleteClick` (dashboard.html) and the users-table delete handler (admin/users.html) now hide `#create-success` on a successful delete. Verified live: created a link, confirmed its success banner + Copy button appeared, deleted that same link, confirmed the banner was hidden immediately afterward (previously it stayed visible with a Copy button pointing at a dead slug).
  - Updated `DESIGN.md` (Elevation & Depth section corrected to document the shadow fix rather than the pre-existing incorrect claim that the theme "never overrides" card box-shadow; Data Tables section documents the mobile column-collapse technique and explicitly warns that `padding-right` does not create sticky-column clearance; Slug Chip component note documents the table's shortened-chip convention) and refreshed `.impeccable/design.json` (Scrollable Data Table and Slug Chip component descriptions extended; 2 new `dos` entries).
  - Regression-verified: full desktop re-check (table no longer overflows at 1400px), sort, Copy, Edit-toggle/Cancel, and a full Delete-with-confirm-dialog round-trip all still work correctly through every CSS change, zero console errors across the entire verification session (only a pre-existing, unrelated `autocomplete`-attribute advisory, not from any code in this repo).

## Considered and rejected

- [x] Client-side destination-URL reachability check on link creation — considered 2026-07-18, decided against, not deferred. The idea: before/without blocking link creation, check that a submitted `target_url` is actually reachable, run from the *browser* rather than server-side (since a real user's browser is far less likely to get bot-blocked by the destination site than a server making the same request). Rejected because neither `redirect` nor `api` has any `allowed_outbound_hosts` entries (confirmed empty/absent in `spin.toml` for both), so the server-side half of that reasoning is moot — the check can only ever run client-side. And a browser-side check against an arbitrary cross-origin URL is limited to a `fetch(..., {mode: "no-cors"})` opaque request, which can detect a hard DNS/connection failure but can never distinguish a real `200` from a `404`/`500` (no readable status across origins without CORS headers from the destination) — not enough signal to justify the added complexity, especially since the check could never be allowed to block submission anyway. Revisit only if a genuinely new mechanism becomes available (e.g. an outbound-allowed validation proxy), not as a plain client-side nudge.

- [x] Per-request CSP nonce injection in `gui-pages` (and its hash-based sibling) — considered 2026-07-31 while planning `docs/plans/csp-drop-unsafe-inline.md`, decided against, not deferred. The idea, and the one the older "Future work" entry reaches for first: generate a fresh nonce per response, put it in both the `content-security-policy` header and every inline `<script>`/`<style>` tag, so the GUI's inline code could stay where it is. Rejected on four counts, the third being fatal: (1) it forces `build_response` to stop being a pass-through and instead do byte-level markup surgery (`body.replace(b"<script>", …)`) on every request, in the one component whose entire job is to be a trustworthy header attacher — a page reformatted to `<script >` or given an extra attribute would silently stop receiving a nonce and start being blocked, a failure that surfaces as a dead page in a browser, not a failing test; (2) it needs a CSPRNG under `componentize-py`, which is unconfirmed and not safe to assume given `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac`'s documented absence in that runtime; (3) **it does not finish the job** — confirmed against MDN's `style-src-attr` page that nonces apply to `<script>`/`<style>` *blocks* only, so the 7 static `style="display: none"` attributes (6 in HTML + 1 in an `app.js` `innerHTML` template) would still be blocked and `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` would have to stay, buying a hardened `script-src` and nothing else; (4) it makes every HTML response uncacheable by construction and leaves 925 lines of JS/CSS stranded inside `.html` files where no editor or linter treats them as JS and CSS. The hash (`'sha256-…'`) variant avoids the per-request work but replaces it with a permanent tax — recompute the hash and hand-edit the CSP string on every edit to any inline block, failing silently — and shares defect (3) exactly. Revisit only if a future page genuinely cannot externalize its script (e.g. server-templated JS), which is not the case for any of the five pages today.
- [x] Serving the new per-page `.js`/`.css` from `gui-pages` instead of the `gui` static component — considered 2026-07-31 while planning `docs/plans/csp-drop-unsafe-inline.md`, decided against. Genuinely attractive: `gui-pages` already owns the `/...` catch-all, so it would add **zero** `spin.toml` routes (versus the 8 exact routes the chosen approach adds) and would express the whole asset list as new entries in `routing.py`'s already-host-tested `ROUTES` dict, sidestepping the `spin_static_fs` path-resolution gotchas entirely. Lost because it routes every subresource request through a `componentize-py` Python Wasm component instead of the purpose-built static fileserver — a Python component instantiation per asset per page load, for zero benefit — and because it would need a new content-type map in `routing.py` (which hardcodes `text/html` today) purely to serve files it has no business serving. More fundamentally it inverts the architecture the 2026-07-25 security-headers pass deliberately established: `gui-pages` serves navigated documents that need headers, `gui` serves static subresources that don't. `CLAUDE.md` already sanctions the chosen path in as many words — "Stick to exact routes for this component if any more assets are ever added to it." A related sub-alternative was also rejected: appending the three pages' CSS blocks to the already-routed `theme.css` to save 3 of the 8 routes. All three blocks are scoped tightly enough (`#links-table`, `#users-table`, `.detail-heading`) that nothing would collide, but it would make every page download 206 lines of rules that apply to one other page, and it would blur `theme.css` — the design-system file `DESIGN.md` describes — with three pages' worth of table-layout workarounds. Route entries are cheap and inert; the muddied boundary is not. Revisit only if the `[[trigger.http]]` list becomes genuinely unmanageable.
- [x] Flash-of-wrong-theme fixes other than a small external `theme-init.js` — considered 2026-07-31 while planning `docs/plans/light-dark-theme.md`, decided against. Four alternatives, all rejected. (1) **An inline `<head>` snippet whitelisted by a `'sha256-…'` CSP hash** — zero new routes, zero new requests, and the CSP stays a static string, but this reopens a decision settled the same day in the entry above: the hash must be hand-recomputed on every edit with a silently dead page as the failure mode, and that entry says to revisit only for a page that genuinely cannot externalize its script, which a 15-line theme-init snippet obviously can. It would also require relaxing `gui-pages/tests/test_no_inline_code.py`'s srcless-`<script>` assertion — the one thing keeping the CSP honest — to save a single inert route entry. (2) **Accept the flash** — free and ships sooner, but this is a five-page multi-page app where every navigation is a full document load, so it is a white strobe on every click, not a one-time startup artifact. (3) **Move `<script src="app.js">` into `<head>` and put the theme logic at the top of it** — the most tempting one: zero new routes, zero new files, zero new requests (`app.js` is fetched on every page anyway and `index.html` already loads it from `<head>`), and behaviour-preserving since `app.js` declares only functions/constants at top level. Lost because it makes a 10 KB shared bundle render-blocking on four pages instead of a ~600-byte file, and permanently couples first paint to the growth of the shared library — the next 200 lines added to `app.js` silently become a paint cost. (4) **A theme cookie with `gui-pages` writing `data-theme` into the served HTML** — eliminates the flash with zero JavaScript and zero routes, but it is ruled out by the user's confirmed client-side-only decision and independently by the same reasoning that killed nonces: it forces `build_response` to stop being a pass-through and start doing byte-level markup surgery in the one component whose job is trustworthy headers. Revisit (3) only if the extra request ever measurably matters; revisit (1) only under the condition its own entry names.
- [x] `light-dark()` (and a duplicated `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` block) as the dark-theme token architecture — considered 2026-07-31 while planning `docs/plans/light-dark-theme.md`, decided against in favour of two explicit `data-theme`-scoped blocks. `light-dark()` is the most elegant option on paper: one token block instead of two, `color-scheme` alone drives the switch, no duplication, correct on first paint with **no JavaScript at all** for the OS-following case, and forcing a theme collapses to a three-line `color-scheme` override. Lost on two counts — it requires rewriting all ~30 existing light declarations into `light-dark(a, b)` form, touching the single block this repo has already gotten silently wrong twice (the `:root` specificity bug, the two-round form-element leak) against an explicit "no light-theme redesign" non-goal; and its degradation is bad rather than graceful, since on an engine without support the declarations are invalid at computed-value time and the affected custom properties resolve to unset — a broken page, not a stale one. The CSS-only variant (duplicate the whole dark block inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme]) { … } }` and use JS only for the explicit override) was rejected separately: CSS cannot share one declaration block between a media-query and a non-media-query context, so ~35 declarations would exist twice, which is exactly the drift the sweep-the-family rule exists to prevent — and with the in-head init script the JS path has no flash either, so the duplication buys nothing. Revisit `light-dark()` if the token block is ever rewritten for an independent reason.
- [x] A two-state light/dark toggle, and a `<select>` as the control's shape — considered 2026-07-31 while planning `docs/plans/light-dark-theme.md`, decided against in favour of a three-button Auto/Light/Dark group. The two-state toggle is simpler and narrower in an already-crowded nav, and the user's own phrasing ("a toggle … that forces light or dark") permits it — but "follow my OS" is the default state, and a two-state control makes it permanently unreachable after the first click, with no affordance anywhere to get back; since persistence is `localStorage`-only, the escape hatch would be clearing site data. The `<select>` shape is more compact than three buttons (~110px vs ~140px) and brings native keyboard/screen-reader semantics for free, but a Pico `<select>` on the navy nav fill needs a fight on three fronts: `width: 100%` by default, a form-element background/colour set that must be overridden for the dark fill, and a chevron whose colour is baked into a `data:` URL rather than read from a variable, so it may render near-invisible and need a bespoke `--pico-icon-chevron` override. Three buttons reuse the already-proven `#logout-btn` white-on-navy treatment instead. Revisit the `<select>` only if nav width measurement forces a more compact control than the plan's pre-approved mobile-wrap fallback can absorb.
- [x] Keeping the primary button white-on-`#276fb8` in dark mode so it stays pixel-identical across themes — proposed and then reversed 2026-07-31 while planning `docs/plans/light-dark-theme.md`. The first draft kept `--pico-primary-background: #276fb8` with `--pico-primary-inverse: #fff` in the dark block, on the argument that the app's single most-clicked control should look the same in both themes and that text contrast (white ink at 5.18:1) outranks the non-text boundary. It measured a fill-vs-card boundary of **exactly 3.00:1** — sitting precisely on WCAG 1.4.11's minimum with zero headroom. Reversed on this repo's own history: it has shipped a thin-margin colour twice (`ok-green` at 4.39:1 against the table cell's real background, and `badge-slate` clearing AA by 0.27:1) and had to fix both after the fact, and a zero-margin value breaks silently the first time anything adjacent moves — here, any future change to `--pico-card-background-color` would invalidate it without the button being touched. The margin could not be bought cheaply either: white ink caps the fill's lightness, so `#2d78c0` (white 4.61:1 / boundary 3.38:1) and `#3079c4` (4.51:1 / 3.45:1) just trade one thin margin for two. Real headroom on both criteria requires changing the ink, so dark mode uses the light-fill/dark-ink convention instead — `#6fb0ee` (the accent itself, constant hue with `#276fb8`, 209° vs 210°) with `--pico-primary-inverse: #0a1628`, giving **6.76:1** fill-vs-card and **7.87:1** label-on-fill. Accepted consequence, recorded so it is not treated later as a bug: **the primary button is deliberately no longer pixel-identical across themes** — light is white-on-mid-blue, dark is navy-on-light-blue — while the hue, the fill-is-the-accent rule, and the "lifting" hover direction all survive. `.identity-avatar` and the theme control's pressed state both read `--pico-primary-background`/`--pico-primary-inverse` rather than hardcoding a fill and a white ink, so neither can drift out of step. Revisit only if cross-theme pixel identity becomes a stated requirement, and then only with a fill/ink pair that clears both thresholds with margin.
- [x] Keeping Fermyon's KV explorer in the committed `spin.toml`, gated only by its required credential variables — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/kv-explorer.md`, decided against. By far the cheapest option: no fragment file, no generator script, no generated manifest, and because `kv_explorer_user`/`kv_explorer_password` would be `{ required = true }`, any deploy that forgot them would fail to start rather than expose an unauthenticated tool. Rejected because it fails the one constraint the whole plan exists to satisfy — "reachable in production unless someone remembers to remove it" is not local-only. It would also put an **unauthenticated** HTML page (confirmed in `explorer/main.go`: `router.GET(spinRoute, UIHandler)` is the one route not wrapped in `BasicAuth`) plus a full-CRUD API on the public origin, and would make two credential variables mandatory on every production run of an app that otherwise has no use for them, turning a dev convenience into a real secret to manage. Revisit only if Spin ever gains genuine conditional/environment-scoped components, at which point the fragment and the generator script both disappear.
- [x] A committed second full manifest (`spin-dev.toml`) run with `spin up -f`, instead of generating one — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/kv-explorer.md`, decided against. Genuinely simpler than the generator: no script, no `.gitignore` entry, and the reviewer's "which manifest exposes the explorer" check is just as easy. Rejected on drift, which is not hypothetical here — `spin.toml` currently carries 16 triggers across four components, and the CSP hardening pass added **eight** routes to it in one change. A committed duplicate would have silently missed all eight, and the failure mode is the bad kind: the dev manifest keeps working while diverging from the one that ships, so local testing quietly stops testing production's routing. The chosen shape (concatenate `spin.toml` + `dev/kv-explorer.toml` into a gitignored `spin-dev.toml` on every run) makes drift structurally impossible for the price of a 15-line shell script.
- [x] Running the KV explorer as its own separate Spin app on a second port, sharing the local state directory — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/kv-explorer.md`, decided against. The strongest possible answer to "must not be reachable in any deployed configuration": the explorer would appear in no file `spin deploy` ever reads, and there would be nothing to generate or guard. Rejected on evidence about the local KV backend: `runtime-config.toml` declares all three stores as `type = "spin"` with **no `path`**, and no `.db` file exists anywhere under the repo or in `~/Library/Caches/spin` after months of local runs (`.spin/` holds only `logs/`), so a second process almost certainly would not see the first's data at all — and even if it did, two Spin processes against one sqlite store is an untested arrangement whose failure mode is confusing rather than obvious. Revisit if the local stores are ever given an explicit `path = ".spin/kv.db"`; at that point this becomes clearly better than a generated manifest.
- [x] Excluding the KV explorer at run time with `spin up -c` / `--component-id` instead of keeping it out of the manifest — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/kv-explorer.md`, decided against. Attractive because it needs no new files whatsoever. Rejected three times over: the Spin docs mark it "[Experimental] … it may change even between minor versions"; it is **opt-out**, so a production run would have to enumerate all four other components and forgetting one exposes the explorer — precisely the failure mode the local-only constraint rules out; and it only narrows the *running* subset, leaving the component in the deployed application. Whether `spin deploy` honours the flag at all is undocumented. Revisit only if Spin promotes it to stable *and* inverts it into an opt-in mechanism.
- [x] Using `SPIN_APP_KV_SKIP_AUTH=1` for the KV explorer instead of real local Basic-auth credentials — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/kv-explorer.md`, decided against. It would drop one env var from the dev command, the `kv_credentials` component variable, and the two `[variables.*]` sub-tables. Rejected for three reasons: `spin up --env` sets the variable on **all** components, not just the explorer; unauthenticated full CRUD on `127.0.0.1:3000` is reachable from any page the developer already has open, because a cross-origin `fetch` with `Content-Type: text/plain` is a CORS simple request (no preflight) and `AddKeyHandler` never checks `Content-Type` before decoding the body — a narrow but real drive-by write onto local link records; and `spin.toml` already establishes the exact pattern to copy (`admin_bootstrap_username = { default = … }` + `admin_bootstrap_password = { required = true, secret = true }`), so matching it costs less than explaining an exception. Revisit only if the credential requirement measurably pushes people toward not using the tool.
- [x] A client-side (or server-side) loop of N single-item requests for bulk create/delete — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against. By far the cheapest option: `gui/dashboard.js` already has `api.post`/`api.delete`, so "bulk" becomes a `for` loop with a progress counter and zero API work. Rejected because it is **incorrect, not merely slow** — every create and delete read-modify-writes the `all_links` and `owner_links:<username>` index keys (`api/links.py:40-73`) and Spin's KV has no compare-and-swap (already disclosed in CLAUDE.md's "Security tradeoffs"), so overlapping in-flight requests silently drop index entries and produce links that exist in KV and resolve at `/r/<slug>` but can never be seen or managed in the dashboard again. The failure will not reproduce on a developer's machine with three rows. A server-side loop over `handle_create` has the identical index defect plus a second one: it would run the pure-Python 100,000-iteration PBKDF2 (`api/auth.py:34-57`, there being no `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` under componentize-py) once per row instead of once per batch. Revisit only if Spin's KV ever gains atomic operations.
- [x] Parsing the pasted/uploaded bulk CSV in JavaScript and posting a structured `rows` array — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against in favour of posting the raw text and parsing it in `api/bulk.py`. Genuinely attractive: the client could show a parsed preview before submitting, the API would take a clean self-describing payload, and it is what most web apps do. Lost on testability — there is no JavaScript test runner in this repo (`find . -name package.json` outside `node_modules` returns nothing; the `Jenkinsfile` runs three Python/Go commands), so the fiddliest logic in the feature (BOM stripping, CRLF normalization, quote stripping, header detection, delimiter precedence) would be the only untested code in it, in a repo whose whole testability convention exists to prevent exactly that. Server-side parsing also yields strictly better errors: it reports the **physical line number of the user's own file**, which a rows-array design discards before the server ever sees it. The user's "read the file client-side" constraint is fully honoured — `FileReader` fills the textarea and there is exactly one submission path. Revisit if a JS test runner is ever added *and* a live parsed preview is actually wanted.
- [x] Multipart file upload to the `api` component for the bulk CSV — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against. The conventional shape for "upload a CSV", and it would let the browser stream a large file rather than reading it into memory. Rejected because it means running a multipart parser inside a `componentize-py` Wasm component, which is precisely the category of stdlib assumption this repo has already been burned by (`hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac`'s documented absence in that runtime), to solve a problem that does not exist: these files are a few KB of text and `FileReader` plus a JSON string field handles them with no new dependency, no new parser and no new failure mode. Revisit only if bulk input ever needs to be megabytes.
- [x] Full RFC 4180 CSV parsing (quoted fields containing delimiters, `""` escapes, embedded newlines) for the bulk format — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against in favour of a first-delimiter split plus a single-pair quote strip. Correct in the abstract and available from Python's stdlib `csv`. Lost because the two fields are a slug (`[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}`, which can never contain a delimiter) and a URL (which can never contain a tab, and whose commas are already handled by splitting on the *first* delimiter only, the destination always being the last field); the one real spreadsheet artifact, a quoted URL containing a comma, round-trips correctly under the cheap rules. Embedded newlines inside a quoted field would break the "one line = one row" contract that makes line-numbered error reporting possible, which is worth more here than completeness. Revisit only if someone produces a real file the current rules mangle.
- [x] Partial success on bulk create/actions — create the valid rows, report the invalid ones — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against (all-or-nothing was a fixed user decision, and it holds up). The most tempting alternative and what most bulk importers actually do: nobody enjoys re-submitting 199 good rows because of one typo. Rejected because with partial success the user must diff what they submitted against what now exists to work out what to retry, and re-submitting the corrected file then collides with the rows that did succeed and produces a second wave of `slug_taken` errors — a fix loop with bookkeeping instead of "edit the file, submit again". The same reasoning extends to bulk delete/enable/disable, where the realistic failure is a stale selection (someone else deleted a link since the page loaded) and the honest answer is "your view is out of date, refresh" rather than "we did 49 of the 50 things you asked for, work out which." Revisit only if real usage shows large submissions failing repeatedly on one or two rows.
- [x] Putting the dashboard's new selection checkbox column last instead of first — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against. This is not a cosmetic preference: at position 8, immediately before the sticky action column, it would shift **zero** `nth-child` selectors and zero `children[]` indices, eliminating an entire nine-row renumbering table and its silent-breakage risk — most sharply `gui/dashboard.js:257-259`, which writes an edited row's saved values into `displayRow.children[2]/[5]/[6]` by positional index, so an off-by-one there writes a formatted date into the wrong cell with no error anywhere. It loses to convention: every table users touch daily puts the checkbox at the left edge, and a right-edge checkbox sitting next to View/Copy/Edit/Delete invites a mis-click on Delete. The renumbering is mechanical, exhaustively enumerated in the plan, and verified by the 390px layout check this repo already has a documented procedure for. Revisit only if the renumbering actually causes a regression that survives verification.
- [x] A modal dialog, or a Single/Bulk tab bar, as the home for the bulk-create form — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against in favour of a second native `<details>` disclosure in the create card. A dialog would keep the create card uncluttered and tabs would be the most explicit framing. The dialog loses because the form is a textarea plus a file picker plus three batch fields plus a potentially 50-row error table — a scroll trap in a modal — and because the app's only `<dialog>` is `confirmDialog`, deliberately a tiny confirm; growing it into a form host makes it a different component. The tab bar loses because no tab component exists in the design system and introducing one for two panels adds a pattern that must then be maintained everywhere. `<details>` is DESIGN.md's own incumbent Do for occasional-use fields, is already styled, already keyboard-accessible, and already has its Pico `summary:focus-visible` gotcha fixed in `theme.css`. Revisit only if the panel grows past what a disclosure can reasonably hold.
- [x] Making the bulk row cap a Spin variable (`bulk_max_rows`) instead of a module constant — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against. It would let an operator tune the cap for a slower host without a rebuild, and `analytics_event_slots` is the obvious precedent. Rejected because that variable exists for a specific reason — `redirect` and `api` must agree on it — while this one is read by exactly one function in one component, and making it a variable costs a `[variables]` entry, a `[component.api.variables]` entry, a `variables.get` + `int()` in `app.py` and a parameter threaded through the handler, to express a safety rail tied to what the runtime can do in one request rather than an operator policy. The `too_many_rows` error body returns `max_rows`, so the UI stays truthful if the constant ever changes. Revisit if a deployment target actually needs a different number.
- [x] `DELETE /api/links` with a JSON body of slugs for bulk delete — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, decided against in favour of `POST /api/links/bulk-action`. The most RESTful shape. Rejected because `gui/app.js:56`'s shared `api.delete` sends no body (`delete: (path) => apiCall(path, { method: "DELETE" })`), so it would have to be widened for a single call site; because a `DELETE` with a semantically significant body is under-specified and inconsistently handled by intermediaries; and because this API already uses `POST /api/links/{slug}/password` for what is logically a `PATCH`, so a POST action endpoint is the incumbent convention rather than a deviation. Revisit only if the API is ever formally speced against a REST style guide.
- [x] A 200-row bulk cap (`MAX_BULK_ROWS`) instead of 50 — proposed 2026-08-01 in the first draft of `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`, overruled by the user the same day in favour of **50**. The draft's reasoning was that the persona finding says "dozens" and 200 gave generous headroom, with a live timing measurement at 200 rows acting as a gate that might force the number down. The user's reasoning is better on both counts: 50 already covers "dozens of campaign links" comfortably, and it moves the unmeasured Wasm-timing question from "a risk the cap has to be sized around" to a non-issue — at 50 rows the per-request work is ~100 KV operations plus at most one PBKDF2 hash, bounded well below anything the redirect path does at scale. The live measurement survives but is reframed as confirmation that a full-cap submission is comfortably fast; if 50 rows turns out to be slow, that is a genuine finding to report loudly, because it would mean something is wrong in the per-row KV path rather than that the cap is too high. Dropping to 50 also deleted a code path — the error table's "first 50 rows, then …and N more" truncation can no longer trigger, since `row_errors` is now bounded by the cap. The accepted cost is that the cap is genuinely reachable: a 120-row spreadsheet export hits it, which is why `too_many_rows` carries `row_count` alongside `max_rows` and the UI names both numbers and the batch count to split into, and why the bulk-action bar disables itself above 50 selected rows instead of quietly acting on a subset. **Raise it later only as a deliberate decision taken with timing evidence from the plan's Verification step 7 in hand** — not because someone found the limit inconvenient — and if it goes past ~100, reinstate the error-table truncation in the same change.
- [x] Plain substring matching for the banned-word slug check — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md`, decided against in favour of whole-segment matching (case-insensitive, split on `-` and `_`). It is the two-line version of the feature and what any quick implementation reaches for. Rejected on the Scunthorpe problem, which a 32-character slug (`CUSTOM_SLUG_PATTERN` = `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$`) walks straight into: substring matching against any realistic list rejects legitimate campaign slugs — `classic-glasses` and `assets-2026` are the two named regression cases, and the tail beyond them is unpredictable — and every false positive costs a rebuild and redeploy to unblock, since the list is a compiled-in constant. **This rejection applies to custom slugs only.** For auto-generated slugs substring is the *chosen* rule: a 7-character base62 string has no separators and therefore no segments for segment matching to ever fire on, and nobody is attached to a particular random string, so the false-positive cost there is one extra iteration of a retry loop that already exists. Two matching rules, one word list, deliberately — do not collapse them while tidying up.
- [x] Folding the banned-word check into `is_valid_custom_slug` and reusing the `invalid_custom_slug` error code — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md`, decided against in favour of a separate `slugwords.banned_slug_segment` predicate called alongside it. Genuinely tempting: `is_valid_custom_slug` (`api/links.py:95`) already has exactly the two call sites that need the check (`handle_create` at `links.py:153` and `validate_bulk_rows` at `bulk.py:131`), so the whole feature would be a three-line diff with no new import and no new error code to thread through. It loses on the error surface, which is the only thing the caller can act on: a boolean tells both callers nothing, so both would report `invalid_custom_slug`, whose user-facing text is *"Custom short links can only use letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores (3–32 characters)"* (`gui/app.js:154`) — sending someone who typed `black-friday-<word>`, which satisfies every one of those rules, to fix a problem that does not exist. It is worse in bulk, where the per-row table is the only feedback and a wrong reason on one row of fifty is genuinely hard to recover from. The same entry settles a related fork: the new `banned_word_in_slug` body **names the offending segment** (`{"error": "banned_word_in_slug", "segment": "<segment>"}`) rather than staying coy. Naming the match is bad practice for a public-facing filter, but the audience here is authenticated, named internal staff, the echoed value is the user's own input rather than a disclosure from the list, and a slug can hold up to sixteen segments — an unnamed rejection turns the fix into a guessing game and does so worst in a 50-row paste. A generic message is kept anyway as the shared `ERROR_MESSAGES` fallback for any surface with no `segment` to hand.
- [x] Leetspeak / homoglyph normalization (`4`→`a`, `0`→`o`, `$`→`s`, Cyrillic lookalikes) before banned-word matching — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md`, decided against, and recorded here because it is the obvious next request. Four reasons. (1) It is an arms race with no end state — every normalization rule invites the next substitution, and the list of substitutions is unbounded. (2) It multiplies false positives exactly where they are most expensive: normalizing digits to letters collides real campaign slugs like `s4le` and `4th-of-july` with the list, undoing the entire point of choosing whole-segment matching. (3) It implies a guarantee the feature does not make — the moment the check looks clever, people assume it is comprehensive, when it is a carelessness guard. (4) It defends only against a deliberate evader, who is explicitly outside the threat model: an authenticated employee intent on publishing something embarrassing has a dozen easier routes, starting with any word not on the list. Revisit only after a real incident of deliberate evasion, and then as a content-policy decision with a named owner, not as a regex someone adds quietly.
- [x] A KV-backed, admin-editable banned-word list with a management UI — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md`, decided against (a static in-code list was a fixed user decision, and it holds up). The attractive version: a non-engineer owns the list, false positives are fixed in seconds, and it matches how the rest of the app's admin surfaces work. Rejected because it needs a key namespace, a CRUD endpoint set, a new entry in `auth.KNOWN_PERMISSIONS` (a deliberately small fixed vocabulary), a new page under `gui/admin/`, and a KV read on every link creation — for a list that will change perhaps twice a year, against `PRODUCT.md`'s principle that self-hosting only pays for itself if it stays operationally simple. The accepted cost is that fixing a false positive requires editing `api/slugwords.py`, rebuilding `api/app.wasm` and redeploying, with no bypass and no override permission anywhere. The check sits behind `banned_slug_segment`/`contains_banned_word` precisely so that conversion later means changing one module's internals plus threading a `store` parameter through two call sites, rather than hunting inlined comparisons. Revisit if false positives become frequent enough that the rebuild loop is a real burden — that is the trigger, not general tidiness.
- [x] Retroactively scanning (or blocking edits to) existing links whose slugs contain a banned word — considered 2026-08-01 while planning `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md`, decided against; the plan instead guarantees existing links are entirely unaffected. A one-off scan is attractive as a "what do we already have out there?" answer. Rejected because there is no rename path — confirmed, not assumed: `UPDATABLE_FIELDS` is `{"target_url", "status", "start_at", "end_at"}` (`api/links.py:219`) and `api/app.py` has no rename endpoint — so the only available action on a flagged legacy link is deletion, which breaks every QR code and printed URL already in circulation. Blocking edits is worse: it would strand a link in a state where the destination cannot even be repointed. `redirect/main.go` never validates slug shape either (bare `store.Exists`/`store.Get`), so legacy links keep resolving with no Go change at all. A read-only report would be more defensible than a scan-and-act, but it needs an endpoint and an admin surface for a question the dashboard already answers by eye. A regression test pins the "edit a legacy banned slug, get a 200" behaviour so a later refactor cannot quietly take it away.
- [x] A per-link `domain` field, and `Host`-header enforcement in `redirect` to make it honest — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/multi-domain-display.md`, decided against; that plan makes domains a pure viewer preference instead. This was the design the 2026-07-18 "Multi-domain short-link hosting" Future-work entry assumed, and it is the first thing any future reader will reach for, so it is recorded in full. The field is attractive: it is what a commercial shortener shows, it lets the dashboard state "this is a `go.example.com` link", and unlike a `localStorage` preference it follows a user between browsers. It loses on one confirmed fact — **`redirect` resolves purely by `slug:{slug}` and never reads the `Host` header**, so every link already works on every domain pointed at the deployment. Storing which domain a link "is for" without enforcing it produces metadata that lies: it would appear in the dashboard, the CSV export, `GET /api/links` and the QR as though binding, and the first person to share an off-brand URL finds it works. That is worse than no field — it converts an honest absence into a confident falsehood, and puts that falsehood in an exported CSV that outlives the session. It also costs a link-record schema change, a migration for every existing link, a new column in the bulk-create format and a new field across three API surfaces. Enforcement, the only thing that would make it honest, was rejected separately: it puts a header parse plus a second KV-field comparison on the one hot path this repo keeps deliberately minimal; it creates a sharp new failure mode where a link works in testing and 404s in production because a CDN, proxy or DNS change rewrote `Host`; and it protects nothing, since slugs are already documented as enumerable and non-secret. Revisit only if a real requirement appears to make a link resolve on exactly one domain — and then take both halves together, plus an explicit decision that a mismatched `Host` returns 404 to match the time-window behaviour.
- [x] A KV-backed domain registry with an admin domain-management page — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/multi-domain-display.md`, decided against in favour of a single comma-separated `public_base_urls` Spin variable (a fixed user decision, and it holds up). Also the 2026-07-18 entry's assumption. Attractive because it is self-service, matches how users and links are already managed, and avoids a redeploy to add a domain. Rejected because the self-service is illusory: adding a domain requires a DNS record, a TLS certificate and an edge routing change, none of which an admin can do from this app — so the page would let someone add `go.example.com` and then discover it resolves nowhere while the app cheerfully offered it in every selector. The variable puts the list in the same place as the deployment configuration it is inseparable from, for one line of `spin.toml`, one pure module and no new endpoint, page, permission, KV key or CRUD surface; it also adds zero new KV usage, sidestepping the Akamai single-`"default"`-store blocker entirely. Revisit only if domains become genuinely self-service — i.e. the app can provision DNS/TLS itself.
- [x] Dynamically-generated per-domain permission strings instead of a separate `assigned_domains` list — considered 2026-07-18, re-confirmed 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/multi-domain-display.md`. Attractive because it reuses the permission plumbing end to end: `KNOWN_PERMISSIONS`, `has_permission`, the users page's checkbox list, the 403 bodies' `required_permission` field. Rejected because `auth.KNOWN_PERMISSIONS` (`api/auth.py:29`) is deliberately a small, fixed, hardcoded frozenset whose whole job is to "reject anything outside this set rather than silently accepting typos" — generating members at runtime from a configuration variable destroys exactly that property. Recorded a second time because it is the first idea anyone reaching for the permission system will have. `assigned_domains` is structurally independent of `permissions` and is *not* consulted by `has_permission`, which is also why (unlike the permissions fieldset) the admin page must not disable it for `admin`-role users.
- [x] Trusting a client-supplied base URL in `GET /api/links/{slug}/qr`, or passing an opaque index instead — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/multi-domain-display.md`. Once the client picks a domain, that choice has to reach the QR endpoint, and the one-line version is `short_url = f"{query_base}/r/{slug}"`. Rejected as a QR-poisoning vector: anyone able to construct a URL could have this app, from this app's origin, render a QR encoding any destination at all — and a QR code's entire purpose is to be printed, handed out and scanned long after the request that produced it, so the artifact outlives any later fix. The chosen design validates `?base=` for membership in the configured list and encodes **the server's own string, never the caller's**, so even a normalization bug cannot smuggle a foreign origin to the encoder; an unrecognised value is a `400 invalid_base_url` rather than a silent fallback, because silently encoding a domain the user did not pick is a quieter version of the same integrity failure and would also hide misconfiguration. The index variant (`?domain_index=2`) is unpoisonable by construction but makes every QR URL positional — reordering `public_base_urls` silently repoints every bookmarked or in-flight request at a different domain — so it lost to allowlist membership on a full, legible URL.
- [x] Backing up KV to S3 or any cloud object storage — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`, dropped by the user before planning began and recorded here in full because it is the first thing any future reader will reach for. The attraction is real: a backup that lives somewhere other than the operator's Downloads folder, can be scheduled, and survives the laptop. It loses on a structural fact, not a preference — **`api` has no `allowed_outbound_hosts` entry, and Spin denies all outbound HTTP when the key is omitted** (confirmed, `CLAUDE.md`'s "Security tradeoffs"). That exact property is the *stated reason* this app has no brute-force rate limiting on login or link passwords, so punching an outbound hole for a convenience feature would spend the component's most load-bearing security property on the least urgent requirement, and `PRODUCT.md` principle 2 ("avoid adding infrastructure … unless a real incident or requirement forces it") says the same. The shipped design is browser download (`Blob` + object URL) and browser upload (`FileReader`), both with working precedents in `gui/dashboard.js`. Revisit only if scheduled off-host backups become a stated requirement, and then as a deliberate `allowed_outbound_hosts` expansion with its own plan — never as a quiet addition to the backup feature.
- [x] Including `password_hash` in the backup file — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`, decided against; hashes are stripped and every restored account needs a password reset. Attractive because it makes restore a genuine one-step recovery where everyone's password still works and nobody has to be contacted. It loses on what the artifact becomes: a PBKDF2 hash is offline-attackable at the attacker's leisure, and this file's whole distribution model is "a JSON document in a Downloads folder, emailed around, dropped in a shared drive, committed to a repo by mistake". The 100,000-iteration cost factor is documented as the *only* mitigation against password guessing, and it only slows an *online* attacker. Stripping hashes also buys something concrete — **the file needs no encryption, no key management and no special handling**, which is the entire reason "no encryption" is a defensible non-goal rather than an omission. The cost is bounded and visible: the admin users table flags exactly who still needs a reset, and the reset flow (`PATCH /api/users/{username}` with `{"password": ...}`) already exists and is already tested. If hash-preserving restore is ever genuinely needed, that is a different feature with encryption and key management attached, not a flag on this one — and this entry must be reversed together with the "no encryption" decision, never separately.
- [x] Encrypting the backup file — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`, rejected as a direct consequence of stripping hashes. Once hashes, `session:*` keys and `_meta:bootstrapped` are excluded, the file holds link destinations, owners, schedules, click counts and the username/role/permission list — internal, not secret: any `links.view_all` user can already CSV-export most of the link half from the dashboard, and the user half is `users.manage`-gated exactly like the endpoint. Encryption would need a key, which means key management, which this app has none of; and componentize-py's WASI CPython is already missing `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac` (confirmed by a build/run spike, see `api/auth.py`'s hand-rolled PBKDF2), a strong signal not to bet a recovery feature on its crypto surface. **The file holds no secrets by construction — that is the reason, and it is only true while hashes are stripped.**
- [x] Merge semantics for restore, and wipe-then-write ordering — both considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`, both rejected in favour of **replace, implemented as write-then-prune**. A merge ("write what's in the file, leave everything else") never empties a store and feels safer, but after a corruption event the operator cannot tell whether a record they see is restored-good or corrupt-surviving, and the indexes end up a union of two eras — `all_links` from the file naming slugs whose records were not in the file, plus surviving slugs absent from the restored index. That is exactly the index/record drift `bulk.py`'s write-ordering rule exists to avoid, manufactured deliberately. Wipe-then-write is the naive reading of "replace" and is simpler, but a failure between the wipe and the writes leaves an **empty** store — strictly worse than the pre-restore state. Write-then-prune (write every entry from the file, then delete every pre-existing key not in the file) gives the same end state on success and a recoverable superset on failure. Revisit only if a real "restore just these links" requirement appears, and then as a separate selective-import feature, not by loosening this one.
- [x] Requiring the operator's password to confirm a restore, instead of a typed `REPLACE` — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`. A password re-prompt is the stronger anti-mistake control and has precedent in other admin tools. It loses on cost and fit: a second PBKDF2 verification on the request path, a password field in a form whose whole purpose is "do not do this by accident", and a new failure mode (wrong password on the one action you take when things are already broken). The typed literal is server-validated (`400 confirmation_required`), costs one string comparison, cannot be triggered by a stray click or a replayed request, and is testable in `pytest` with no crypto — with the count-bearing `confirmDialog` already established by the Bulk Action Bar on top of it. Also rejected in the same pass: **a different permission bar for restore than for backup**, because there is no higher tier to promote it into — `users.manage` is already equivalent to the `admin` role by escalation (`users.handle_update` has no self-promotion guard, so a `users.manage` holder can PATCH their own record to `role: "admin"`). If a self-promotion guard is ever added, revisit and require `role == "admin"` for restore specifically.
- [x] Putting the backup/restore UI on `admin/users.html` instead of a new admin page — considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`, and it was close. Genuinely cheaper: no new page, no new `spin.toml` route, no `ROUTES` entry, no nav item, and — the real prize — **no nav overflow re-measurement**, which DESIGN.md records has bitten this nav twice already (the theme control forced the 480px wrap fallback; the domain selector needed a four-breakpoint re-measure in both themes). It loses on placement: the users page is routine, frequent work (reset one password, flip one permission), and restore is the one action in the app that replaces three KV stores with no undo and ends the session. One page puts the most destructive control a mis-click from the most routine one, and `PRODUCT.md` principle 5 asks for admin surfaces to stay distinct.
