Recorded rather than silently dropped because it is the closest neighbour to the plan's own pre-approved fallback — if the nav measurement fails, the nav item is dropped and `admin/users.html` gains a plain in-body link, with the separate page kept.
- [x] Restore rebuilding or repairing the indexes, and a per-value "JSON or base64" encoding discriminator — both considered 2026-08-02 while planning `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`. Index repair is attractive because it would turn restore into a fix for exactly the corruption that motivates backups; it requires deciding whether an unindexed `slug:X` is orphaned junk to drop or a live link to re-index, and whether an `all_links` entry with no record is a dangling reference or a failed write — getting either wrong deletes data, silently, in the one operation an operator runs when they are already in trouble. Restore therefore reproduces the file faithfully, inconsistencies included; a read-only consistency-check endpoint is the honest shape for repair and is filed under Future work below. The encoding discriminator would make most of the file human-readable (nearly every value in these stores is already JSON) but costs a per-entry discriminator, doubles the encode/decode branches and the test matrix, and creates a real ambiguity where a value that *is* valid JSON but was written as opaque bytes round-trips through a different path than it arrived on. Uniform base64 costs ~33% of file size on an already-capped file and keeps exactly one code path; keys stay plaintext, which is enough to eyeball a file without decoding it.
- [x] A server-side whole-tag bulk action (`DELETE /api/tags/{tag}`, or `bulk-action` taking a tag instead of a slug list) — considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, decided against by the user before planning and recorded here because it was a live option, not a strawman. The idea: "delete/disable every link tagged `q3-2025`" in one request, unbounded by `MAX_BULK_ROWS`. Rejected because the blast radius is invisible at the moment of clicking — the operator sees a tag name, not the 300 links it resolves to — and there is no undo (bulk-delete undo needs a tombstone record and a retention policy that do not exist; see the Future-work entry above). `MAX_BULK_ROWS` was deliberately cut from 200 to 50 to keep a single request's work bounded, and an unbounded whole-tag action reintroduces exactly that unboundedness in the one operation where being wrong is unrecoverable. The shipped design instead filters the table by tag and reuses the existing select-all + bulk bar, so the count is on screen, the rows are on screen, and the confirmation dialog states the number. Revisit only if >50 links per tag becomes a routine workflow **and** undo exists.
- [x] A `tag:<tag>` → slug-list KV index — considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, decided against. Attractive because every other "find links by X" need in this app is served by an index (`all_links`, `owner_links:<user>`). Rejected on four counts: nothing in the feature reads it (the dashboard already holds every visible link in `allLinks`, so a tag filter is a client-side array filter over data already in memory — the same observation the CSV-export entry made); it would be the only index a *single-link edit* has to touch two of, since retagging means removing from every old tag's index and adding to every new tag's index, up to 20 racy read-modify-writes per `PATCH` under the 10-tag cap with no compare-and-swap available; it adds a second durable source of truth that can silently disagree with the records, a drift hazard `bulk.handle_bulk_create` already spends N extra KV reads defending against for `all_links`; and it becomes a permanent backup obligation, since a `tag:` key type must be added to `backup.INDEX_KEYS["links"]` and `restore_write_order` or restore silently mis-orders it. Revisit only as part of a paginated, server-filtered list endpoint, if `handle_list`'s existing O(all visible links) walk ever becomes the bottleneck — not as a bolt-on to today's load-everything dashboard.
- [x] A `_meta:tags` registry for tag autocomplete — considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, decided against in favour of deriving the suggestion list client-side from the links already loaded. The precedent is real (`auth.USERNAMES_INDEX_KEY`'s `_meta:usernames` is the repo's only enumerable set) but the shapes differ: a username index has exactly one record per name and `handle_delete` removes exactly one, whereas a tag registry goes stale the moment the last link carrying a tag is deleted or untagged, and de-staling it needs refcounting or the O(all links) walk the registry existed to avoid. It would also be read once per page load and written on every create/edit/bulk-create/bulk-tag — a racy read-modify-write on one hot key, for a read nothing needs. The client-derived list is additionally *better* scoped: it reads `allLinks`, already ownership-scoped by `handle_list`, so a user without `links.view_all` is suggested only tags they have used rather than being shown every other team's campaign names. Accepted limitation, stated in the plan: two people can independently create `black-friday` and `blackfriday`. Revisit only if tag drift between teams becomes a real complaint, at which point the honest fix is the admin-curated vocabulary that was already rejected, not a registry.
- [x] A dedicated Tags column in the dashboard links table — considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, decided against; tags render as chips inside the existing Short-link cell instead, after the Custom/Password badges. A real column would be sortable and is where a spreadsheet user would look, but `gui/dashboard.css` spends ~60 lines of live-measured fixes defending a table that already overflows at ordinary desktop widths, including a `@media (max-width: 600px)` block that hides columns by `nth-child` index. Those indices already shifted once when the select column landed and `gui/dashboard.js` carries the comment "This fails silently if wrong" about the positional `displayRow.children[n]` writes that depend on them. A ninth column shifts them again, changes three `colspan="9"` values, and requires redoing the 600px clearance measurement. Revisit only as part of rebuilding the table's responsive strategy.
- [x] Clickable tag chips as the dashboard's tag-filter affordance — considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, decided against in favour of a `<select id="tag-filter">`. The most discoverable option, and half of the user's own "clicking or selecting" phrasing. Rejected because a clickable chip must be a `<button>` or carry `role="button"`, both of which DESIGN.md's sitewide tap-target floor puts `min-height: 44px` on — ten 44px chips in a table row is an enormous row, and exempting them is a design-system change rather than a feature change (DESIGN.md's own history shows the nav anchors being *raised* to 44px rather than the rule being narrowed). The `tabindex="0"` + Enter/Space escape hatch that `#links-table th.sortable` uses is available but would add ten focus stops to every row. Revisit only if DESIGN.md deliberately exempts in-table micro-chips from the 44px floor.
- [x] Owner reassignment via `PATCH /api/links/{slug}` or a dedicated `POST /api/links/{slug}/owner` endpoint — both considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, both rejected in favour of a `reassign` action on the existing `POST /api/links/bulk-action` (a single-link reassign is a one-element `slugs` list). Adding `owner` to `links.UPDATABLE_FIELDS` would put two different permission gates in one handler — `can_edit` for every other field, `users.manage` for this one — which is exactly the shape that produced the `links.view_all` bug family where four handlers gated on `role != "admin"` and none checked the permission they named. A dedicated `/owner` endpoint mirroring `/password` is clean but implements the three-write index dance twice, once for one slug and once for many, in the single highest-risk operation in the feature; `handle_bulk_action`'s existing validate-every-row-then-write-nothing-on-error structure is precisely what that operation needs.
- [x] Requiring per-row `can_edit` on owner reassignment in addition to `users.manage` — considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, decided against, making reassignment the one bulk action that does not apply the per-row edit gate. It would break the motivating case outright: reassigning a departed employee's orphaned links means acting on links you do not own and cannot edit, so requiring `can_edit` makes the feature useless unless the operator also holds `links.edit_all`, a separate grant nobody would think to pair with it. And it buys no security — `api/users.py`'s `handle_update` lets a `users.manage` holder set `role` on any username including their own, with no self-exclusion, so `users.manage` is already equivalent to full admin access. Same argument `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md` used for its own gate. Revisit only if `users.manage` ever stops being self-escalatable.
- [x] A per-row tags column in the bulk-create pasted-text format, and a dedicated tag-management admin page — both considered 2026-08-03 while planning `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`, both rejected. The text parser is first-delimiter-wins on two columns, so a third column lands inside the destination and fails as an invalid URL; supporting it needs a real CSV parser, a much larger change than a tags feature justifies, and the batch-level tags field (matching how batch password/schedule already work) covers the actual need. A tag-management page was rejected on discovery grounds before design: the nav is full — a Backup nav link was built, measured at `scrollWidth` 716 vs `clientWidth` 700 at 768px in both themes, and reverted to an in-body link — and tags need no management surface anyway, since there is no registry to curate and untagging is done from the dashboard's own bulk bar.
- [x] Cascade-deleting a user's links when the user is deleted — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against in favour of refusing the delete with a `409`. Attractive because it is one round trip and leaves nothing dangling by construction, and it is what "delete this user and everything they own" means in most admin tools. Rejected because it breaks live short URLs: a URL shortener's entire promise is that a published short link keeps resolving, and the links most worth caring about are exactly the ones already printed on something, handed to a third party, or encoded into a QR code that will outlive any later fix. The blast radius is unbounded and invisible at the moment of clicking — the operator sees a username, not 300 destinations — there is no undo (bulk-delete undo needs a tombstone record and a retention policy that do not exist, per the Future-work entry below), and it would be the single most irreversible operation in the app, hidden behind a confirmation dialog whose text is about deleting a *user*. The capability is not lost: filter the dashboard by owner, look at the rows, and use the existing count-bearing bulk delete, where the confirmation names the number of links because deleting links is what you are doing. Revisit only if a deployment genuinely wants "offboarding destroys the links" as a stated policy, and then as an explicit, separately-confirmed bulk action, not as a side effect of deleting an account.
- [x] Requiring an explicit link disposition in the delete request (`reassign_to: "bob"` or `delete_their_links: true`) — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against in favour of a `409` that names the link count. Genuinely the strongest alternative: one round trip, and it makes the decision *mandatory* rather than merely blocked, which is a real advantage over a refusal an operator might satisfy by cascade-deleting in a hurry. Lost on four counts. (1) There is nowhere clean to put it — `gui/app.js:56`'s shared `api.delete` sends no body and this file already rejected a semantically significant `DELETE` body on 2026-08-01, leaving `DELETE /api/users/carol?links=reassign&to=bob`, a strange and easily mistyped place for an irreversible instruction. (2) It reintroduces unbounded per-request work — N record writes plus index writes for an uncapped N, in a handler that today does three KV operations, with no transaction — in a codebase that deliberately *lowered* `MAX_BULK_ROWS` from 200 to 50 to keep exactly this bounded. (3) The decision is made blind, from a page where the links, their destinations and their real count are not visible — the same shape rejected on 2026-08-03 for whole-tag actions ("seeing-before-hitting over raw power"). (4) It implements reassignment a second time, which the tags plan's trade-off #6 already rejected for the single-link case. Revisit if users routinely own several hundred links each, at which point the right answer is a paginated server-filtered list endpoint and a raised cap, not a disposition parameter.
- [x] Auto-reassigning a deleted user's links to the deleting admin — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against. The "just make it work" option: no link is ever lost, nothing dangles, and the operator is never blocked. Rejected because it hides the decision at exactly the moment it should be made, and makes the deleting admin the owner of record for links they may know nothing about — which is worse than an obvious orphan, because it looks correct. One admin who offboards five people ends up owning several hundred links, an unbounded `owner_links:<admin>` index and a dashboard they can no longer use. It also mutates a store the request was not ostensibly about, with unbounded writes and no operator awareness that they happened, so an interruption leaves a half-moved set nobody knows to re-drive. A deployment that wants this policy can enact it deliberately for one extra click.
- [x] A tombstone / reserved-usernames list to prevent username reuse — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against in favour of removing what a reused name could inherit (a `409` gate so a deleted user can never still own links, plus deleting `owner_links:<username>` and purging every `session:` record naming the user). A tombstone does not fix the defect — this app has no user identity beyond a string, and that stays true after one is added; it just makes the defect unreachable through the admin UI, so a future username-keyed feature (an audit log, per-user analytics, a saved view) reintroduces the inheritance and nobody thinks to check. It is also the wrong shape for the product: usernames here are employee identifiers, reusing `jsmith` for a different John Smith is ordinary, and to be sound the reservation would have to be permanent — a reservation shorter than "forever" is just a bet about how long a stale artifact survives, and the only artifact with a natural expiry (the 8-hour session) is now deleted outright. A permanent block with no escape hatch gets worked around within a month (`jsmith2`); an escape hatch restores the vector on the exact path an operator uses when in a hurry. Two near neighbours were rejected with it: **stamping a stable `uid` into each session record and comparing it in `resolve_session`** (more robust and O(1), but existing user records and existing sessions both lack the field, so `None == None` passes and precisely the accounts that predate the change keep the vulnerability — the opposite of what a security fix should do; making it fail-closed signs everyone out on deploy and still needs a backfill), and **a `user_sessions:<username>` index** to make the purge one read instead of a key walk (another read-modify-write index with no compare-and-swap, written on every login and logout, to speed up an operation that happens a handful of times a year — and a drifted session index fails in the direction of *not* purging, which is the failure the change exists to prevent). Revisit the `uid` if a fourth username-keyed artifact appears that cannot be cleaned up at deletion time.
- [x] Deleting an `owner_links:<owner>` key when its list becomes empty, in the shared index helpers — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against. It would eliminate the whole class of dangling empty index keys, including the one that repairing an orphan leaves behind for a user who has already been deleted and so will never be deleted again. Rejected because an empty `owner_links:` key is indistinguishable from an absent one in every code path — `links._owned_slugs` returns `[]` for both (`api/links.py:41-43`), `handle_list` shows nothing either way, `add_slugs_to_indexes` refills either way, and backup captures an empty array that restore writes back harmlessly — so the change is tidiness with zero behavioural payoff, paid for by touching two of the most load-bearing helpers in the component and invalidating the "exactly one index write per distinct owner" assertions in `test_links.py:757-759` and `test_bulk.py:616-617`, in the same commit as a security fix. `users.handle_delete` does delete `owner_links:<username>`, but that is one line in a new code path, justified by "deletion leaves nothing behind under that username" being a statement worth being able to test. Revisit if the KV consistency endpoint below ever wants to enumerate index keys and empty ones become noise worth removing at the source.
- [x] A one-shot orphan-repair endpoint (`POST /api/admin/reap-orphans`) for deployments that already have links owned by nonexistent users — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against; the dashboard's owner filter plus the existing bulk reassign is the whole repair story. Attractive because an existing deployment gets fixed in one click instead of 50 links at a time. Rejected because it is another unbounded, mutating server-side action whose blast radius is invisible at the moment of clicking — the third time that shape was rejected in one plan — and because it overlaps a backlog item that is already scoped and deliberately read-only (the KV consistency check below, which exists precisely because it "reports and never silently fixes"). Building the repairing sibling before the reporting one gets the order backwards, and the realistic scale is one departed employee's links, once, per deployment.
- [x] Filtering the dashboard by owner with a substring match on the existing free-text filter, instead of a dedicated `<select>` — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`, decided against. It is one line (add `link.owner` to the existing match) and needs no new markup. Rejected because the filtered set feeds a bulk reassign: a substring match on `carol` also matches the slug `carols-secret` and any destination containing the string, so select-all-then-reassign would eventually move a link that was never carol's. Exact equality is the entire point, and a `<select>` is already the established affordance in that row (`#tag-filter`, itself chosen over clickable chips for the 44px tap-target reason recorded in `DESIGN.md`).

- [x] Checking the `analytics` store in the consistency endpoint — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-consistency-check.md` (trade-off #1), rejected: `links.handle_delete` never removes analytics keys, so `count:`/`events:` records for deleted slugs are **normal state**, not drift. Reporting them would make every healthy deployment show findings, which is how a checker gets ignored. Re-open only if deletion is ever changed to purge analytics.
- [x] A repair mode on the consistency endpoint (`?fix=true` or `POST /api/admin/repair`) — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #2), rejected: the 2026-08-02 backup plan already refused to build a silent repairer, and both prior plans that touched this shape rejected unbounded server-side mutation whose blast radius is invisible at the click. Moved to Future work with an explicit trigger — real reports from a real deployment, since a repair tool designed before anyone has seen one is designed from imagination.
- [x] A separate `gui/admin/consistency.html` page — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #3), rejected: it would cost a new file, a new exact `spin.toml` route, a `routing.py` entry and a `test_routing.py` case, and the nav is full (`DESIGN.md` records the next nav item as a redesign). The report goes on the existing `admin/backup.html`, which is already the operator-maintenance page and is where the check is most useful — right after a restore.
- [x] API-only with no GUI — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #4), genuinely live and rejected: a diagnostic nobody can reach is a diagnostic nobody runs, and the backup page cost no new route.
- [x] A single global finding cap instead of per-check — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #5), rejected: one noisy check would starve all the others out of the report.
- [x] Making `MAX_FINDINGS_PER_CHECK` a Spin variable — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #6), rejected on the same reasoning as `MAX_BULK_ROWS`: one function in one component reads it, so it is a safety rail rather than operator policy.
- [x] An input cap refusing to scan a large store — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #7), rejected for now with no evidence either way; the E2E task measures a real report against the 84 ms / 4,402-entry restore baseline, and that measurement is what any future cap must be argued from.
- [x] Reporting expired `session:` records and empty `owner_links:` keys — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #8), rejected: both are normal, self-correcting state rather than drift, and reporting them would be noise. This also answers `docs/plans/user-deletion-link-ownership.md`'s deferred question about deleting emptied index keys at the source — empty keys are never reported by any check, so the stated trigger is not met and that entry stands unchanged.
- [x] Doing nothing — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #9), rejected: `users.handle_delete`'s `409` gate reads only the `owner_links:` index, so a record that has drifted out of it does not block its owner's deletion and is orphaned by the very flow built to prevent orphans. Nothing detects that at scale today.
- [x] Automatically disabling existing links that violate a newly-added destination rule — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/destination-url-policy.md` (trade-off #1), genuinely live and rejected. Attractive because it is the only option where saving a rule *does* something immediately, and disabling is reversible unlike deleting. Lost on three counts: it turns a configuration edit into an unbounded, unpreviewable bulk mutation of link records, and with no compare-and-swap and no transaction in Spin KV a partial failure leaves an arbitrary subset disabled with no record of which; the operator already has one-click bulk Disable, so the automation saves two clicks and costs the preview; and it breaks third parties relying on links that were legitimate when created, with no human deciding the trade was worth it. Bulk-disabling violators is still the recommended remediation — as the operator's action after reading the violations report, not as a side effect of saving a rule. Revisit only as an explicit "Disable all N" button *on* the report (which keeps the preview), and only when a real report has more violators than a person wants to select by hand.
- [x] Deleting existing links that violate a newly-added destination rule — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #2), rejected with little argument: irrecoverable, it leaves orphan `count:`/`events:` analytics keys behind (which `links.handle_delete` never removes), and it is strictly dominated by disabling, which produces the same `404` at `/r/<slug>` because `redirect` already checks `status`.
- [x] Giving a destination policy no retroactive effect at all — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #3), rejected. This is exactly the posture `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md` took ("Effect on existing links: None, and this is a guarantee"), so it has real precedent here, and it is free. Lost because the two cases are not analogous: a banned word in a slug is visible in the short URL itself and self-evident in the dashboard, whereas a bad *destination* is precisely the thing nobody can see, and the harm is ongoing rather than historical — the link is still being clicked. "We have a policy and no idea whether anything already violates it" is not a policy. Its one good idea was kept as an explicit guarantee: a legacy violator stays fully editable, because `handle_update` re-checks the policy only inside the `if "target_url" in payload:` branch.
- [x] Reporting destination-policy violations as a thirteenth check on `GET /api/admin/consistency` — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #4), live and rejected in favour of a separate `GET /api/admin/url-policy/violations` endpoint on its own page. It would have reused a walk that already reads every `slug:` record and landed on a page the operator already visits. Lost on three specifics: `consistency.py` is scoped to *structural* drift — every one of its twelve checks compares an index against the records it describes — whereas a policy violation is a perfectly coherent store whose *rule* changed underneath it; it would poison `ok`, since `build_report` sets `ok = findings == 0`, so a structurally flawless deployment adopting a policy with any legacy violator reports `ok: false` forever, and the page's own "run it again, a real finding shows up on both runs" guidance is about transient write races and is simply false for a stable, reproducible policy finding; and the remediation is opposite — consistency findings deliberately have no GUI repair path (rejected as trade-off #2 on 2026-08-04) while policy violations have an obvious one, the existing bulk Disable/Delete, which the report should point at.
- [x] "Most specific match wins" precedence between destination allow and deny rules — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #5), rejected in favour of "a deny rule always wins". Specificity ranking (an exact 3-label rule beating a 2-label subdomain rule, the way DNS and cookies work) is strictly more expressive and is the one thing the chosen model cannot do: carve an allowed exception out of a denied tree. It lost on failure direction. Under specificity, an `allow evil.example.com` silently defeats a `deny example.com` — a misunderstood rule **fails open**. Under deny-wins, a misunderstood rule fails closed: someone gets an unexpected `400`, tells an admin, and it is fixed in a minute. The workaround for the missing case is stated in the UI (invert `default_action` to `deny` and enumerate). Revisit only if the exception-inside-a-denied-tree case turns up for real *and* inverting the default is genuinely unworkable.
- [x] A per-rule `include_subdomains` toggle on destination rules, and path or port matching — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-offs #6 and #7), both rejected. One always-on semantic (a rule matches the host and every subdomain of it, always) means there is nothing for an operator to pick wrong, and the over-broad-allow case a toggle would solve — an allow rule for a shared-subdomain provider like `github.io` — is already repairable with a deny rule, which wins. Path matching is precision theatre: `/safe/` is reachable via `/safe/../bad`, via percent-encoding, via a `;` parameter or a fragment, and the URL a QR code hands out never shows the path anyway. A port rule is bypassed by using the default port. **The host is the unit of trust.**
- [x] Two separate destination lists (an allow-list field and a deny-list field) instead of one list with a per-rule `action` — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #8), rejected. One list plus a single `default_action` covers every real configuration (pure deny-list, pure allow-list, and allow-a-tree-minus-one-subdomain), has a precedence rule that fits in a sentence, and makes "which list is authoritative" a question that cannot be asked.
- [x] Storing the destination policy in a Spin variable instead of a KV key — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #9), rejected, and this is the storage decision the 2026-07-18 Future-work entry explicitly left open. `public_base_urls` is a Spin variable because a display domain needs DNS and routing anyway, so it is already deploy-time configuration; a destination policy has no such coupling and must be editable by an admin at runtime without a rebuild and redeploy — which is precisely the cost `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md` accepted for its compiled-in word list and flagged as that design's main liability. One KV key per rule was rejected too: it would turn one read into N on every single link creation, and would introduce an index (and therefore index/record drift, and therefore real new work in `consistency.py`) for a list of tens of entries.
- [x] A new `links.policy` permission for the destination policy — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #11), rejected in favour of `users.manage`. `auth.py`'s `KNOWN_PERMISSIONS` is a deliberately small fixed vocabulary and an addition to it is cheap but permanent; `users.manage` is already the bar for backup, restore, consistency, user CRUD and owner reassignment, and is not the weaker bar, because a holder can already promote themselves to admin through `users.handle_update`. A compliance/abuse role that is deliberately *not* an account administrator is a real organizational shape, but not one PRODUCT.md's two populations describe. Trigger to revisit: an actual request for that role.
- [x] Letting admins bypass the destination policy — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #12), rejected. An admin who needs an exception edits the policy, which is one action and leaves an `updated_by` trail; a silent per-request bypass leaves none, and it would make bulk-create enforcement conditional, which is the "enforced in two of three places is not enforced" failure in a different costume.
- [x] Per-rule `POST`/`DELETE` endpoints for the destination policy instead of a whole-document `PUT` — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #13), rejected. Spin KV has no compare-and-swap, so a per-rule endpoint is a read-modify-write race either way; one handler beats three; and full replacement matches the established `PATCH {"tags": [...]}` precedent. The disclosed cost is last-write-wins between two concurrent admins, with no warning to the loser.
- [x] Putting the destination policy UI on `gui/admin/backup.html` as a fourth article — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #14), rejected. Cheapest option by far and it fires no new routes, but the backup page is *operator maintenance* (three destructive-or-diagnostic one-shot actions) and this is *standing configuration* an admin returns to and edits, which PRODUCT.md principle 5 keeps distinct; a rules editor with an add form, a table, per-row removal and a Save is also too much content to bolt under a Restore control the page already warns can't be undone. **A fifth nav item was not even attempted** — `DESIGN.md`'s "The nav is full" paragraph already measured one at 768px and reverted it. The new page is reached by an in-body anchor on `admin/users.html`, the same pattern `backup.html` uses, which is also why the deferred "rename backup.html when a fourth operator tool lands there" trigger has **not** fired.
- [x] Blocking non-ASCII destination hosts outright, and policy-checking `backup.handle_restore` — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-offs #16 and #17), both rejected. `urlparse` does not IDNA-encode and rule hosts are ASCII LDH only, so a Unicode-host destination matches no rule: blocked under `default_action: "deny"` (fail-closed, correct) and allowed under `"allow"` (fail-open, i.e. a deny-list evasion). Blocking such hosts outright would break legitimate IDN destinations for every deployment to close a hole that deny-lists are inherently open to anyway — picking a domain that isn't on the list works just as well — so it is disclosed rather than fixed, in the same terms `banned-word-slugs.md` used ("a carelessness guard, not a content-moderation system"). Restore is exempt because it is a faithful replacement of a snapshot rather than an authoring action; checking it would make a backup un-restorable after a rule change, a far worse failure than a legacy violator the violations report lists on the next run.
- [x] Resolution-time destination enforcement in `redirect` — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/destination-url-policy.md`, rejected and costed rather than merely asserted. It would add a second KV read (`_meta:url_policy`) to every `/r/{slug}` click, a 100% increase in the hot path's resolution round trips (confirmed: `redirect/main.go`'s `resolveLink` does exactly one `slug:` read), and it would require reimplementing `normalize_rule_host`/`destination_host`/`host_matches` in Go — a second independently-maintained copy of the one rule the whole feature turns on, the drift class `analytics_event_slots` needed a shared Spin variable to avoid, and that was for a single integer rather than a matching algorithm. It buys nothing the authoring-time check plus the violations report does not: a legacy violator is reported and one bulk Disable away from `404`ing through the `status` check `redirect` already performs.
- [x] Doing nothing about destination URLs — considered 2026-08-04 (trade-off #18), live and rejected. The status quo is that any authenticated account can point the organization's short domain at anything, with no way to prevent it and no way to find out afterwards: `api/links.py`'s `is_valid_target_url` checking `scheme in ("http","https") and bool(netloc)` is the whole of today's control, and a short link laundering its destination is the specific harm — a recipient sees `go.example.com/r/promo` and cannot tell where it leads, so a bad destination borrows the organization's credibility.
- [ ] Flattening the KV prefixes into every key literal instead of a prefixing view — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` (trade-off #1), rejected. This is the literal reading of CLAUDE.md's own description of the Akamai fix: change `f"slug:{slug}"` to `f"links:slug:{slug}"` everywhere so the string in the source is the string in the store, which is genuinely what a developer debugging through the KV explorer wants and costs no indirection to learn. It loses on blast radius and on upgrade safety. ~55 key literals across eight non-test modules and ~257 lines across nine test files each become a place to typo a prefix into a silent wrong-namespace write; `backup.py`'s `is_excluded_key`, `redact_user_value`, `INDEX_KEYS`, `restore_write_order` and `validate_backup` all need prefix-aware rewrites and `consistency.py`'s twelve-check key classification with them; and the backup file's key space changes, which forces a `schema_version` bump, a growing `SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSIONS` and a v1 converter — turning what is otherwise a free backup→deploy→restore upgrade path into a feature. The view confines the change to `api/app.py` plus one new module and keeps all 474 existing api tests as a regression suite for the refactor. Revisit only if the view's indirection is ever measured to be causing real debugging cost, which would be an argument for better tooling before an argument for flattening.
- [ ] A config seam preserving three-store separation for local dev only — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` (trade-off #3), rejected by user decision. A Spin variable selecting one-store vs. three-store mode would have kept the KV explorer denied the `users` store at the Spin host boundary, preserving the one guarantee the consolidation gives up. Rejected because it makes the deployed configuration different from the one anyone develops or tests against — a far more expensive property to own than a dev-only credential exposure inside a tool that already holds full CRUD over every other key. Dropping the explorer instead was also rejected: repairing bad local test data is half its value. The exposure is accepted and documented rather than mitigated.
- [ ] Deleting `runtime-config.toml` once the default store auto-provisions — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` (trade-off #4), rejected. Spin provides `"default"` with no runtime config and Akamai Functions ignores runtime configuration entirely ("Runtime configuration is also unavailable" — techdocs quotas-and-limits), so the file has no remaining hard requirement, and a file with no purpose misleads. Kept anyway because every documented command, `dev/kv-explorer-up.sh`, and a long trail of TASKS.md entries pass `--runtime-config-file runtime-config.toml`; deleting it turns a mechanical refactor into a change that breaks a script and invalidates documentation for a tidiness gain. Reduced instead to one `[key_value_store.default]` block with a comment saying it is optional locally and inert on Akamai. Revisit when someone is already editing the dev script.
- [ ] Caching the physical KV key enumeration per request — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` (trade-off #5), rejected for v1 and moved to Future work. After consolidation `_kv_keys` enumerates the whole app rather than one store, so a backup walks the full key space three times; a single-shot cache in `scoped_list_keys` would make it one walk and be strictly faster than today. Rejected because it couples silently to `backup.handle_restore`'s prune, which calls `list_keys` *after* writing specifically to find pre-existing keys — a cached pre-write snapshot happens to produce the same stale set today only because newly written keys are in `entries` by definition, which is a coincidence of the current code rather than a stated property. The call *count* is unchanged from today; only each call's size grows.
- [ ] A Spin variable for the KV key prefixes — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` (trade-off #7), rejected. `analytics_event_slots` is a shared Spin variable precisely because two components must agree on it, which is the same shape as this problem. It loses because a prefix is structural, not operator-tunable: changing it orphans every existing record, and a mismatch between the Go and Python sides is silent — links get written that `/r/{slug}` cannot find, with no error anywhere. Hardcoded constants in both languages plus a test in `api/tests/test_kvprefix.py` that reads `redirect/linkgate/keys.go` and pins the equality is the stronger guard, because it fails at CI time rather than at runtime.
- [ ] Reducing the redirect hot path's KV operations as part of the consolidation — considered 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md`, rejected as scope. Research corrected a fact this repo has asserted twice (in CLAUDE.md's Akamai section and in the "Resolution-time destination enforcement" entry above): the hot path does **two** KV data operations per resolution, not one — `lookupLink` at `redirect/main.go:147` calls `store.Exists("slug:"+slug)` and then `store.Get("slug:"+slug)` — and both places name a function `resolveLink` that does not exist. Dropping the `Exists` and treating a `nil` `Get` as absent, and passing the already-open store into `recordAnalytics` to save one `kv.Open` per recorded click, are both plausible and both deliberately excluded, so that any regression in the consolidation is attributable to the consolidation. Moved to Future work; wants real timing evidence on Akamai first.
- [x] Per-operation KV log lines for v1 — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected and deferred to a future `verbose` level. One stderr write measured **≈13 µs** in Go (isolated from the 404-miss probe row: `lookupLink` 28,291 ns containing only `Exists` 15,125 ns, one `Fprintf` and a key concatenation, with no JSON parse), so seven per-click operations would add ~91 µs to a 137–180 µs handler — a 50–66% increase — and inflate the very durations being collected. On `backup`/`restore`/`consistency`, which perform thousands of operations against Akamai's 30-second handler limit, 5,000 operations means 5,000 lines and ~65 ms of pure logging. It also carries a hidden prerequisite: without a per-request ID, interleaved lines from concurrent requests cannot be attributed to a request at all — plus key redaction and a volume guard. The per-request rollup is a strict prefix of it (the collector visits every operation regardless), so this defers in one direction only; starting here would build IDs, redaction and volume guards up front for detail that may never be needed.
- [x] A KV-backed runtime logging toggle — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected. A `_meta:log_config` key would be changeable without a redeploy, which is genuinely what a Spin variable cannot do (`spin aka app` has no variables subcommand — confirmed), but it costs a KV read on every request to decide whether to time KV reads. Self-defeating for the stated use case, and it spends the 1,000 read RPS budget on configuration. The per-request `X-SS-Debug` token buys the same no-redeploy property for free.
- [x] Gating the api component's per-request tracing on the `users.manage` permission — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected. It would avoid introducing a new shared secret and would reuse the repo's existing authorization vocabulary, but `redirect` has no session, cookie or principal of any kind and cannot implement it at all, so one feature would activate two different ways in two components. Revisit only if the shared token proves awkward to rotate.
- [x] JSON log lines instead of logfmt — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected. `spin aka logs` returns plain text to a terminal and nothing in this repo consumes structured logs programmatically; logfmt is readable unaided and `awk`-able, JSON is neither without tooling that does not exist here.
- [x] Emitting the `Server-Timing` header whenever `log_level=summary` — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected. It would hand internal timing data to every visitor of a deployment that merely turned baseline logging on. Tying the header to the debug token keeps the disclosure deliberate; the same reasoning added `Vary: X-SS-Debug` to token-bearing api responses.
- [x] Removing `recordAnalytics`'s second `kv.Open` while wiring the collector through it — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected. Threading the handler's already-open store into `recordAnalytics` would drop one `kv.Open`, measured at 12–33 µs against a 137–180 µs handler — a real 8–20% win, and exactly the hot-path optimisation the Future work entry below defers pending Akamai timing evidence. Rejected because it would change the baseline that every future measurement is compared against, inside the very change that builds the measuring instrument. A successful redirect stays at 7 KV operations before and after.
- [x] Reading the logging variables per request rather than caching them for the instance lifetime — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`, rejected. A `variables.get` measured ~25 µs in Python, paid on every request forever to re-read a value that cannot have changed: Spin variables are fixed for the lifetime of an instance both locally (restart) and on Akamai (redeploy). **This must be revisited if Akamai ever ships variable updates without a redeploy**, at which point the cache would silently serve a stale level.
- [ ] Append-only click keys (one unique KV key per click, aggregated on read) as the fix for Akamai click under-counting — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`, rejected in favour of sharded counters. It is genuinely attractive: with no read there is no update to lose, so it is *exact* at any rate under any mechanism, including the app-wide-contention model that would kill sharding. It lost on the read side, which this app cannot absorb. Spin's KV enumerates the **whole physical store** (`get_keys`) with no prefix scan, so counting one slug's clicks means enumerating every key in the app and filtering, on a host where a data operation costs 5.5–16.7 ms against a 30 s handler limit. `api/backup.py`'s export already enumerates and reads every analytics key against `MAX_BACKUP_ENTRIES = 5_000` — today's ~31 analytics keys per slug already put that ceiling near 160 links, and one popular link's click keys would break backup for the whole application, not just for analytics. Compaction answers both and this app has no trigger to run it from: Akamai Functions supports neither cron nor custom triggers, so it would be an admin button someone remembers to press, or a GET that writes and races another concurrent reader into double-counting. It trades a bounded, measured, quantified inaccuracy for an unbounded, unquantified operational failure. **Revisit only if the per-key/app-wide probe in `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md` shows contention is app-wide** — sharding would then be worthless and this becomes the only exact option, as its own plan with the compaction trigger designed first.
- [ ] In-instance batching of click counts (accumulate in a package-level counter, flush every K clicks or T ms) — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`, rejected. It would collapse N writes into one and so fix both the under-counting and the ~25 clicks/second write-RPS ceiling at once, which is why it keeps suggesting itself. It loses because a Wasm instance on a FaaS can be torn down at any moment with no shutdown hook: every unflushed click is lost outright and silently, and the loss is *unbounded* rather than merely rate-dependent — strictly worse than the bounded, measured loss it is trying to fix. It also reintroduces exactly the package-level shared state `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md` designed out of this component (the collector is per-request context, never a package variable, because concurrent requests interleave). Revisit only if Spin/WASI ever exposes a real instance-shutdown hook *and* instance lifetime becomes observable.
- [ ] Making the analytics shard count a Spin variable rather than a constant pinned across the two languages — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`, rejected. CLAUDE.md's own rule says a value two components must agree on becomes a variable, which is why `analytics_event_slots` is one; this looked like the same case. It is not. A mismatched `analytics_event_slots` produces a lossier *sample*, whereas a shard count the reader sets **lower** than the writer silently deletes click history from every total, with no error anywhere — the same failure shape the KV prefixes carry, and the repo's answer to that shape is a constant per language pinned by a cross-language test (`api/tests/test_kvprefix.py`), not an operator knob. The constant also removes the "operator lowers it in a hurry" foot-gun entirely and makes the raise-only rule reviewable in a single commit touching both languages. Revisit only if a deployment genuinely needs a per-environment shard count, and then only with a read path that reads a fixed maximum rather than the configured value.
- [ ] Instance-sticky shard selection for the click counter (draw one shard per Wasm instance at startup) — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`, rejected in favour of per-request random selection. Under the stale-read model it looks strictly better: an instance always reads back its own last write, so read-your-writes would eliminate self-collision entirely. It lost on two grounds. If the staleness lives in the KV backend (replica lag) rather than a per-instance cache, stickiness buys literally nothing. And if Akamai creates one Wasm instance per request — plausible on a FaaS, and **unconfirmed** — sticky selection *is* per-request selection, with the added hazard that two long-lived instances that draw the same shard are welded to it permanently instead of colliding 1-in-16 of the time. Same expected loss, strictly worse tail, more code. Revisit only if instance lifetime on Akamai is confirmed to be long-lived *and* the staleness is confirmed to be instance-local.
- [ ] A deploy-instrumented step to confirm the click-loss mechanism before designing the fix — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`, rejected as the *gating* step (the experiment itself is recorded in that plan's "Key technical facts" for whoever wants it later). Writing a sentinel value, immediately re-reading the same key and logging whether the read was stale would settle whether this is read staleness or read-modify-write overlap. But the design depends on exactly one property — whether contention is **per-key or app-wide** — and that is measurable *today* on the running deployment with `curl` and sixteen extra links, because N distinct slugs are indistinguishable from N shards of one slug as far as the KV store is concerned. No build, no deploy, no code. The mechanism question is separately worth answering; it is not worth a deploy-instrument-deploy cycle in front of a fix that works under either answer. Trigger to revisit: the deployed verification failing in a way the per-key model does not explain.
- [ ] **[SUPERSEDED 2026-08-07 — see the "EventSlot hashing fix" section. The blocking reason below expired: the investigation it was protecting closed with the cause proven, so the fix was made — as a hashing change that keeps `EventSlot` deterministic, NOT as the random-selection variant rejected here, which would have deleted the function.]** Replacing `linkgate.EventSlot` with random slot selection as part of the click-count work — considered 2026-08-06 while planning `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`, carried as an OPTIONAL task, then **dropped on 2026-08-06 by user decision before any code was written.** The idea was nearly free once `ShardFor` and `clickEntropy` existed: the recent-events ring buffer picks its slot from a timestamp hash that is documented to collide far more than uniform (8 local requests 300 ms apart retaining 3 distinct events), and a random slot is strictly the correct way to draw a sample. It was dropped because deleting `EventSlot` would orphan the open "Find the real cause of the analytics recent-events slot collisions" investigation, which the probe made *more* interesting rather than less: **app-wide write throttling is now a plausible additional cause of event loss on the deployment** — a throttled events write is indistinguishable from a slot collision when read back. Note precisely what that does and does not explain: throttling cannot account for the original observation, which was made locally under `spin up`, and local sqlite has no write cap, so `EventSlot`'s hashing remains a live suspect for the local case. Whoever picks that investigation up now has two candidate causes to separate, which is exactly why its subject has to stay alive. Revisit only after that investigation reports.
- [x] Reporting orphaned analytics as a **13th consistency check** — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected. Attractive because it is the obvious home: `consistency.py` already walks stores and reports drift, and "orphan `count:<slug>` for a link that no longer exists" sounds exactly like a consistency finding. Rejected on the reasoning `docs/plans/kv-consistency-check.md`'s own rejected alternative #1 already established, whose stated revisit trigger is **"deletion being changed to purge analytics"** — and this plan deliberately does *not* change deletion, so orphans remain normal, expected state between operator-run purges. A check over them would pin `ok: false` on a structurally flawless store on every deployment with any deletion history, which is exactly "a diagnostic that always finds something is a diagnostic nobody reads." CLAUDE.md already applies this identical argument to the destination-policy violations endpoint ("a policy finding would pin `ok: false` on a structurally flawless store, and its 're-run to confirm' and 'never repairs' framings are both wrong"), and every clause transfers — including that "re-run to confirm" is actively misleading here, since orphan findings are perfectly stable. That precedent also supplied the answer: a separate endpoint pair plus its own article, exactly like `/api/admin/url-policy/violations`. It additionally avoids colliding with the *other* pending 13th check (physical keys under no known prefix), which genuinely is structural drift and keeps its own trigger. Revisit only if link deletion is ever changed to purge analytics inline.
- [x] A server-side resumable purge with a cursor KV key — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected in favour of client-driven chunking. Attractive because one call would do the whole job and "resumable" sounds strictly better than "the client loops". Rejected because it needs a new KV key type, which CLAUDE.md prices at three mandatory obligations (`backup.py`'s `INDEX_KEYS`/`restore_write_order`, `consistency.py`'s key-shape recognition, a `STORE_PREFIXES` prefix) purely for bookkeeping with no user-visible value — and worse, it needs a *mutable* cursor with no compare-and-swap anywhere, so two operators, or one operator with two tabs, would corrupt each other's progress undetectably. The resumability it buys is already free: the purge is idempotent and the report is re-runnable, so "resume" means "click the button again". Revisit only if Spin's KV ever gains a compare-and-swap.
- [x] Purging analytics inline in `links.handle_delete` and the bulk delete path — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected on arithmetic rather than taste. A single delete writes 3 keys today; purging inline adds up to 95 deletes at 20–26 ms per write on Akamai — **~2–2.5 s added to every link deletion**, consuming ~2 seconds of the entire app's 50-writes/second budget while live clicks compete for it — plus a full-store enumeration (~66 ms today, ~690 ms at 10,000 keys) in a request that currently makes none. For **bulk delete it is not merely expensive but impossible**: 50 links × 95 keys = 4,750 writes ≈ **95 s against a 30-second handler limit**, so the request would be killed mid-write and a currently reliable feature would start half-working. A conditional variant ("purge inline only for links with few analytics keys") was dropped in one line: knowing how few requires the enumeration, which is most of the cost, and a delete whose duration depends on click history is worse to reason about than one that never purges. Revisit only if a host ever offers a batched or ranged delete.
- [x] Having the purge client send the **key** list rather than the **slug** list — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected. Attractive because the report already knows every key, so the purge could skip its per-request enumeration entirely — worth ~40 full-store walks on a large cleanup. Rejected because the server would then be deleting client-supplied strings, so it would have to re-derive each key's slug and re-check liveness anyway (the same work, minus the guarantee that the key exists and belongs where it appears to), and because a key list from an earlier report goes stale: clicks recorded between report and purge write *new* shard keys a stale list does not contain, so the count would never reach zero. The enumeration is ~66 ms against a 5–15 s request, about 1%, and buys exactness plus a smaller trust surface.
- [x] All-or-nothing semantics on the purge endpoint, matching every other bulk endpoint — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected deliberately rather than overlooked. CLAUDE.md's stated reason for all-or-nothing is that "a partial-success design would leave the user needing to diff what they submitted against what exists just to know what to retry" — which does not apply here, because the response names exactly which slugs were purged, which remain and which were skipped and why. The alternative is worse twice over: a 250-key write budget means a 50-slug submission is routinely partial *by design*, so making that an error makes the endpoint unusable; and a fatal `link_exists` would stall the GUI's loop permanently (the report keeps offering a drifted slug, the purge keeps rejecting the whole batch). The line taken instead: **input validation is all-or-nothing; state-dependent per-slug outcomes are reported and skipped.**
- [x] Requiring a typed confirmation string in the purge GUI, as restore does — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected while keeping the server-side `{"confirm": "PURGE"}` gate (that one matters — the endpoint is reachable by `curl`). The typed field is calibrated to restore's blast radius: everything including the users store and the operator's own session, no undo, no partial. A purge deletes data that is already unreachable, for links that no longer exist, from a list the operator is looking at, behind a dialog quoting both exact totals. Adding a typing ritual to the lesser action trains operators to type through rituals, which makes restore's field weaker rather than the purge safer.
- [x] Reporting each orphan slug's click total alongside its key count — considered 2026-08-10 while planning `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, rejected. Attractive because "you are about to erase 4,120 clicks of history" is a more honest confirmation than a key count. Rejected because it costs one gathered read per orphan `count:` key — ~900 reads on the measured store — to produce a number nobody can act on: the link is gone, the data is already unreachable through every UI in the app, and no operator choice changes based on the answer. Keys are what the enumeration walks and what the cost is measured in, so keys are the honest unit.
- [x] Blind-deleting a deleted slug's 95 candidate analytics keys with no enumeration — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`, rejected. Attractive because `delete` on a missing key is a documented no-op (`spin-key-value@3.0.0/key-value.wit:21-24`, "No error is raised if a tuple did not previously exist for `key`"), so the handler could skip the enumeration entirely and issue `count:<slug>`, `count:<slug>:0..63` and `events:<slug>:0..29` unconditionally — no read at all, no store-size dependence, simplest possible code. Rejected because it costs **95 writes on every single delete**, including the never-clicked link that is the whole motivating case: ~2,185 ms and 95 writes where the enumeration variant spends ~24 ms and zero. It inverts the scarcity model — writes are cap-bound at 50 RPS app-wide while reads have 1,000 — and it would make the delete path construct keys from `COUNT_SHARDS`/`analytics_event_slots` rather than discover them, losing the legacy-key and future-key-type coverage `classify_analytics_keys` gives for free.
- [x] A key-count cap that defers heavily-clicked links' inline purge to the operator tool — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`, rejected **as a policy** while being kept as a rail. Attractive because the enumeration reveals the count for free (the very inversion that revisit corrected) and a cap of ~32 would hold every delete under ~900 ms. Rejected because the links it would defer — heavily clicked ones — are exactly the links carrying the most orphan keys, so it opts out of most of the benefit while keeping all the complexity; because it invents a caller-visible `deferred` state the non-technical audience cannot act on; and because the harm it bounds is shallower than it looks: a sequential delete loop runs at ~40–50 writes/second whatever the cap, so a cap shortens the contention window rather than reducing its depth, and the shipped purge endpoint already sustains that window for 5.75 s per 250-key chunk. What is kept is `MAX_INLINE_PURGE_KEYS = 128`, a rail that cannot fire at shipped configuration (64 shards + 1 legacy + 30 event slots = 95), pinned by a test against `COUNT_SHARDS + 1 + 30`.
- [x] Purging a deleted slug's analytics **before** removing its record — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`, rejected. Attractive because it would close the tens-of-milliseconds window in which another user could recreate the same slug between the record delete and the enumeration. Rejected because it inverts the write ordering: an interruption after the analytics deletes but before the record delete leaves a **live, resolving link whose click history is gone**, silently and unrecoverably, with nothing that reports it — against orphan analytics keys, which are recoverable by a shipped tool and are today's normal state. The race it closes costs at most one click on a link created inside that window.
- [x] Rendering the inline purge's result in the dashboard — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`, rejected. Attractive because silent behaviour is usually worse than visible behaviour, and the `deferred`/`failed` statuses are real information. Rejected because the audience is explicitly non-technical marketing staff: "6 analytics keys removed" is noise, and "some keys were left for an administrator" names a person they cannot summon and an action they cannot take. The information's correct home is the Store maintenance page's orphan report, read by the operator who *can* act. The `analytics_purge` field stays in the JSON response for `curl` and tests. The delete confirmation text is likewise left unchanged — the analytics became unreachable the moment the link was deleted, purge or no purge, and saying so here but not in the bulk dialog (which does not purge) would advertise a distinction the user cannot see.
- [ ] Paginating `GET /api/links` now — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/links-pagination.md`, rejected and deferred. Attractive because an unbounded list endpoint is a real smell, CLAUDE.md's own "Parallel KV reads" section names it as the remaining unfixed item, and one KV read per link per dashboard load draws on the same app-wide 1,000 reads/second cap the redirect hot path draws from. Rejected on arithmetic: at 100 links averaging 50 clicks a dashboard load fires ~3,600 KV reads and `GET /api/links` is **103 of them — 2.9%** (the other 97% is `GET /api/analytics/click-totals`, MODELLED from the coupon-collector key formula and not yet measured against a clicked store). It also buys no latency at reachable sizes — measured **~173 ms at 50 links against ~178 ms at 14** once `gather_reads` landed — while costing a seven-feature client-side cascade (tag autocomplete, the record-derived owner filter that is the documented repair path for orphaned links, text/tag filtering, sorting, sorting by Clicks specifically, CSV export whose own comment says it needs no endpoint *because* `allLinks` is complete, and bulk select-all) plus re-opening the settled decision to have no `tag:` index. Revisit on either trigger in the Future-work entry below.
- [ ] Landing the API-side pagination groundwork only (`?limit=`/`?offset=` with no client change) — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/links-pagination.md`, rejected. Explicitly offered as an acceptable smaller scope and it still loses: parameters designed against no client get designed wrong. The design work established that a cheaply-paginated endpoint can serve **index order only, with no filter and no sort** — every sortable column lives in the link record, not in the index, so sorting server-side means reading every record, which is the exact cost pagination exists to avoid. An endpoint offering only index order is not what any client wants, so the parameters would be dead on arrival and redesigned the moment a real client appeared. Landing nothing is the right amount of code.
- [ ] Cursor-based pagination for `GET /api/links` — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/links-pagination.md`, rejected in favour of offset/limit. Attractive as the textbook answer, and made to feel necessary by `spin:key-value/key-value@3.0.0`'s `get-keys()` having no cursor. But pagination never enumerates — it slices the app's own `all_links`/`owner_links:<u>` index, which is a **single JSON array read wholesale in one `get`**, so a cursor and an offset cost identically and there is no seek to avoid. Offset additionally wins on drift: `add_slugs_to_indexes` appends, so a concurrent create never shifts an earlier page, while a cursor naming a slug deleted between requests needs a fallback policy that offset does not. Complexity with no corresponding benefit.
- [ ] Widening `all_links` from a slug array into a per-link summary array — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/links-pagination.md`, rejected. **The most attractive alternative considered**: holding `{slug, owner, target_url, status, created_at, tags}` per link in the index would make `GET /api/links` **O(1) KV reads instead of O(N)** — strictly better than pagination rather than a mitigation of it — and every client-side feature would survive untouched. Rejected on the identical argument that killed the `tag:` index: `handle_update` touches no index today, and this adds an index read-modify-write to every single-link `PATCH`, every password change and every bulk tag action, with no compare-and-swap anywhere in Spin KV. It also caps the deployment hard — at ~250 bytes per summary, Akamai's 1 MB max value size is reached near 4,000 links, converting a slow dashboard into a write failure — and a summary silently drifting from its record is a whole new class of consistency finding. Revisit only if a compare-and-swap primitive ever appears.
- [ ] Moving filtering and sorting server-side as part of pagination — considered 2026-08-11 while planning `docs/plans/links-pagination.md`, rejected. It is the only design that preserves correctness under pagination, which is why it keeps suggesting itself: without it, filtering and sorting silently apply to the current page only, and "I can't find my spring-sale link" presents to a non-technical author as data loss rather than as a paging artifact. It loses because filtering or sorting on any field requires the records — every sortable column lives in the `slug:<slug>` record and Clicks lives in a third store — so it reads all N anyway, unless backed by new indexes, which is the summary-index entry above or the already-rejected `tag:` index wearing a different hat.
- [ ] A denormalised `analytics:total:<slug>` written as a **third** KV write on every click — re-costed 2026-08-12 against the measured read numbers (see `docs/plans/denormalised-click-total.md`), rejected again, **but on a different reason than the one recorded in `api/analytics.py`'s docstring, which is wrong and is being corrected.** The docstring says "writes are the binding constraint"; on the two caps alone that is now the *weaker* half of the argument — a 33% cut in a 25-clicks/second sustained ceiling this deployment has never approached (busiest link: 524 clicks lifetime) is a smaller real cost than 613% of the app-wide read budget per dashboard load, and the extra write costs no TTFB at all because `sendRedirectThenRecord` (`redirect/main.go:380-398`) hands the 302 to the host before any analytics runs. The read-side win is real and large: `1 + N` reads with no traffic term and no full-store enumeration, a 60× reduction at 100 links × 200 clicks. **It loses on accuracy.** `analytics:total:<slug>` is one key per slug, read-modify-written per click, with no compare-and-swap anywhere — byte for byte the pre-sharding `analytics:count:<slug>` shape whose loss curve was MEASURED live 2026-08-06 at **0% below ~2.7 clicks/s and 25% at 9.4 clicks/s on one slug**. The 64-shard sum stays exact, so the dashboard's Clicks column (which carries no accuracy caveat) would silently under-report a busy campaign link while the detail page (which does carry one, `gui/links/detail.html:60`) reports it correctly, breaking `PRODUCT.md`'s "accurate running totals" commitment on the summary view only. **The escape does not exist on this host:** `wasi:keyvalue/atomics`' `increment` is documented unsupported by Akamai (see the separate entry below); sharding the total is what `count:<slug>:<shard>` already is; and a blind `set` cannot accumulate, because the redirect knows its own shard's new value and nothing about the other 63. Second-order, MODELLED on this repo's own k²/2S collision model: 6 data ops instead of 4 raises in-flight concurrency ~1.5× and shard collisions ~2.25×, so it makes the counter that is currently right slightly less right in order to add one that can be wrong. Also carries a **fourth** new-key-type obligation the general rule omits — `analytics.parse_analytics_key`/`analyticsorphans.classify_analytics_keys` would route it to `unrecognized`, making it a permanent unpurgeable orphan for every deleted link — and a chunked operator backfill endpoint, because the cheap-looking lazy shard-summing fallback would keep the full-store enumeration in the dashboard path forever. Revisit **only** if Akamai ships `wasi:keyvalue/atomic` support or Spin's KV gains a compare-and-swap.
- [ ] The same denormalised total with the `events:` ring-buffer write **dropped**, keeping two writes per click — considered 2026-08-12 while re-costing the above, rejected, and recorded separately because it **defeats the original rejection completely**: writes/click stays at 2, so the app-wide 25 clicks/second ceiling does not move at all and the "trading read cost for write cost is backwards" argument has nothing left to stand on. It additionally cuts analytics keys per link from up to 95 to up to 65 (−32%), slowing every enumeration in the app. **It was the most attractive alternative considered and it still loses, because it pays for the wrong problem:** it buys back the write budget, which was never the real objection, and leaves the accuracy objection above fully intact — the `total:` key is still one key per slug on the same measured loss curve. It also still adds an op to the hot path (7 vs 6, shard collisions ~1.56× MODELLED), still needs the fourth obligation and the backfill endpoint, and it reopens the user's 2026-08-10 decision that recent events stays. **The line taken: keep the two questions apart.** "Drop the events write to double the click ceiling" remains live on its own merits as a Future-work entry with two independent justifications; "denormalise the total" is rejected on its own merits. Revisit only as two separate decisions, never as one trade.
- [ ] `wasi:keyvalue/atomics`' `increment` as the fix for the denormalised total's contention — considered 2026-08-12, rejected as a **documented dead end rather than deferred as a spike.** It is the one primitive that would make a single-key total correct, and the bindings genuinely ship in both SDKs (Go `imports/wasi_keyvalue_0_2_0_draft2_atomics.Increment`, Python `spin_sdk/wit/imports/wasi_keyvalue_atomics_0_2_0_draft2.py`) with the Spin world importing the whole family (`spin-go-sdk/v3@v3.0.0/wit/world.wit:24`, `include wasi:keyvalue/imports@0.2.0-draft2;`) — **which makes it a trap, not an option**, since it would compile and might even work locally while failing on the only deployment target that matters. `techdocs.akamai.com/akamai-functions/docs/use-the-key-value-store`, fetched 2026-08-12: *"the `wasi:keyvalue/atomic` interface is not supported because it requires a consistency guarantee not provided by our global store."* (`developer.fermyon.com/wasm-functions/using-key-value-store` 301-redirects to that same page, so there is one source, not two.) The same sentence confirms `wasi:keyvalue/store` and **`wasi:keyvalue/batch` are supported**, which is where the surviving read-side option came from. Note also that `kv.Store` wraps `spin_key_value_3_0_0_key_value.Store` while both atomics and batch take a `wasi_keyvalue_0_2_0_draft2_store.Bucket`, so either interface needs a second, separate open against a different WIT interface. Revisit only if Akamai's documentation changes.

- [ ] `wasi:keyvalue/batch`'s `set_many`/`delete_many` for the write paths — considered 2026-08-15 while planning `docs/plans/batch-kv-reads.md`, rejected outright rather than deferred, and recorded here so the symmetry with the adopted `get_many` is not mistaken for an oversight. It is genuinely tempting: the same interface exposes them, `backup.handle_restore` does up to `MAX_BACKUP_ENTRIES` (5,000) sequential writes and the orphan purge does up to 250 sequential deletes at the 2026-08-15 measured **~75 ms each — ~19 s for one purge request**, so the wall-time prize is far larger than anything on the read side. **It loses on the arithmetic that underwrites every read-side change in this repo:** reads are capped at 1,000 RPS app-wide and writes at 50, so reads are latency-bound (there is headroom to exploit by overlapping) while writes are already cap-bound. A batch of K writes therefore either still consumes K against the 50/s cap — in which case it queues exactly as today and the only thing that changed is that the queueing became invisible — or it does not, in which case a single handler can silently spend the whole service's write budget, including the budget every concurrent redirect's two analytics writes draw from. Neither outcome is one to own. It also dissolves the interruption-safety story: the WIT states verbatim that batch writes "do not guarantee atomicity, implying that some key-value pairs could be set while others might fail" and that they are "not guaranteed to be set in the order they are provided", while **every** write path in this app depends on a stated ordering — records before indexes in both bulk handlers and in `restore_write_order`, `owner_links:` → sessions → `user:` → `_meta:usernames` in user deletion, record → indexes → analytics in the inline purge — each chosen so that an interruption leaves the stronger invariant. A partially-applied unordered batch has no such story and no way to learn what landed. CLAUDE.md's "**Never gather writes**" rule is the whole safety argument for the read-side work; extending batching to writes would remove the argument along with the rule. Revisit only if Akamai documents batch **write** quota accounting *and* the host provides an ordering or atomicity guarantee the WIT itself disclaims.
- [ ] Per-finding consistency repair — the client submits the findings it wants fixed — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/consistency-repair.md`, rejected in favour of per-check submission. Attractive because it is maximally granular and reads as "the operator is in control". It loses three ways. (a) It re-introduces exactly the stale-report hazard `analyticsorphans.handle_orphan_purge`'s `exists()` pre-check exists to close, with a **much** longer window — the operator's think time between fetching a report and clicking a button — where per-check submission lets the repair re-detect everything in-request and trust the client for nothing but intent. (b) `consistency.analyze` truncates `findings` to `MAX_FINDINGS_PER_CHECK = 100` while `count` stays exact, so **the 152 `missing_link_record` entries of the real 2026-08-15 incident could not be submitted at all** — the operator would repair in waves and never see the tail. That is not hypothetical: it is recorded in this file's "BOTH SPIKES ANSWERED" section as one of the reasons the drift was repaired by hand-editing a backup instead. (c) Once a finding's index key is scheduled, every further finding on that key costs **zero** marginal writes, so per-finding granularity buys an option nobody wants — there is no meaningful "repair 80 of these 152 entries". Revisit only if a check is ever added whose repair cost is genuinely per-finding rather than per-index-key.
- [ ] `?fix=true` on `GET /api/admin/consistency` — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/consistency-repair.md`, rejected outright rather than deferred. Attractive because it is one query parameter and no new route. It loses because a GET that writes is a category error: it is CSRF-reachable by plain navigation, cacheable in principle, retried by intermediaries, and it destroys the one property that makes a diagnostic trustworthy — this file and CLAUDE.md both state "it reports; it never repairs" as a load-bearing fact about that endpoint, and a flag would make the sentence conditional. A `POST` to a distinct path additionally keeps `obs.route_template`'s log line honest about which requests mutate. Nothing would justify revisiting; if the ergonomics ever matter, the answer is a button, not a verb change.
- [ ] Repairing `owner_index_mismatch` automatically by "the record wins" — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/consistency-repair.md`, rejected for now and re-filed under Future work with a trigger. It is the most defensible of the four non-repairable checks: `links.can_edit` is `record["owner"] == principal.username`, so the record is *already* authoritative for permissions, and the only realistic producer of a mismatch is an interrupted `links.move_slugs_between_owners` (which adds to the new owner first, then removes from each old one), where "record wins" is exactly the completion of the interrupted reassignment. It loses on three counts. The repair is a **removal** from a user's index, which makes a link vanish from that user's dashboard; deciding which of two conflicting owner assertions reflects *intent* is not derivable from the store, and it is the one repair in the set that is not; and the operator already has `POST /api/links/bulk-action` with `action: "reassign"` for precisely this. Decisive on the feature's own terms: **the observed 2026-08-15 drift contained zero mismatches**, and the whole trigger for building the repair companion was "designed from observed drift rather than imagined drift". Revisit on seeing a real mismatch in a real report.
- [ ] Repairing `unreadable_value` or `unrecognized_key` by deleting the key — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/consistency-repair.md`, rejected. Attractive because these two are the only findings that can hold a store at `ok: false` with no automatic path to `ok: true`. It loses because deleting an unrecognised key is **precisely how a new KV key type the checker has not been taught about yet gets destroyed** — this repo already holds the opposite rule in the analogous place, `analyticsorphans.classify_analytics_keys`, whose docstring calls routing an unknown shape to `unrecognized` "the safety valve: a future analytics key type must show up as something a human is told about, never as something this feature quietly deletes". And an unreadable value's content is by definition unknown, so both candidate repairs — delete, or rewrite — are guesses about data nobody can read. Both stay manual, with shipped GUI copy naming the tool to use instead. Nothing would justify revisiting.
