- [ ] Blanket-refusing every repair while any `unreadable_value` finding exists — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/consistency-repair.md`, rejected in favour of three precise per-finding guards (`missing_link_record`, `orphan_owner_index_entry` and `dangling_owner_index` all require the slug's absence from `collect`'s new `present_slugs` set). Attractive because it is one condition instead of three, and it is genuinely the *safe* direction. It loses because a single corrupt key anywhere in the store would block every repair on it — the shape of tool operators stop using — and because the precise guards do strictly more: they report the specific blocking slug back to the operator with a `record_unreadable` reason and a next step, where a blanket refusal reports only "no". Revisit only if the guards ever prove unable to enumerate a hazard cheaply.
- [ ] A fifth `<article>` on the Store maintenance page for consistency repair — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/consistency-repair.md`, rejected in favour of rendering repair controls inside the existing consistency article's result. Attractive because it matches the page's existing structure — four articles, one tool each — and it was the shape originally suggested. It loses because **a repair is meaningless without the report it repairs**: a standalone article would hold a button with no findings beside it, and the operator would scroll between two articles to connect a finding to its fix. The analytics purge already set the precedent in the right direction — its "Delete these analytics keys" button renders *inside* `#orphans-result`, after the report, not as its own article — and following it costs no new file, no new `spin.toml` route and no new `gui-pages/routing.py` entry. Revisit only if repair ever gains inputs of its own that make sense before a report exists.
- [ ] String-matching `'too many requests'` to decide whether a failed KV write is retryable — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected **for control flow** and kept only as a label. Attractive because it is precise: `spin:key-value/key-value@3.0.0` has no dedicated rate-limit variant (`Error = Union[Error_StoreTableFull, Error_NoSuchStore, Error_AccessDenied, Error_Other]`), so the string is the only thing distinguishing a throttle from a permanent fault, and matching it would let `Error_AccessDenied` fail instantly instead of wasting attempts. It loses on the direction it degrades: **if Akamai rewords the message the match silently stops firing and the app reverts to exactly today's behaviour** — no retries, bare 500, invisible — so a vendor copy-edit could un-ship the feature with nothing anywhere reporting it. It also cannot live in a pure module: `componentize_py_types` is absent from the host venv (confirmed by `find`), so a host-testable module cannot import `Err` or the variants at all and the string is the only available discriminator regardless. The chosen policy — retry **any** write error, bounded by attempts and a per-request sleep budget — wastes at most 2 extra attempts and ~400 ms on a request that was going to fail anyway, and `AccessDenied` on a KV write is a deploy-time fault that fires on the very first request. The match survives as `kvretry.classify_write_error`, feeding the log line and the response's `write_error` field, where being wrong costs only a less specific message. Revisit if Akamai ever publishes a stable machine-readable throttle signal.
- [ ] Retrying `redirect`'s two analytics writes under throttling — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected outright rather than deferred, and agreed with rather than merely deferred to. Attractive because the redirect path is where the 50 writes/second cap actually binds — two writes per click, ~25 clicks/second app-wide. It loses three times over. The loss is already documented, measured and accepted as mechanism M2, and CLAUDE.md is explicit that only *fewer writes per click* addresses it. A retry would add wall time to a visitor's redirect for bookkeeping they have no stake in, on a path where `recordAnalytics` already runs *before* `http.Redirect` — itself flagged as a problem. And retrying into a saturated cap actively worsens M2 for every other caller, since the redirect path is the largest consumer of the write budget and therefore the last place that should re-issue writes. The hot path stays at 6 KV operations. Revisit only alongside the "reduce the redirect's KV writes per click from two to one" Future-work entry, never independently.
- [ ] Transparent retry inside `kvprefix.PrefixedStore.set`/`delete` — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected. By far the most attractive option: one edit, every write path in the application covered, impossible to forget at a call site. It loses for three reasons. It makes wall time unbounded and invisible — a 50-row bulk create could silently grow by 50 × the full backoff schedule with no per-request budget anywhere, against a 30-second handler limit. It puts write-cap policy inside the module CLAUDE.md designates as "the only Python module that knows prefixes exist", whose single responsibility is namespace separation. And decisively, it removes the handler's ability to make the decision that matters most: **stop, and index what landed.** A transparent retry can only succeed or raise; it cannot know that abandoning the remaining 40 records and spending the budget on the index write is the right trade. The explicit `write(...)` call site is what makes that choice expressible. Revisit only if the explicit form is measured to have been forgotten at a real call site.
- [ ] Making bulk *execution* all-or-nothing by rolling back on a failed write — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected. Attractive because it would make the documented "all-or-nothing" true of execution as well as validation and would need no new response shape at all. It loses because a rollback is *itself writes*, issued into the same saturated cap that just rejected the forward write, with no transaction and no compare-and-swap to make it correct — and a rollback that fails halfway leaves a store that is neither the before-state nor the after-state and about which nothing can be said, strictly worse than a reported partial. Same reasoning that made restore write-then-prune rather than wipe-then-write. The line taken instead extends the analytics purge's 2026-08-10 precedent: **validation is all-or-nothing; execution is best-effort and fully reported.**
- [ ] Retrying `analyticsorphans.purge_slug_analytics`, the inline purge on single-link delete — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected deliberately rather than overlooked, and it is the plan's stated answer to "where should the shared helper NOT be used". It runs *after* the link is already deleted, so its failure cannot corrupt anything; its failure mode is orphaned analytics keys, which CLAUDE.md documents as "expected, normal, intended state between purges" with a shipped operator tool; and it already catches every exception and reports `{"status": "failed", ...}` rather than turning a successful deletion into a 500. Retrying would spend the request's write budget — and add wall time to a delete already measured at 1.9 s — on the least valuable writes in the application, while worsening app-wide cap pressure for everyone else.
- [ ] Retrying `backup.handle_restore`'s write loop — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected in favour of report-only. A full-cap 5,000-entry restore already cannot finish inside Akamai's 30-second handler limit (~100 s of writes at the cap), so adding sleeps makes a doomed request slower for no gain. Restore replaces rather than merges and is therefore idempotent, so "run it again" is a genuine next step. `handle_restore` gets no `write` parameter at all and `api/backup.py` imports no `kvretry` — the clearest demonstration in the plan that **retry and report are independent decisions** and one can be taken without the other. Revisit alongside the existing chunked/resumable-restore Future-work entry, not before.
- [ ] Accepting the concurrent index lost update and leaning on the consistency repair — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected. Genuinely live, and the strongest version of "do nothing" this repo has had: zero code, and the repair is proven cheap — 65 findings in **2 writes** on 2026-08-17, the O(distinct index keys) property confirmed live rather than modelled. It loses on three counts. The damage is **silent**: the user gets a clean `201` and a dashboard missing their links, with no in-product signal anywhere. The repair is gated on `users.manage`, so the population that *creates* the drift (non-technical marketing staff creating and deleting links heavily) cannot fix it and has no reason ever to open the Store maintenance page — the same argument that retired the identical option a day earlier for the throttle work, only stronger here because the trigger is lower. And the trigger is embarrassingly low: **two overlapping bulk creates**, with a race window of one KV round trip per authoring request, measured to lose an entire request's three additions at ~10 writes and 0.7 s. It would be the right answer if the fix were expensive; the measured cost of deriving the index at the current store size is **−1 ms** (`list_keys` 23.9 ms replacing a `get` at ~25 ms). Revisit only if the derived design's enumeration cost is measured to bind before its benefit lands.
- [ ] Verify-after-write on the index — re-read `all_links`/`owner_links:` after writing and re-apply if your own slugs are missing — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected as the primary fix and retained only as the fallback if the enumeration turns out not to be read-your-own-write fresh. Attractive because it is ~10 lines, needs no enumeration, costs nothing on the happy path and converges probabilistically. It loses because the read-back is exactly as untrustworthy as the read that caused the problem: Akamai KV has a documented staleness artifact (a deleted key still reported present by `exists()`, TASKS.md 2026-08-16) and an inferred ~100 ms cross-instance propagation window from the click-counter loss curve. Worse, a re-apply writes a full array derived from a possibly-stale read, so **a repair attempt can itself clobber a third request's additions** — and the extra writes land precisely when the store is already contended, cutting directly against the write-throttle plan's own "abandon rather than hammer into a saturated cap" rule. It converts a rare permanent loss into a rarer permanent loss plus a new failure mode. Revisit only as the named fallback, i.e. if measurement M1 in `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md` fails.
- [ ] Sharding the link index the way the click counter was sharded — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected. Attractive by precedent: `CountShards` worked, is raise-only, needed no migration, and is the option a reader reaches for first. The precedent does not transfer. A count shard holds a **commutative integer** whose loss is a statistical error already disclosed as best-effort; an index shard holds **set membership** whose loss is a link disappearing from its owner's dashboard. Sharding divides collision probability by S and eliminates nothing — at 16 shards roughly 1 in 16 simultaneous writer pairs still collides, forever. It also costs a new KV key type (all three obligations: `backup.py`'s `INDEX_KEYS`/`restore_write_order`, `consistency.py`'s key-shape recognition, `kvprefix.STORE_PREFIXES`), a migration off `all_links`, a removal path that must read every shard to locate a slug, rewritten consistency checks and repairs, and a `get_many` over S × owners on every read. Maximum machinery for a partial fix. Revisit only if a design appears that makes index membership commutative.
- [ ] Serialising index writes behind a single owner — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected as **not implementable** rather than undesirable. There is no compare-and-swap, no lock primitive, no queue, and `wasi:messaging` is unsupported on Akamai Functions; both components declare `allowed_outbound_hosts = []`, so an external coordinator is out for exactly the same reason the login rate limiter is (see "Security tradeoffs"). Revisit only if Spin/Akamai ever ship an atomic KV primitive, which would also retire half the reasoning in this file.
- [ ] Deriving `all_links` only and keeping `owner_links:<owner>` maintained (the split answer) — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected. Attractive because it halves the change and dodges the one genuinely expensive derivation: deriving per-owner membership means reading every link record to learn its owner, even for a user who owns 3 of 900. It loses on **who it leaves broken** — an ordinary account has role `user` and no permissions, so a plain user's dashboard reads `owner_links:<them>` and nothing else, and the measured 2026-08-17 incident produced 28 `unindexed_owner_link` alongside 37 `unindexed_link`. This option fixes only the half that admins read, leaving the symptom exactly as visible for the population that hits it. The cost that motivates it is also smaller than it looks: reading every record is one `get_many` host call (~10 ms at K=1,000, measured not to bill as K reads), and `handle_list` already does exactly that for admins today.
- [ ] Deriving `all_links` from `users:_meta:usernames` + `owner_links:<U>`, with no enumeration at all — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected, and the most interesting of the rejected options: one `get` plus one `get_many` over K owner keys, O(users) and bounded, killing the single hottest shared key outright and saving a write per authoring request without paying for any key walk. It loses three times. It does not fix **same-owner** concurrency, which is precisely what every measured run exercised. It makes `dangling_owner_index` catastrophic rather than cosmetic — a link whose owner is missing from `_meta:usernames` becomes invisible to *everyone*, and CLAUDE.md documents the admin dashboard's owner filter (which surfaces links whose owner no longer exists, marked "— deleted account") as **the repair path** for deployments that orphaned links before the `409` gate existed. And it substitutes one read-modify-write shared key for another on the link path, which is a smaller blast radius, not a different property.
- [ ] Rebuilding the link index from an enumeration on every WRITE instead of deriving it on read — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, rejected. Attractive because it keeps `GET /api/links` at one cheap `get` and confines the enumeration to authoring requests, which are rarer. It loses because two concurrent rebuilds still clobber each other — the outcome merely becomes order-dependent (whoever enumerates last and writes last wins, and a writer that enumerates before a peer's record write still drops it) rather than race-free — and it puts a whole-store walk on every write path instead of every read path, at a moment when the write cap is the binding constraint. Strictly worse than deriving on read, with the same enumeration bill.
- [ ] Doing nothing, on the grounds that the consistency repair already fixes throttle damage in one click — considered 2026-08-17 while planning `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md`, rejected. Genuinely live and stronger than it was a week ago: the repair shipped 2026-08-17 cleared the 174-finding incident in 13 KV operations and 368 ms. It loses because **it requires a human to notice**, and both recorded incidents (2026-08-15 and 2026-08-17) were noticed by an engineer running `/api/admin/consistency` for an unrelated reason. The audience — non-technical marketing staff doing bulk work at the 50-row cap — has no reason to ever open the Store maintenance page, and the failure is silent by construction: the links resolve, the dashboard just doesn't show them. Revisit if the audience ever changes to one that monitors store health.
- [ ] Disabling the recent-events write reversibly, via `analytics_event_slots = 0` as an off switch — considered 2026-08-18 while planning `docs/plans/drop-events-write.md`, rejected. Attractive because it looked like a no-code-change, no-deploy-of-new-code way to buy the write-cap win back if it turned out to be a mistake. It fails on every part of that. **It does not actually disable the write:** `EventSlot(now, 0)` delegates to `ShardFor(_, 0)`, whose `numShards <= 1` guard returns `0`, so the component keeps writing `events:<slug>:0` on every single click — the headline benefit (one fewer write per click) is not delivered at all, and making it a real off switch needs a code change in `recordClickEvent` anyway. It also lands squarely in the partial state the whole change was scoped to avoid: the read side builds `range(num_event_slots)`, which at 0 is empty, so the link detail page would show **"No recent events yet" forever on every link** — reading as broken rather than as removed — and fixing *that* means the API publishing an events-enabled flag and the GUI branching on it, i.e. more surface, not less. Finally it leaves dead code plus a config-dependent behaviour difference, which this file already rejected once (the config seam preserving three-store separation, on the reasoning that a deployed-vs-developed configuration mismatch is a worse property to own). Reversibility was worth less than it looked: the ring is a 30-slot sample, not history, so re-adding the write later is a small `git show`-recoverable diff. Revisit only if a future feature genuinely needs a runtime-tunable analytics write, which nothing does today.
- [ ] Sampling the recent-events write (write it 1 click in N) instead of dropping it — considered 2026-08-18 while planning `docs/plans/drop-events-write.md`, rejected, and previously flagged in this file's own "two to one" Future-work entry. The obvious middle ground: 1-in-4 gives 1.25 writes per click and a ~40 clicks/second ceiling while keeping some referrer data. It loses on the flaw that entry already named and that nothing has since answered — **an unconditional sample thins the events list most for LOW-traffic links, which are exactly the links whose events are worth reading** (a link with 8 clicks would record 2 events), while a rate-adaptive sample needs to know the rate, which needs state, which needs a read, which is circular on the hot path. It also retains 100% of the code, tests, GUI and maintenance surface for a fraction of the data — the worst of both columns. Revisit only if a rate signal ever becomes available on the redirect path for free.
- [ ] Stopping the events write while keeping the read path and the Recent events table — considered 2026-08-18 while planning `docs/plans/drop-events-write.md`, rejected outright. It is the cheapest possible diff (delete one function call) and it is the worst outcome: the detail page would render a frozen list of pre-cutover events under a heading that says "Recent" — presenting stale data as current — and, on any link with no leftover `events:` keys, "No recent events yet" permanently. This is why the read-side and GUI removals are sequenced **with or before** the write removal and never after. Not revisitable; it is a sequencing error rather than a design option.
- [ ] Building the leftover-`events:`-key sweep in the same change that stops writing them — considered 2026-08-18 while planning `docs/plans/drop-events-write.md`, deferred rather than rejected (see the Future-work entry below for the trigger). Three reasons it did not ship alongside. The residual is **frozen, not growing** — no new `events:` key is created after the change, and existing ones decay as links are deleted, because both `links.handle_delete`'s inline purge and `analyticsorphans.handle_orphan_purge` enumerate-then-classify rather than constructing candidate keys, so they already remove `events:` keys for free. A sweep **cannot reuse the existing purge's safety argument**: `handle_orphan_purge`'s load-bearing property is that it re-checks `exists("slug:<S>")` and therefore never deletes a live link's analytics, and a sweep of a retired key type must delete them for live links too — inverting that property, so it would need its own endpoint, confirmation string and justification, never a mode on the existing one. And on the store as it stands (14 links, 37 analytics keys, `list_keys` already at its ~24 ms floor) it would reclaim a rounding error, which fails this repo's own measure-before-building standard. The plan ships the measurement instead (`totals.obsolete_event_keys` in the orphan report).
- [x] A bounded retry of the link `Get` inside `redirect` when a KV read fails — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-read-failure-not-404.md`, rejected outright rather than deferred. The most attractive of the three options the filed bug named: it is the only one that keeps the link *working* rather than merely honest, and the repo already built a retry seam for writes (`api/kvretry.py`), so it looks like a consistent move. It loses on the mechanism, and the difference from the write case is the whole argument. A throttled **write** retries into *headroom* — it defers into a later 50/s window that is usually idle. This failure is **read-cap saturation of a 1,000/s app-wide budget**: at the measured 947 rps, 31% of requests are already failing, so retrying spends more of the exact resource that is exhausted, converting a partial failure into a retry storm that degrades every concurrent request including the ones that would have succeeded. Secondary reasons, each sufficient on its own: it adds latency to the one path this repo protects hardest (CLAUDE.md's "Write-throttle resilience" Trade-offs #2 excluded `redirect` from the retry seam for a weaker version of this same reason); any sleep long enough to outlast a per-second cap window is far longer than a visitor will wait; and **whether `time.Sleep` even works inside this component is UNCONFIRMED** — the Python side needed `wasi_clocks_monotonic_clock…wait_for` because `asyncio.sleep` raised, and nothing equivalent has ever been tested in Go here. The correct place for a retry decision against a saturated origin is the **client**, which is exactly what `503` + `Retry-After` buys at zero origin cost. Revisit only with a measurement showing the read cap has headroom at the moment of failure — the 690/726/947/1292 rps sweep says it does not.
- [x] Serving a remembered redirect from in-instance memory when the KV read fails — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-read-failure-not-404.md`, rejected. The only option on the list where the visitor still reaches the destination: cache `slug → target_url` in process and use it *only* on a read failure. It loses to CLAUDE.md's "Redirect caching" section, which is emphatic that resolution must re-read KV on every request — the `status` check, the `[start_at, end_at)` window, deletion, repointing and the destination-policy remediation path are each correct *only* if no layer serves a remembered answer. "Only on failure" does not soften that; it means serving a remembered answer at precisely the moment the app cannot verify it, so a deleted or disabled link keeps redirecting for as long as the store is saturated — and saturation is exactly when an operator most needs a kill switch to work. Wasm instance lifetime on Akamai is also unknown and unpredictable, so both the hit rate and the staleness window are unknowable. Revisit only if "keep redirecting through saturation" becomes a stated product requirement, and then as a deliberate decision about serving stale redirects with a bounded TTL and an explicit list of the guarantees being traded away — never as a fallback smuggled in behind an error branch.
- [x] Keeping the plain `404` for an unparseable link record — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-read-failure-not-404.md`, rejected in favour of `500`, and it was close. Three real arguments for keeping it: it preserves probing resistance perfectly (a `500` reveals the slug has a record); a 5xx invites a visitor and a crawler to retry a *permanently* broken link forever, where a 404 lets a search engine deindex it; and an operator already has three other surfaces for a corrupt record (`422 link_record_unreadable` on six `api` paths, `unreadable_value` in the consistency report, and the record being skipped from `handle_list`), so a fourth adds little. It loses on the principle the whole fix rests on: **404 means "we read the store and there is no link available to you" — absent, disabled, out-of-window, all intentional product states — while a corrupt record is a fault, and answering a fault with a product state is the same lie, in miniature, that this plan exists to remove.** Note this reverses the reasoning in `api/links.py`'s `UnreadableLinkError` docstring, which rejected `500` because it "tells an operator to retry a transient fault when it is a permanent data fault": that objection was correct while `500` was the only error status on the path, and dissolves once `503` owns "transient, retry" and `500` means "permanent fault" by contrast. The API keeps its `422` — it has a JSON client that can be told something specific; a browser navigation does not. Revisit if a deployment ever sees corrupt records at a rate where the 5xx noise costs more than the honesty buys, which would itself be a signal that something upstream needs fixing.
- [ ] Gating KV-failure logging on `log_level=summary` instead of making it unconditional — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/observable-kv-failures.md`, rejected. Attractive because it is the mechanism that already exists, needs no new bound and no new argument. It fails the actual requirement three ways: it needs one redeploy to arm and a second to disarm, it carries the "remember to turn it off" hazard, and it cannot catch a failure that happens next week — which is the whole point, since the redirect read fault has now failed to reproduce on demand twice. **The volume objection that justifies `log_level=off` does not transfer**: that is ~130 bytes on EVERY request at ~50 rps sustained, while a failure line is ≤3 per faulting `api` request and ≤32 distinct messages per `redirect` instance. Note the proposed framing "a KV failure is rare by definition" is arithmetically wrong per-request — one throttled 50-row bulk create can fail 150 times in a single request — which is why the shipped bound is dedup-based rather than "log every failure". Revisit only if a captured run shows the dedup bounds being reached routinely.
- [ ] Logging `redirect`'s swallowed analytics `Get`/`Set` failures — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/observable-kv-failures.md`, rejected, and it was the most attractive option on the table: it is the ONE place in the app that would directly capture Akamai's **write**-failure message, in the clean unwrapped Go form (`errorVariantToError` passes `Other` through verbatim), with no experiment needed at all. Rejected because it is the highest-frequency write in the application and the one already known to fail routinely above ~50 clicks/second (mechanism M2 — documented, measured, accepted), making it the single worst place to attach an unconditional log; `api`'s bulk path reaches the same host and gets the same message at human-scale request rates. Revisit if the `api` capture comes back empty AND someone wants a counter-only signal (never a line) to attribute M2 loss — filed under Future work in that shape.
- [ ] Putting the sanitized host error message in the API response body (a `write_error_detail` beside the existing `write_error`) — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/observable-kv-failures.md`, rejected. Attractive: no log access needed, visible immediately to whoever ran the bulk operation, and outside the 7-day `spin aka logs` retention window entirely. Rejected because that body is rendered in the dashboard for ORDINARY users, not just `users.manage` holders, so it would put raw host error text in a user-facing surface and disclose backend detail to every authenticated account, for a field only an operator can act on — and the operator who needs it already has `spin aka logs`. Keeping it out also keeps the whole change clear of `gui/` and its restart-required staleness trap. Revisit if an operator-only surface ever exists to put it on.
- [ ] A post-delete `exists` verification read to catch the ghost DELETE — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/observable-kv-failures.md`, rejected on evidence rather than taste. Attractive because it would turn "seen once 2026-08-18, unreproducible in 10 attempts" into "logged whenever it happens". Rejected because TASKS.md already records (2026-08-15) Akamai's `exists()` reporting a *deleted* key as still present, so a positive result cannot distinguish a lost write from documented eventual consistency — it would fire on normal state, which is exactly how a checker gets ignored (the same reasoning that kept orphaned analytics out of the consistency check). It also costs a KV read on every delete. `dev/delete-verify.sh` gets the same evidence with no production cost and no ambiguity, and a harness is what the filed entry actually asked for.
- [ ] Making the WIT error variant name (`etype`) control flow — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/observable-kv-failures.md`, rejected FOR NOW and filed under Future work with a trigger. Genuinely attractive, and newly *possible*: `type(exc.value).__name__` identifies the variant with no import, so the 2026-08-17 conclusion that string matching was the only option available to a pure module was too broad. Rejected here purely on sequencing — this plan is diagnostics only, and the right order is to observe which variants actually occur before writing a policy against them. Note what must NOT be inferred from this entry: the standing prohibition is on the **message string** becoming control flow (a vendor copy-edit must not be able to un-ship a feature); a variant check is a different mechanism and does not inherit that prohibition, but it does inherit the obligation to be justified by observation rather than a hunch.
- [ ] Adding a `kv_err`/`read_failed` op type to either collector, or a field to the existing per-request summary line — considered 2026-08-19 while planning `docs/plans/observable-kv-failures.md`, rejected, upholding both prohibitions `docs/plans/redirect-read-failure-not-404.md`'s "Observability changes: none, deliberately" section set down. A field on the summary line is invisible unless tracing is already on, duplicates `status=`, and costs the traced path; a collector op type would change `kv_ops`, which CLAUDE.md defines as counting HOST operations, and would shift every existing trace under a change whose only purpose is to observe. **What that earlier section did not consider, and what this plan reopens deliberately, is a SEPARATE line emitted only from the fault arm** — it costs the success path nothing and carries the one thing a status code cannot: the host's own message and variant. The status code stays the frequency signal; the line is the content signal.
- [ ] Styling only the 404 and the 503 on `/r/{slug}`, leaving the 500 a bare `http.Error` string — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-error-pages.md`, rejected. Attractive on the filed Future-work entry's own scope logic: the 500 is by far the rarest of the three (it needs a link record that will not parse, which only a hand-edited store produces — it has never been seen outside a deliberately-corrupted local key) and it is the only one implying *operator* rather than visitor action, so its audience is arguably nobody. It loses for exactly the reason that entry's "never just one" rule exists: leaving one of three statuses as a raw Go string reproduces the inconsistency the rule was written to prevent, one status later. It is also the cheapest of the three to include, since the CSP, the render helper and the test guard are all already paid for by the other two — one more static file and one more one-line call-site swap. And the rarity argument inverts: the 500 is the page most likely to be seen at the worst possible moment, by the recipient of a printed campaign URL an operator has not yet noticed is broken. Revisit only if a template turns out to cost something this analysis missed.
- [ ] Loading `/theme-init.js` on the `/r/{slug}` error pages so they follow the OS light/dark preference — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-error-pages.md`, rejected; the pages always render light. Genuinely newly available: the reason `prompt.html` refuses a script (it is the app's one credential-entry page, so `script-src 'none'` outranks theme-following) does not apply to a page with no credential on it. Rejected on four counts. (a) It widens the strictest CSP in the app from `script-src 'none'` to `'self'`, on the most publicly-exposed route the app has, to buy an aesthetic. (b) These are public pages, so almost no visitor has an `ss-theme` key and the feature reduces to "follow the OS" — nice-to-have, not a fix. (c) It adds a render-blocking subresource to a page whose 503 variant is by definition served when the system is degraded, and a `theme-init.js` 404 there produces exactly the unstyled failure `gui/app.js`'s `window.ssTheme` guard exists to contain elsewhere. (d) Consistency inside one component: a visitor hitting a password prompt and then an error page would see two different themes from the same route. **What it would cost to reverse, recorded so the reversal stays cheap and visible:** one `<script src="/theme-init.js">` line per template, `script-src 'self'` in `errorPageCSP`, and loosening the new no-`<script`-at-all assertion in `gui-pages/tests/test_no_inline_code.py` — that last one is the point, since it makes the change show up in a diff instead of silently.
- [ ] A single parameterized `error.html` with the three pages' copy in Go string constants — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-error-pages.md`, rejected in favour of three static, data-free `go:embed`ed files. Attractive: one embed, one guard entry, and no duplicated `<head>` block across three near-identical files. It loses twice. First, it moves the copy out of the file a human edits copy in and into Go constants, putting the 404's non-distinguishing-wording guard out of reach of the HTML-file guard that already exists (it would have to read a `.go` file — possible, per `api/tests/test_kvprefix.py`'s precedent of a Python test reading `keys.go`, but a worse fit). Second, it reintroduces a template parameter on the one page whose defining property is that it must render identically for three different causes; "the template takes no data" is a strictly stronger guarantee than "we always pass the same data". The real duplication cost is mitigated by a guard assertion that every `error-*.html` links both stylesheets with a leading slash.
- [ ] Moving the error templates and a `Disposition → (status, page)` mapping into `redirect/linkgate/` so a Go test could pin them — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-error-pages.md`, rejected. Legal (`go:embed` is stdlib, so `linkgate` would stay free of `spin-go-sdk` imports) and it would buy the only host-runnable Go assertion available for this work, since `package main` is not host-testable at all. What it would actually pin is thin: `Resolve` already collapses absent/disabled/out-of-window into one `DispositionNotFound` (pinned by `resolve_test.go`), so a mapping test can only assert one disposition maps to one page, which a `switch` in `main.go` makes true by construction either way. Against that it drags served HTML out of the component root where `prompt.html` lives, splits the two kinds of served HTML across two directories, makes the Python guard's glob follow, and puts presentation assets inside the package whose stated purpose is pure logic. The honest position: this change contains no logic and therefore gets no Go test.
- [ ] Registering `mux.HandleFunc("/r/", ...)` so `GET /r/` (no slug) and method mismatches also get a styled page — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/redirect-error-pages.md`, rejected. Those two shapes are answered by `ServeMux` itself, not by this component's code (net/http's own plain-text `404 page not found`, and its own `405`), so they keep their raw strings after the error-page work. A subtree pattern would catch them, but a method-mismatched request matches *only* the subtree pattern, so the `405` would silently become whatever the new handler returns — a status change, which the error-page work forbids outright as presentation-only. Doing it correctly needs method-aware routing. Accepted as a residual instead, on the reasoning that neither shape is one a human reaches by clicking a shared link. Revisit only on evidence anyone actually lands on `/r/` with no slug — note a `log_level=summary` build would not even show it, since those requests never reach a handler that logs.
- [ ] Serving `gui-pages`' error-page markup from a file under `gui/` through the injected `read_file` — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/gui-pages-error-pages.md`, rejected in favour of an inlined `bytes` constant in a new pure `gui-pages/errorpages.py`. Genuinely attractive: the component already mounts `gui/`, `build_response` already takes a `read_file` callable, a designer would get a real HTML file with syntax highlighting, and `test_no_inline_code.py`'s existing `PAGES` guard already reads files from `gui/`. It loses on circularity, which is decisive: **the `500` branch exists precisely because `read_file` can fail** (a `ROUTES`-vs-filesystem drift), so fetching the error page's own markup through the same callable puts a possible failure inside the failure handler, and *that* failure needs its own fallback — which is a `bytes` constant, i.e. the rejected option, now carried in addition to the file. Two further nails: there is **no `go:embed` equivalent for componentize-py** (only `spin.toml`'s `files` mapping is a runtime filesystem and it maps `gui/`, so a data file in `gui-pages/` is unreachable — UNCONFIRMED but not depended on), and reading it eagerly at module import just moves the same failure to instance startup where there is no response to attach `SECURITY_HEADERS` to at all. The duplication objection is also weaker here than it was for `redirect`: one shared `_render` shell means **one** `<head>` block for both pages, against the three near-identical ones `redirect` accepted. Note this is the exact mirror of the "copy in Go constants" rejection above, and both of that entry's reasons flip in Python — a module constant is *importable* by the guard (no source-file parsing), and `#` comments live outside the guarded bytes, so the comment-stripping regex `error-404.html`'s guard needed never arises. Revisit only if these pages ever need per-deployment copy, which would be a Spin variable, not a file.
- [ ] Giving `gui-pages`' error responses a tightened, `redirect`-style CSP (`default-src 'none'; script-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; …`) instead of the component's existing `SECURITY_HEADERS` — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/gui-pages-error-pages.md`, rejected. Attractive on two counts: it matches the sibling error pages one route over, and `img-src 'self' data:` (which exists only for Pico's chevron/search/calendar affordances) plus `form-action 'self'` are dead permissions on a page with no form, no table and no Pico affordance. Rejected on three. First, **what it would protect against cannot happen**: the tightening's value is containing injected content, and these bodies are rendered at import time from module constants with no request data reaching them — `redirect`'s prompt page earned its strict policy because it has real parameters (`.Slug`, `.Error`); these have none. Second, it introduces a second header set inside the one module whose entire purpose is to have one, on the exact two branches whose stated guarantee is "`SECURITY_HEADERS` still set", and it would force both existing `for key, value in SECURITY_HEADERS.items()` loops in `gui-pages/tests/test_routing.py` to be loosened — weakening the pin on that guarantee to buy a theoretical hardening. Third, a future addition to `SECURITY_HEADERS` would then silently not reach the error responses. **Revisit trigger: these pages interpolating anything derived from the request** (which that plan forbids) — tighten the CSP in the same change if that ever happens.
- [ ] Following `redirect`'s always-light, no-`<script>` decision on `gui-pages`' error pages — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/gui-pages-error-pages.md`, rejected; these two pages **do** load `/theme-init.js`, deliberately diverging from the sibling pattern. Four reasons the same question answers differently in this component. (a) **Consistency runs the other way here**: every page `gui-pages` serves loads `theme-init.js` as the first element of `<head>`, so a script-free error page would be the odd one out *at the same origin*, and a dark-mode console user who mistypes a URL would get a white page — whereas in `redirect` no page loads script, so the opposite choice is the consistent one there. (b) It costs **no CSP widening**, because that plan keeps the component's existing `script-src 'self'` — which is exactly why the argument that defeated this for `/r/` (widening the strictest policy in the app) does not carry over. (c) The degraded case *is* `redirect`'s behaviour: with `theme-init.js` blocked or 404ing, no `data-theme` is set and `theme.css`'s unconditional light block renders the page light, so this is strictly additive with a graceful fallback rather than a dependency. (d) `gui/app.js`'s `initHeader` guard exists because an unguarded `window.ssTheme` call would kill a whole page's init chain — an error page has no init chain to kill. **Residual cost, stated plainly:** the guard cannot assert "no `<script>` at all" on these two pages, so enforcement is `INLINE_SCRIPT` (no srcless script) plus a leading-slash assertion on `/theme-init.js` — the same bar every other page in this component is held to. **Neither decision may be "harmonised" onto the other**; both are recorded in CLAUDE.md for that reason.
- [ ] Echoing the requested path back on `gui-pages`' 404 ("No page at `/promo`"), and/or adding a "Go to the dashboard"/"Sign in" link to it — considered 2026-08-23 while planning `docs/plans/gui-pages-error-pages.md`, both rejected. The echo is the most obviously helpful thing the page could say and is the one thing it must not do: it puts request-controlled input into HTML, turning a data-free constant into a template needing escaping, invalidating the "no injection point" argument the CSP decision above rests on, and making the page a reflection surface on one of the app's two most public routes. The detail line names the likely *cause* instead (a short link missing its `/r/`), which is more actionable than repeating the path the visitor just typed. The navigation link loses on audience: the dominant visitor here is the public one who dropped the `/r/` from a shared link, for whom a link to a login page is a dead end that also points the merely curious at the internal console; the console user who mistyped already has the back button. **Revisit trigger for the link only: an actual report of a console user stranded on this page.**
- [ ] `<select multiple>` as the dashboard's multi-tag filter — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`, decided against in favour of a chip input plus a two-option `<select id="tag-rule">`. Attractive because it is native, needs no new component and no keyboard model. Rejected on three counts: it has nowhere to *state* the combining rule, and the Future-work entry that opened this work says the combining rule "is the actual decision, not the widget"; multi-select needs ctrl/cmd-click, which is undiscoverable and effectively unusable on touch; and its rendered height is unpredictable in a filter row `DESIGN.md` has already measured as tight (the links table overflowed its container once at a realistic desktop width). It also offers no type-to-add path, which the chip input gets from `<datalist>` for free once the buffer's whole value is one token. Revisit only if the filter row is redesigned and the rule moves somewhere else.
- [ ] A two-button segmented `role="group"` with `aria-pressed` for the all-of/any-of rule — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`, decided against in favour of a two-option `<select id="tag-rule">`. Genuinely the more legible control (both options visible at rest, and `.theme-toggle` is a shipped precedent for the exact shape). Lost on width — two `min-width: 44px` buttons plus Pico's group borders against one ~110px `<select>`, in the row `DESIGN.md:211` records as having already overflowed — on focus stops (2 vs 1), and because `DESIGN.md:213` already establishes a `<select>` as the affordance in that row (`#tag-filter`, `#owner-filter`). A `<select>`'s rendered value is itself a statement of the rule, which is the property that mattered. Revisit if the filter row ever gets more horizontal budget.
- [ ] Any-of (OR) as the default tag-filter combining rule — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`, decided against; all-of (AND) is the default and any-of is a switch. Attractive because "pick several tags" often means "either" colloquially, and because any-of never returns zero rows when each tag individually matches something. Lost on three counts, the third decisive: any-of *grows* the result set as chips are added, which inverts what a filter means; the tag filter already ANDs with `#links-filter` and `#owner-filter`, so OR-among-chips would put two combining semantics in one row with nothing on screen distinguishing them; and **the filtered set feeds bulk Delete and Reassign** — an operator filtering `q4` + `sale` intending the intersection, getting the union, then select-all → Delete, deletes links they never meant to. That is the same argument that rejected owner substring-matching on 2026-08-04, applied to the same table. All-of can only under-match, which is recoverable. Revisit only if a real workflow needs the union *and* bulk actions are no longer reachable from the filtered set.
- [ ] Exempting input chips from `DESIGN.md`'s sitewide 44px tap-target floor, or extending each chip's hit area past its ink — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`, both decided against; the input chip is a real `<button>` and takes the floor with no exemption and no new CSS to reach it. The narrowed-rule option is the cheapest CSS and the lightest visuals, and `TASKS.md`'s clickable-in-row-chips entry named "DESIGN.md deliberately exempts in-table micro-chips" as its own revisit trigger. Rejected because no exemption is needed — `gui/theme.css`'s sitewide `button` rule already supplies `min-height`/`min-width: 44px`, and the field row is already 44px tall from the `input`/`select`/`textarea` rule, so a 44px chip beside a 44px input adds no height at all — and because `DESIGN.md`'s history is of the floor being *extended* twice (nav anchors at 38.4px, then `<select>`) and never narrowed. The overlay/negative-margin variant (44px hit area, ~24px ink, the `.checkbox-hit` letter) was rejected on its own merits: adjacent chips' hit areas would overlap, so a tap near a boundary removes the **wrong** tag — worse accessibility than the thing it optimises. `.checkbox-hit` works only because its 44×44 wrapper *is* the layout box. **The in-row table chips stay inert `<span>`s regardless; that decision is untouched.**
- [ ] A hand-rolled ARIA combobox/listbox for tag suggestions, replacing the shared `<datalist>` — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`, decided against. Attractive because it could annotate each suggestion with a usage count ("sale (12)") and would not depend on browser `<datalist>` quirks. Rejected because `<datalist>` becomes *honest* the moment the input's whole value is a single token, which is exactly what the chip input makes true — so the last-comma prefix trick this work exists to retire is retired without adding ~150 lines of `aria-activedescendant` keyboard plumbing the app has no other instance of, in a component that is instantiated once per editable table row. Revisit only alongside the deferred "tag counts in the suggestion list" Future-work entry.
- [ ] Converting only some of the four authoring tag inputs to chips (e.g. leaving the bulk bar's field as plain text) — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`, decided against. Less work and less risk per placement. Rejected because `refreshTagDatalist`'s last-comma prefix trick would then have to survive, and retiring it is the stated point of the Future-work entry — and because two different tag-entry idioms on one page is exactly the drift this codebase fixes at the cause rather than the symptom (see the `ALL_PERMISSIONS` fix that stopped the create and edit permission lists from diverging).
- [ ] Bulk slug editing — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-schedule-and-repoint.md`, rejected outright rather than deferred. It was one of three ideas bundled into the "Bulk editing of existing links — destination, schedule, and slug" Future-work entry, and that entry already argued against it: unlike `schedule` and `repoint`, which are pure `slug:<slug>` record rewrites, changing a slug is a **delete plus a create** — two writes with no atomicity, no compare-and-swap, and an interruption window that can leave a link with no record under either name. Worse, it silently breaks every QR code, printed asset and shared URL already in the wild, since there is no redirect-from-old-slug concept in this product and adding one means a new KV key type (with all three obligations that imposes: `backup.py`'s `INDEX_KEYS`/`restore_write_order`, `consistency.py`'s key-shape recognition, and `kvprefix.STORE_PREFIXES`) plus a retention policy for the alias. **What would justify revisiting: a decision to ship slug aliases as a feature in their own right** (old slug keeps resolving, new slug becomes canonical). At that point renaming is a byproduct of aliasing and costs almost nothing extra; before it, renaming is a data-loss tool with a friendly button.
- [ ] Always setting BOTH window sides in a bulk schedule (the bulk-create panel's batch Starts/Expires semantics) — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-schedule-and-repoint.md`, rejected in favour of a per-link merge mirroring `links.handle_update`. Attractive because it sidesteps the merge entirely: one validation, one verdict, no dependence on each record's stored state, and it is exactly what the bulk-*create* controls already do. Lost because on *existing* links it silently destroys data the operator never mentioned — "these 12 links expire Friday" would wipe the start date off every link that had one, visible only after the reload. The objection that a per-link verdict complicates the all-or-nothing rule does not hold: `handle_bulk_action` already has that exact shape in the `too_many_tags` per-row check, which returns `400 bulk_validation_failed` having written nothing. Revisit only if the per-link merge is measured to be confusing in real operator use, and then by improving the row-error copy rather than by clobbering.
- [ ] Skipping `urlpolicy.evaluate` on bulk repoint, on the reasoning that the destination policy is an authoring-time control and repointed links already exist — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-schedule-and-repoint.md`, rejected. Genuinely tempting, because `docs/plans/destination-url-policy.md` says existing violators are reported and never mutated, so "editing an existing link" can be argued to sit outside enforcement. It fails on inspection: `links.handle_update` already enforces the policy on a single-link destination change, so repoint is a bulk edit of the same field on the same records, and exempting it would let any `links.edit_all` holder bypass the policy at 50× throughput behind the organisation's own short domain. The existing-violator carve-out is about links nobody has touched since the rule appeared, not about new destinations chosen after it. Hence `repoint` is the FOURTH enforcement path and `api/tests/test_url_policy_enforcement.py` gained a fourth case. Nothing would justify revisiting this short of removing the policy feature.
- [ ] A new `PATCH /api/links/bulk` endpoint instead of two `handle_bulk_action` variants — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-schedule-and-repoint.md`, rejected. The more REST-shaped answer: a bulk PATCH taking a field map reads better than an `action` discriminator and would extend to future fields for free. Lost on three counts — the user scoped this work as variants on the existing endpoint; `gui/app.js`'s `api.patch` helper would need the whole selection/partial/`not_applied` machinery `handle_bulk_action` already carries, duplicated; and a second bulk endpoint with its own caps and error shapes is precisely the API-inconsistent-with-itself outcome `docs/plans/write-throttle-resilience.md` rejected `207 Multi-Status` over. Revisit only as part of a deliberate whole-API redesign, never for one more action.
- [ ] A client-side pre-check of merged windows against `allLinks` before submitting a bulk schedule — considered 2026-08-24 while planning `docs/plans/bulk-schedule-and-repoint.md`, rejected. The dashboard holds every visible record in memory, so it could grey out the offending rows before a round trip. Lost because it reimplements the server's merge rule in a second language, where the copy can silently drift out of step and would then be wrong in the reassuring direction. The existing `wireWindowValidation` already catches the one case needing no stored state (both inputs filled and inverted), and the server's per-row error carries both merged dates, so the round trip explains itself with real values rather than a guess.
- [ ] Table-driving `handle_bulk_action`'s per-action payload validation (an `ActionSpec.prepare` coroutine per action) — considered 2026-08-25 while planning `docs/plans/unify-bulk-write-loops.md`, rejected as part of that change. Attractive because it would make "an action added with no validation" as structurally impossible as "an action added with no write branch" now is. Lost because the four payload blocks share nothing: `reassign` awaits a user lookup on the users store, `tag`/`untag` parse a tag list, `repoint` awaits `urlpolicy.load_policy` and runs two checks, `schedule` parses two window fields by key presence — each returns a different 4xx body. A uniform `prepare` hook would be eight bespoke functions behind one signature: the same code, one indirection further from the reader. They are also independent `if` guards with no catch-all, so unlike the write dispatch they never had a fall-through hazard. The one genuinely uniform piece, the permission check, IS hoisted onto the spec as `ActionSpec.required_permission`. Revisit only when a future action's validation is actually uniform with an existing one's, at which point move just that shared piece onto the spec the same way.
- [ ] Folding `handle_bulk_create`'s record-write loop into the shared `_apply_mutations` loop — considered 2026-08-25 while planning `docs/plans/unify-bulk-write-loops.md`, rejected. Attractive because it is a ninth copy of the same try/`write`/`except kvretry.WriteFailed`/break/append shape. Lost because it is ONE loop, not eight — there is no duplication to remove there — and its failure report is a different shape: `not_created` rows carry `line` numbers derived from `assigned[idx:]`, and the success body needs the `created_records` list for `links.public_link`. Sharing would force `_apply_mutations` to return a failure *index* and both callers to reconstruct their own reports from it: more coupling, wider blast radius, nothing deduplicated. Revisit only if a second create-shaped bulk path ever appears.
- [ ] Planning each bulk mutation lazily inside the write loop instead of materialising the list first — considered 2026-08-25 while planning `docs/plans/unify-bulk-write-loops.md`, rejected. Attractive because it preserves today's exact plan/write interleaving, so a record the loop never reaches is never even mutated in memory. Lost because it puts the `ActionSpec` — and therefore the action name — back inside the write loop, which is precisely the property the change buys: with planning hoisted, `_apply_mutations` has no way to know what action it is serving and `test_apply_mutations_takes_no_action_parameter` can say so. The delta it costs is in-memory-only and unobservable — the store is the only observable surface and it is untouched, pinned by the existing `after3 == before3` assertions in the repoint/schedule ThrottlingStore tests. Revisit only if a planner ever gains a side effect outside the record dict, which would make the interleaving observable.
- [ ] A contentless `ev=record_unreadable` line (slug only), leaving `linkgate.Resolve`'s error contract untouched — considered 2026-08-25 while planning `docs/plans/disposition-unreadable-logging.md`, rejected. This was the shape the Future-work entry itself filed, and it is genuinely attractive: zero contract change, no rewrite of `TestResolve_ErrorIsNilForEveryOtherDisposition`, no question about what a decoder message might echo from the record, and it still answers "which slug", which is what an operator needs in order to go fix it. **It lost because the operator's very next question is "why", and nothing in the application answers it.** `api/consistency.py` appends `{"store", "key"}` with no reason (lines 203/212/240/254), `api/links.py`'s `UnreadableLinkError` carries the slug, and `Resolve` discards the one real answer — `json.Unmarshal`'s error — before any caller sees it. A truncated write (`unexpected end of JSON input`) and a schema mismatch between what `api` writes and what `linkgate.Link` expects (`json: cannot unmarshal number into Go struct field Link.status of type string`) need different fixes, and a contentless line makes the operator reproduce the parse by hand to learn which one it is — which on a deployment means the KV explorer, and that is dev-only. The contract change is two tokens plus an honest doc comment, and the invariant it breaks ("non-nil error ONLY alongside `DispositionUnavailable`") is one no caller actually relies on, because both handlers switch on the disposition before ever reading the error. Revisit only if a decoder message is ever observed carrying record content worth keeping out of a 7-day retention window.
- [ ] Wrapping `Resolve`'s parse error in a sentinel (`ErrUnreadableRecord` / `errors.Join` / `fmt.Errorf("%w")`) so `errors.Is` can still separate a store failure from a corrupt record — considered 2026-08-25 while planning `docs/plans/disposition-unreadable-logging.md`, rejected. Attractive because it keeps a mechanically *checkable* invariant instead of a documented convention, now that a non-nil error can arrive with two different dispositions. Rejected twice over: the `Disposition` already separates them exhaustively and visibly in a `switch`, so a sentinel is a redundant second discriminator that can drift out of agreement with the first; and wrapping destroys the `%T` classification the new log line's `etype` field gets for free (`*json.SyntaxError` vs `*json.UnmarshalTypeError`), replacing it with exactly the kind of hand-maintained English-string table `classifyKVFailure` only has because `spin-go-sdk` flattens the WIT error variant and leaves it no alternative. `TestResolve_UnreadableErrorIsUnwrapped` pins the no-wrapping rule with a `%T` assertion.
- [ ] A parallel dedup map/mutex/cap in `redirect/main.go` dedicated to `ev=record_unreadable`, leaving `shouldEmitFailureLine` untouched — considered 2026-08-25 while planning `docs/plans/disposition-unreadable-logging.md`, rejected. It respects "don't touch the existing failure-line path" most literally. Rejected because two independent 32-entry budgets make the instance's real stderr bound 64, growing with every future event kind, and the duplicated mutex/map/cap trio is precisely the code a later reader would be right to consolidate. Moving only the *key construction* out of the shared function — into `linkgate.KVFailureDedupKey` and `linkgate.RecordUnreadableDedupKey`, where it is host-testable — is both the smaller change and the one that makes "what counts as novel" a per-line-kind decision instead of a hardcoded `(op, msg)`.

- [x] **The mobile column-hiding rule also hides the edit form AND the empty state, so below 600px editing is unreachable and an over-filtered table explains nothing** — found 2026-08-24 while verifying `docs/plans/tag-ux-chips-and-filtering.md`; **pre-existing and unrelated to tags** (confirmed: the rule is untouched by that diff). `gui/dashboard.css`'s `@media (max-width: 600px)` block hides `#links-table td:nth-child(1)` to drop the select-checkbox column — but the edit row is `<tr class="edit-row"><td colspan="10">` and the empty state is `<tr><td colspan="10" class="empty-state">`, and each is `nth-child(1)` **of its own `<tr>`**, so both are hidden too. **Reproduced in a real browser at 390px, not inferred from the CSS:** the edit row's `<td>` computes `display: none` with height 0 and its `<form>` is unreachable, and with a filter matching nothing the message "No links match your filter." is `display: none` with the whole `#links-body` rendering at **0 height** — a blank table with no explanation. **The second half is newly worse:** the tag-UX plan deliberately added empty-state copy naming the active all-of/any-of rule precisely so an over-narrow filter explains itself, and that copy is invisible on the viewport where a mistaken filter is easiest to make. The fix is cheap and the hook already exists — the edit row already carries `.edit-row`, so scoping the hide (e.g. `#links-table tr:not(.edit-row) td:nth-child(1)`, plus an equivalent for `.empty-state`) is CSS-only; heed DESIGN.md's repeated warning about specificity traps in this file, and re-measure at 1400/768/480/390 in both themes afterwards. **Trigger: none needed — a plain bug, filed rather than fixed only because it is outside the tag work's scope.** — **FIXED 2026-08-24.** One-token guard: `#links-table td:nth-child(1)` became `#links-table td:nth-child(1):not([colspan])`, on the principle that a cell spanning every column is not a column, so a column-hiding rule must never match it. Deliberately NOT the neighbouring `tbody > tr:not(.edit-row)` idiom already used by the nth-child(2)/(6) width rules in the same file — that idiom misses the empty state, whose `<tr>` carries no class, which is exactly how this survived. Guarding only nth-child(1) is sufficient because a single-cell full-width row can never be any other child index. **Verified in a real browser, including the negative check that matters:** at 390px and at 480px in both themes the checkbox column is still hidden (the rule's actual purpose survives), the edit form is reachable (706px tall, was 0), and the empty state renders with its text (36px, was 0). At 768px in both themes the rule is correctly inactive and the edit form works; 1400px was not probed separately because the change lives inside `@media (max-width: 600px)` and provably cannot apply above it. `#links-figure` scrolling at 768px (1074/676) is pre-existing and by design — it is `overflow-x: auto` and the page itself measures 753/753. `#users-table` was checked and is NOT exposed: it hides only nth-child(3), and a full-width cell is always nth-child(1).**

- [x] **Concurrent bulk creates lose index updates, and retry cannot fix it — MEASURED 2026-08-17, FIXED AND VERIFIED 2026-08-18.** Closed by `docs/plans/derived-link-indexes.md`, both stages shipped, deployed and traced: the indexes are gone entirely, so there is no shared read-modify-write key left to clobber. The same 4-concurrent-create run that produced 10 `unindexed_link` + 10 `unindexed_owner_link` now leaves `ok: true` with zero findings on the deployed build, and concurrent bulk *deletes* are clean too. Of the four options this entry listed, the one taken was "make `all_links` derivable rather than authoritative" — and it went further, deleting the keys rather than merely not trusting them. Original entry follows. Raised by the write-throttle trace (see `### DEPLOYED AND TRACED (2026-08-17)` below), which set out to confirm "a throttled bulk run leaves zero `unindexed_link`" and found the opposite under concurrency. **The control run is the important part: 4 concurrent 5-row creates, ~28 writes, far under the 50/s cap, all four `201` with zero retries and zero write failures — and still 5 `unindexed_link`.** A later 2-request, ~10-write run lost an entire request's 3 additions, so the threshold is roughly "any two overlapping bulk creates", not "a busy store". Reproduce either with `dev/bulk-concurrent.sh`. `links:all_links` and `links:owner_links:<owner>` are read-modify-write with no compare-and-swap, so concurrent requests clobber each other's index additions; last writer wins. This is **independent of throttling** and therefore untouched by every retry constant in `api/kvretry.py`. **Both incidents that motivated the write-throttle work were reproduced with concurrent bulk creates**, so this is a demonstrated contributor to them, not a hypothetical. Options, none costed yet and none obviously right: serialise index writes behind a single owner; make `all_links` derivable rather than authoritative (it is already only an index — `handle_list` tolerates missing entries, and the consistency repair rebuilds it in one write); shard the index the way the click counter was sharded; or accept it and lean on the repair tool, which fixed 65 findings in 2 writes. **Do not reach for retry — the control run proves nothing was failing.**
- [ ] **Find out what Akamai's actual KV write-failure message is — `write_error` reports `other`, not `throttled` (2026-08-17).** Every failed write in the traced run classified as `other`. The classifier is not at fault: `str()` on a faithful reconstruction of `Err(Error_Other(value='too many requests'))` does surface the message, so `api/tests/fakes.py`'s stand-in is accurate and the substring match would fire on it. Akamai's real message is therefore different, **and nothing anywhere logs the exception string** — not the log line, not the response. Control flow is deliberately unaffected (every write error retries regardless), so this is an observability gap, not a correctness one: an incident report says `other` and names nothing. Fix needs a diagnostic build surfacing `repr(exc.cause)` on the partial response or in the log line, deployed, and one concurrent bulk run to capture it — then either widen `classify_write_error`'s match or record that the message is unstable. Note the standing rule this must not break: the match is **observability-only** and must never become control flow.
- [x] **A memoised `list_keys` hit is still counted as a KV op, inflating `kv_ops` — MEASURED 2026-08-17, FIXED 2026-08-18.** Fixed by the second option this entry named: `scoped_list_keys` no longer records an op when the underlying call never reached the host. The memoisation moved from a private closure in `api/app.py` (untestable — `app.py` is excluded from pytest) into `kvprefix.memoized_raw_list_keys`, which sets a `cache_hit` attribute that `scoped_list_keys` reads via `getattr(..., False)` so every non-memoized call site is untouched. Mutation-verified: recording cache hits again fails `test_memoized_cache_hit_records_no_kv_operation` with `assert 2 == 1`, the exact traced symptom. Original entry follows. `GET /api/analytics/click-totals` traces as `list_keys=2` on the `55dea50-derived-reads` build even though only one raw walk occurs: the two ops total 26,400 µs while the slowest single one is 26,396 µs, so the second is a 4 µs memoised hit. CLAUDE.md defines `kv_ops` as counting **host** operations, and a memoised hit is not one — so this both overstates `kv_ops` and, worse, tells a reader the whole-store walk happens twice per request when it happens once. Cost is unaffected; this is purely observability, which is why it was filed rather than fixed during a measurement deploy. Fix is in `api/app.py`'s per-request memoisation wrapper (record the op only on a miss) or in `api/obs.py` (a distinct op name for a cache hit, e.g. `list_keys_cached`, which keeps the hit visible without pretending it cost a round trip). **Whichever is chosen, re-trace afterwards** — the point of the field is that a reader can trust it. Note this becomes more misleading, not less, once Stage 2 lands and the enumeration is the only way the app learns which links exist.
- [ ] **A single-link DELETE returned `200` but did not remove the record — SEEN ONCE, 2026-08-18.** During the M2 probe on `88f4f4c-no-indexes`, slug `m2t01` was created, deleted, and was still present in `GET /api/links` and still returning **302** from `/r/m2t01` minutes later; a second DELETE removed it cleanly. **It did not recur in 10 further create-then-immediately-delete cycles, all of which returned `200` and removed the record.** The probe did not capture the failing DELETE's status code, so the cause is unknown. Most plausible reading: a create→delete race where the DELETE's own record `get` did not yet see the just-written record, so it 404'd and deleted nothing — which would make the observed "200" a mis-memory and the real response a 404, or would mean the delete write itself was lost. **Do not treat either explanation as established.** Reproducing needs a loop that records the DELETE's status code AND an `X-SS-Debug` trace (the `delete=` op count in the log line distinguishes the two: a 404-and-do-nothing shows no `delete` op at all, a lost write shows `delete=1`). Note this is NOT the same phenomenon as the sub-second redirect staleness recorded alongside it in the M2 section — that one self-heals in under a second and this one persisted until a second DELETE.
- [ ] **[CLOSED 2026-08-19, see `docs/plans/redirect-read-failure-not-404.md` and CLAUDE.md's "The `/r/{slug}` status contract" — a KV read failure now answers `503` + `Retry-After: 2`, never `404`.]** **A live link returns 404 when the KV read fails — MEASURED 2026-08-18, a correctness bug under load.** `lookupLink` (`redirect/main.go`) collapses a KV *failure* and a genuinely *absent* link into one `false` (`if err != nil || len(raw) == 0`), so the caller answers `http.NotFound`. Measured on `43d66c6-no-events` with `hey -disable-redirects`: clean at 690 req/s, **7% of requests wrongly 404 at 726 rps, 31% at 947, 43% at 1292**, with the link resolving normally at rest immediately afterwards. A successful redirect performs 2 KV gets, so ~700 rps is ~1,400 reads/second against Akamai's documented 1,000 — this is read-path saturation surfacing as a lie about the link. **Why it deserves a fix rather than a note:** a 404 is a claim about the *link*, not the server, and this codebase deliberately makes it indistinguishable from a disabled or expired link (a probing-resistance feature, "Security tradeoffs"), so a visitor is told a live campaign URL is dead. `Cache-Control: no-store` is the only reason it does not also get cached. **The fix is a judgement call and wants its own plan**, not a one-line patch: options are a `503` with `Retry-After` (honest, but a new status on the hot path), a bounded retry (adds latency to the one path the repo protects hardest, and `redirect` deliberately has no retry today — see "Write-throttle resilience" Trade-offs #2), or threading an explicit absent-vs-unreadable distinction out of `lookupLink`. Note the same collapse exists for an unparseable record (`ParseLink` error), which the API side already treats as a *reportable* condition (`unreadable_value`). **Cheap first step if this is picked up: the traced log line already distinguishes them** — a failed get shows as a `get` op with `status=404`, so a deployed build with `log_level=summary` could confirm whether this ever happens in real traffic before anyone designs a fix.

See CLAUDE.md's "Deployment: known Akamai Functions blocker" section for the confirmed finding and exact prefix scheme. Touches `spin.toml`, `redirect/main.go`'s `kv.Open` calls, `api/app.py`'s `key_value.open` calls, and every key literal across both components' non-test and test code. — **SCHEDULED 2026-08-04**, see `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md`. The create-link form should show a domain multi-select (checkboxes: one, several, or all of the user's assigned domains) only when the user has any assigned domains at all. One design question deliberately left open for whenever this is actually picked up, not resolved now: whether `redirect`'s hot path should validate the incoming `Host` header against a link's `domain` (an extra server-side check) or treat `domain` purely as display/QR metadata, since `/r/{slug}` resolution is currently Host-header-agnostic. - [x] Add a `links.edit_all` permission letting non-admin users edit/delete/password-protect other users' links — raised and implemented 2026-07-24. Plan confirmed with the user before writing (below), then built and verified end-to-end.
  - **Backend** — file(s): api/auth.py, api/links.py, api/analytics.py, api/qr.py — done when: added `"links.edit_all"` to `KNOWN_PERMISSIONS`; added two shared helpers in `links.py` — `can_view(principal, record)` (owner OR `links.view_all` OR `links.edit_all` OR admin) and `_can_edit(principal, record)` (owner OR `links.edit_all` OR admin, module-private since only `links.py` needs write-gating) — replacing five duplicated owner-or-admin checks across `handle_list`/`handle_get`/`handle_update`/`handle_delete`/`handle_set_password`. Fixed each 403 body's `required_permission` field to name whichever permission is actually checked at that call site (`links.view_all` for view-gated paths, `links.edit_all` for edit-gated ones) instead of all four hardcoding `links.view_all`.
  - **Pre-existing bug fixed** (found during planning, confirmed in scope): `handle_get`/`handle_update`/`handle_delete`/`handle_set_password` previously gated non-owner access on `principal.role != "admin"` only — none actually checked `links.view_all`, even though `handle_list` already used it to decide list visibility. A `links.view_all` user saw Edit/Delete/View buttons for links they didn't own, and every one of those buttons 403'd. Now fixed via `can_view`.

Fixed by importing and reusing the same `can_view` helper from `links.py` in both files (no cyclic import risk — both already imported `get_link` from `links.py`). Added matching regression tests to `api/tests/test_analytics.py` and `api/tests/test_qr.py`.

Sequenced `loadMe()` before `loadLinks()` (previously concurrent) since `renderLinksTable()` now reads `currentPrincipal` — running them in parallel risked a first-paint race where even the owner's own Edit/Delete buttons could render hidden. `links/detail.html` mirrors the same `canEdit` logic for its Edit button, sequencing `initHeader()` before `loadLinkInfo()` for the same reason.

Fixed by defaulting both buttons to `display: none` in the markup and only revealing Copy unconditionally (reaching that line already implies `can_view` passed) and Edit conditionally on the success path — fail-closed instead of fail-open.
  - **Verified live via Playwright**, not just via the test suite: created three real non-admin test users (`links.edit_all` only, `links.view_all` only, no permissions) against a link owned by `admin`, logged in as each, and confirmed: the `edit_all` user sees "All links", full View/Copy/Edit/Delete, can actually PATCH the link via the real API, and the detail page's QR/analytics/Edit all load with zero console errors; the `view_all`-only user sees "All links" and the link with View/Copy only (Edit/Delete correctly hidden), and the detail page loads fully (QR, analytics, Details) with Edit hidden; the no-permissions user sees "Your links" with the link absent entirely, and direct navigation to its detail page shows the existing friendly 403 error with the button group empty (no dangling Copy/Edit).

Akamai Functions publishes a 30 s request-handler duration and a **50 KV write RPS** cap, so a restore at the existing `MAX_BACKUP_ENTRIES = 5_000` cap needs roughly 100 s of writes and cannot complete inside a single request — even though the identical restore measured 84 ms locally (see the KV backup and restore verification note above, which is exactly the "timing evidence, not a hunch" baseline that rule asked for, taken on the wrong host). Export is read-bound and safer (1,000 read RPS) but has no entry cap of its own, only a 5 MiB body cap, and a store with many `analytics:events:` keys enumerates and reads far more than 5,000 keys. Trigger: a deployment whose real data exceeds what one request can move inside 30 s — measure against the deployed round-trip timings recorded by the consolidation's Akamai smoke test before designing anything.

It is deliberately never passed to `backup.handle_restore` — the exact caveat this entry names, since restore enumerates AFTER writing to compute its prune set and a pre-write snapshot would silently change what it prunes. **What remains is the backup/export case this entry was originally about** (three full walks per backup), which needs that restore hazard handled rather than avoided. Original entry: raised 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` and rejected for that change (see "Considered and rejected"). Must not be done without first handling `backup.handle_restore`'s post-write `list_keys` call, which relies on a fresh enumeration to compute the prune set. — **Now priced, 2026-08-10:** an enumeration costs **~68.7 µs per physical key, linearly** (see the measurement section at the end of this file), so each walk this would eliminate is worth ~66 ms at today's 962 keys and ~690 ms at 10,000. It helps `consistency.collect` (2 walks) and `backup` (3), and **does nothing for `/api/analytics/click-totals`, which makes only one walk and is the path that runs on every dashboard load** — so this is no longer the fix for the risk that motivated it. **A prefix-scoped enumeration is confirmed not to exist** (`get-keys()` takes no arguments in either SDK), so the only remaining lever for `click-totals` is avoiding the walk entirely.

Before consolidation the same key would have surfaced as `unrecognized_key`.
