- [x] Reduce the redirect hot path from two KV data operations to one — raised 2026-08-04 while planning `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md` and deliberately excluded from it. `lookupLink` (`redirect/main.go:147`) does `Exists("slug:"+slug)` then `Get("slug:"+slug)`; a `nil` `Get` already means absent, so the `Exists` is removable. Separately, `recordAnalytics` opens the store a second time on every recorded click rather than receiving the handler's already-open one. Both are performance changes and want real timing evidence from the deployed Akamai app, not a local hunch. — **MEASURED ON AKAMAI 2026-08-06, and the result inverts the local reasoning.** With the logging build deployed and `X-SS-Debug` tracing a real click, the per-operation split is `open=2/307µs exists=1/21677µs get=2/42460µs set=2/52251µs` (means over 6 traced redirects; `kv_us≈116.7ms` of `dur_us≈120.4ms`, so **KV is ~97% of handler time**). Two consequences: (1) **`kv.Open` is nearly free on Akamai — ~154 µs each, versus 12–33 µs locally — so removing `recordAnalytics`'s second open saves ~0.2% and is NOT worth doing.** That half of this entry should be dropped; the local measurement that made it look like an 8–20% win does not transfer. (2) **Dropping the `Exists` in `lookupLink` is worth ~21.7 ms, about 19% of the redirect's KV time**, and is the real optimisation here. Data operations run 1,400–3,000× slower than local (exists 21.7 ms vs 13–18 µs, get 21.2 ms vs 5–9 µs, set 26.1 ms vs 5–12 µs) while `open` is only ~7× slower — so on Akamai the cost is per *data operation*, not per store handle. This entry now has the deployed timing evidence it was waiting for; re-scope it to the `Exists` removal alone before building anything. — **DONE 2026-08-06, re-scoped to the `Exists` removal only.** `lookupLink` now performs a single `Get`: the SDK returns `([]byte(""), nil)` for a missing key, so absence is detected with an explicit `len(raw) == 0` check rather than a prior `Exists` probe. A successful redirect drops **7 → 6** operations; a miss stays at **2** (`open` counts, so it swapped `exists` for `get`). **Deployed and measured: 5.2 ms of 38.8 ms, 13.5%**, compared like-for-like against the 7-op build in the same latency window — NOT against the 116.7 ms figure that motivated the change, because Akamai KV latency swung 3× between those two windows and attributing that swing to this edit would be wrong. One operation's worth, ~14%, is the durable claim. The `kv.Open` half of this entry was **deliberately not done** — measurement showed it is ~0.2% on Akamai, not the 8–20% the local numbers implied. Verified locally across all three paths (302 hit, 404 nonexistent, 404 disabled link) with the op counts read off the log lines.

Locally this was invisible: the same three operations cost ~19 µs of an 80 µs budget. **No obvious fix exists** — a Spin/WASI handler has no after-response hook and the instance may be torn down once it returns, so "record it asynchronously" is not automatically available and needs a spike before it is a plan. Options worth costing: dropping the `events:` ring-buffer write on the hot path (1 of the 2 sets, ~26 ms, and it is already documented as a lossy best-effort sample), or accepting the latency. Do not start without measuring whether a post-response write is possible at all. — **DONE 2026-08-06. All analytics now runs after the response**, cutting median untraced warm-connection TTFB from **98.0 ms to 74.3 ms (~24 ms)**. The stated blocker — that WASI offers no after-response hook — turned out not to bind: `wasiHandle` hands the response to the host as soon as the first `Write` calls `send()`, so post-response work runs while the response travels. Two things were needed: the 302 is now **bodyless with an explicit `Content-Length: 0`** (its courtesy body had no length, so a client could not tell the message was complete until the stream closed, which only happens when the handler returns), and the empty `Write` is load-bearing because `Write`, not `WriteHeader`, is what calls `send()`. **A wrong turn worth recording:** an intermediate 'split' (count before the response, event after) was built and deployed on the belief that deferring the count lost clicks — 8 of 10, twice. A controlled A/B disproved it (85/100 not deferred vs 86/100 deferred); at the real ~85% baseline rate those readings were ordinary noise, and the split's own gain was ~5.5 ms, inside the noise band. The lesson: a ~15% background loss rate makes any 10-sample accuracy comparison worthless.

Two claims in the text below are now known to be **wrong** and are kept only because this is the record of how the question was opened, not a live specification: (1) the loss curve's 34/s and 65/s rows are contaminated by the app-wide write cap and describe a different mechanism entirely; (2) the "stale read across instances" mechanism guess was never confirmed and the measured evidence fits per-key read-modify-write overlap, which is what sharding fixes. **The "~25 redirects/second is academic" framing at the end is explicitly retracted** — it is the real and now sole binding constraint. - [ ] **[CLOSED, see the "Click-count accuracy (sharded analytics counters)" section below — `CountShards = 64` fixed the per-key contention this entry measured; confirmed live at both 9.4/s (0.5% loss, against 25% pre-sharding) and 34/s.]** ~~Fix Akamai click under-counting~~ — `analytics:count` loses ~15% under rapid sequential requests — raised 2026-08-06 from the analytics-deferral A/B and **the most product-significant finding of that exercise**. Measured against the live deployment: 25 rapid sequential requests from a *single* client recorded 21–22, reproducibly (85/100 and 86/100 across two builds). CLAUDE.md previously claimed `count.total` was "exactly accurate" and that only the recent-events log was lossy; that was true of the local sqlite store (20/20 in the same test) and false on Akamai. **It is ordering-independent** — the A/B moved the write before and after the response and changed nothing — because `analytics:count:<slug>` is a read-modify-write and Spin's KV has no compare-and-swap. It cannot be resequenced away and needs a different counter shape. Options to cost: sharded counters (`analytics:count:<slug>:<n>` summed at read time, trading a wider read for a narrower race, and multiplying key count against the 2 GB store cap); append-only click keys aggregated on read (exact, but unbounded growth and an expensive read); or accepting the loss and documenting the real number. **The loss curve has now been measured — do that no more; design the fix.** **Measured loss curve (2026-08-06, live deployment, 20 requests per condition, fresh link):** 0.5/s → 0%, 0.9/s → 0%, 1.6/s → 0%, 2.7/s → 0%, **9.4/s → 25%**, 34/s → 70%, 65/s → 75%. **There is a cliff, not a gradient: zero loss across 80 requests at or below ~2.7/s, severe loss above ~9/s.** The losses are permanent, not eventual-consistency lag — a 25-request burst recorded 19 and was still 19 at t+60s. A simple local read-modify-write collision model does not fit (it over-predicts at low rates and under-predicts saturation), so the likelier mechanism is a stale read across instances — request N+1's `get` not yet seeing request N's `set`, with a propagation window on the order of 100 ms. **The mechanism is unconfirmed and does not change the options**, since both candidate fixes address either cause. **The practical headline: this app's click analytics is trustworthy below ~3 clicks/second and unusable above ~9.** That also makes the '~25 redirects/second write-RPS ceiling' recorded elsewhere in this file academic — at 25/s roughly 70% of clicks are already being lost, long before any write cap binds. Sharded counters divide the collision probability by the shard count and keep a bounded key space; append-only click keys eliminate the read entirely and so cannot lose an update at all, at the cost of unbounded growth and an expensive aggregation on read. Verify any fix against this same curve, on a fresh link, at 9.4/s and 34/s where the effect is unambiguous.

**PROBE RESULT 2026-08-06 — the plan's gating probe was RUN and PASSED, but its design had a confound worth recording.** Run as specified (16 slugs, 38.5 req/s aggregate) it showed 32.5% loss and looked like a failure. That run was measuring the **app-wide write cap**, not key contention: 38.5 req/s x 2 writes = 77 writes/s against Akamai's published 50 write RPS. Re-run under the cap, the signal is unambiguous — **1 slug at 9.4 req/s (18.8 writes/s) loses 25%, while 16 slugs at 9.2 req/s aggregate (18.5 writes/s, same app-wide write load) lose 0%**; 16 slugs at 19.7 req/s (39.4 writes/s) also lose 0%. Identical write rate, one hot key versus sixteen: sharding works.

**There are TWO independent mechanisms and the original single-slug curve blended them:** (1) per-key contention on one hot counter, which sharding fixes; (2) app-wide write throttling above ~50 writes/s = **~25 clicks/second**, which sharding cannot fix and which only fewer writes per click would move. **Any future probe must hold aggregate writes/s below 50, or it measures mechanism 2 and tells you nothing about mechanism 1.**

**This also retracts a claim made earlier the same day in this file and in CLAUDE.md: that the ~25 redirects/second write-RPS ceiling is 'academic'. It is not — it is the real, measured, app-wide ceiling**, and the 70%-loss-at-25/s figure that motivated calling it academic came from single-slug runs confounded by per-key contention.

- [x] Find the real cause of the analytics recent-events slot collisions, and correct CLAUDE.md's explanation — raised 2026-08-06 while measuring for `docs/plans/toggleable-logging.md`. CLAUDE.md's Analytics section attributes the collisions to "the WASI clock having deliberately limited resolution"; measurement found the opposite — consecutive `time.Now()` calls differ by 750–1000 ns in Go and 400–800 ns in Python, `time.get_clock_info('monotonic')` reports `clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC)` at 1 µs, and requests 15–18 ms apart received distinct microsecond-resolution wall-clock timestamps, so requests 300 ms apart cannot possibly share a `UnixMilli` value. `linkgate.EventSlot`'s hashing is the obvious suspect and has never been examined against real timestamps. **Do not correct the documentation without finding the cause**, or the section will simply assert a different unverified thing. — **CAUSE FOUND 2026-08-07**, incidentally, while mutation-testing `ShardFor`'s new timestamp-distribution test (see the sharding section below). It is `EventSlot`'s hashing, and it is arithmetic aliasing, not the clock. `EventSlot` is `(unixNano × 2654435761) mod numSlots`. Multiplication distributes over the modulo, so for two clicks Δ nanoseconds apart the slot advances by a **constant stride** of `(Δ × 2654435761) mod numSlots`, and the reachable slots are therefore just one additive cycle of length `numSlots / gcd(stride, numSlots)` — never the full ring. The multiplier is ≡ 1 (mod 30), so the stride collapses to `Δ mod 30`, and every millisecond-scale Δ is divisible by high powers of 2 and 5 while `30 = 2·3·5` shares them. Verified numerically against the real formula: at the default `numSlots=30`, clicks **1 ms apart reach only 3 of 30 slots** (stride 10) and clicks **300 ms apart reach exactly 1** (stride 0); 1 s and 107 ms also give 3. This reproduces the exact documented observation ("8 requests spaced 300 ms apart retained only 3 distinct events") without invoking clock resolution at all — the timestamps are perfectly distinct, they just alias onto the same slots. It is also not confined to 30: at `numSlots=16` every millisecond-scale spacing reaches **1** slot, which is what the Go mutation test showed as 100,000/100,000 draws into shard 0. **DOCUMENTATION CORRECTED 2026-08-07**, together with the sharding section's "Document both mechanisms" task as planned — CLAUDE.md's Analytics section now carries the stride/gcd derivation and the spacing-vs-slots table, and explicitly retracts the clock-resolution claim. **Both halves of this item — find the cause, correct the documentation — are therefore done.** What remains is not investigation but the actual code fix to `EventSlot`, which is the separate OPTIONAL task above; `splitmix64` (already in `linkgate` as `mix64`) is the fix, and is immune because a finalizer with xorshifts is not linear over the modulus and so has no constant stride.

Reading `net/http`'s `ServeMux` wildcard behaviour, a wildcard value is the *unescaped* segment, so `/r/a%20b` would emit `slug=a b` and split one logfmt field into two; a `%0A` would be worse. **UNCONFIRMED** — it needs a live `spin up` build with an induced `open`/`get` failure (the documented technique is temporarily removing `key_value_stores` from `[component.redirect]` in `spin.toml`) and a request to a percent-encoded slug. The new `ev=record_unreadable` line is NOT affected: reaching that arm requires a stored record at `links:slug:<slug>`, and only `api` writes those, always against `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$`. Fix if confirmed: reject or escape a slug that does not match that same pattern before it reaches a log field — `redirect/linkgate/` is the right home for the predicate, since `package main` is not host-testable. **Trigger: confirmation, or any log-analysis tooling that parses these lines as logfmt.**

## Security response headers

- [x] Add security response headers (CSP, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `X-Frame-Options`, HSTS) to all 3 routable surfaces — raised 2026-07-25 (a `CLAUDE.md`-documented gap since Phase 5). Plan confirmed with the user before writing: research first established that `spin_static_fs.wasm` (the `gui` component serving all of `gui/`) supports only a `CACHE_CONTROL` env var and has zero custom-header capability at all — confirmed both via web search of upstream `spin-fileserver` docs and by reading `spin.toml` directly. Since security headers are only meaningful on the navigated document itself (not a `.js`/`.css` subresource), the user chose to split the GUI's routes rather than replace the static-fileserver wholesale: keep `spin_static_fs.wasm` for the genuinely static assets, add one new small component for just the HTML pages.
- [x] **New `gui-pages` component** (Python, `componentize-py`, same toolchain as `api` since this isn't a hot path) — file(s): gui-pages/app.py, gui-pages/routing.py, gui-pages/tests/test_routing.py, gui-pages/pyproject.toml, spin.toml — done when: `routing.py` holds a fixed path→file allowlist (`/`, `/index.html`, `/login.html`, `/dashboard.html`, `/admin/users.html`, `/links/detail.html` → the 5 real HTML files) and the shared `SECURITY_HEADERS` dict; `build_response(uri, read_file)` takes the file-read as an injected callable so it's host-testable without real file I/O (mirrors `api/responses.py`'s `Request`/`Response`-dataclass pattern for the same reason — keeps everything except the real WASI entrypoint `app.py` unit-testable). Because it's a fixed, known allowlist rather than a general-purpose static file server, there's no dynamic filesystem path resolution against request input and therefore no path-traversal surface to defend, unlike a hand-rolled general fileserver would have. 14 new tests in `gui-pages/tests/test_routing.py`, all passing.
- [x] **`spin.toml` routing split** — done when: `gui` (spin_static_fs.wasm) narrowed to 3 exact routes (`/app.js`, `/theme.css`, `/vendor/pico.min.css`); `gui-pages` takes over the `/...` catch-all. Confirmed via Spin's own docs that route specificity (not declaration order) decides precedence, so the 3 exact routes correctly win over the new catch-all for those paths. **Two real gotchas found and worked around during implementation, not anticipated in the plan**: (1) a directory `files` mapping to a non-root destination (`{ source = "gui/vendor", destination = "/vendor" }`, to narrow `gui`'s virtual filesystem for tidiness) 404'd live despite matching Spin's own documented file-mapping semantics — reverted to the original `{ source = "gui", destination = "/" }` full mapping, which still works correctly since the narrowed *routes* (not the files list) are what actually restrict reachability; (2) confirmed live that once the `gui` component has more than one trigger route, `spin_static_fs`'s internal path resolution breaks specifically for wildcard (`/...`) routes — a `/vendor/...` wildcard 404'd on every request, while the identical file under the exact route `/vendor/pico.min.css` served correctly. Since `vendor/NOTICE.txt` is never referenced by any page (confirmed via grep), one exact route fully covers this directory's real usage.
- [x] **Headers added to `api`** — file(s): api/responses.py, api/qr.py — done when: `json_response`'s shared header-merge now includes a new `SECURITY_HEADERS` dict (`default-src 'none'` CSP, appropriate for a pure JSON API that should never render/execute/frame). Also fixed `qr.py`'s one direct `Response(...)` construction, which bypassed `json_response` entirely and would otherwise have missed these headers on every QR-code response. `uv run pytest` — 131 tests, unchanged pass count (no strict header-equality assertions anywhere in the suite to break).
- [x] **Headers added to `redirect`** — file(s): redirect/main.go, redirect/passwordgate.go — done when: a `setSecurityHeaders` helper, called from the `spinhttp.Handle` closure before dispatching to the mux, sets the baseline 4 headers on every response (redirects and error pages alike — `http.Error`/`http.NotFound`/`http.Redirect` only ever `Header().Set` their own specific keys, never clearing the whole map, so these survive). `renderPasswordPrompt` additionally sets its own stricter CSP (`script-src 'none'` — the page has zero `<script>` tags, confirmed by reading `prompt.html`; `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` for its one inline `style="color: red"` error attribute). `go test ./linkgate/...` unaffected (main.go/passwordgate.go aren't host-testable either way).
- [x] **A real CSP violation found and fixed during live verification, not anticipated in the plan**: `gui-pages`'s initial CSP used `img-src 'self'`, which broke live with 3 confirmed CSP-violation console errors — Pico CSS renders several UI affordances (sortable-column chevrons, the search-box icon, the datetime-local calendar icon) as inline `data:image/svg+xml` background-images, not `<img>` tags, so they need `img-src 'self' data:`. Caught only by loading the actual dashboard page and reading the console, not by reading the CSS or the CSP string.
- [x] **Full regression-verified after every fix**, not just spot-checked: logged in, created a link, sorted, toggled an edit row, viewed a link's detail page (confirmed the QR `<img>` still loads real pixels — a same-origin `/api/.../qr` fetch, unaffected by `gui-pages`'s CSP since `api`'s own CSP governs that response), created a user, confirmed self-delete-hide and the admin-promotion confirm dialog both still work, deleted the test user — zero console errors across the entire session. `detect.mjs --json gui/` unchanged (same 2 known false positives). `uv run pytest` (131, api) + `uv run pytest` (14, gui-pages) + `go test ./linkgate/...` all pass.
- [x] Updated `CLAUDE.md`: Architecture section documents the 4th component and the routing split (including both gotchas above); new "Security response headers" section documents exactly what each component's CSP allows and why; the "Security tradeoffs" section's old "no security response headers" bullet replaced with the one remaining accepted gap (`gui-pages`'s CSP allows `'unsafe-inline'` — see the new Future Work item below); Commands/Tests sections updated for the 4th component and its own `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock`/test suite.
- [x] (Deferred at the time, **since done** — see `## CSP hardening — drop 'unsafe-inline'` below, completed 2026-07-31.) Harden `gui-pages`'s CSP by dropping `'unsafe-inline'`, which requires either externalizing ~700 lines of inline `<script>`/`<style>` or per-request nonce injection. Both figures in that sentence turned out wrong: the inline code measured 925 lines, and nonce injection could never have finished the job, since a `style="…"` attribute cannot carry a nonce. Externalization was the approach taken.
- [x] Independent code review of the security-headers commit (6bc7a66) + all 4 findings fixed — raised 2026-07-25. A fresh agent with no prior context reviewed the diff adversarially (path-traversal safety, CSP correctness, header-merge order, Go middleware ordering, test coverage, and the two claimed "gotchas"), and each finding was independently re-verified before fixing (not taken on trust) — confirmed live via `urlparse` edge-case testing, direct file reads, and re-running the test suites.
  - **[Confirmed] Header-merge order let caller-supplied headers silently override security headers** — file(s): api/responses.py, api/qr.py, api/tests/test_responses.py (new), api/tests/test_qr.py — done when: `json_response` and `qr.py`'s merge both now apply `SECURITY_HEADERS` *last* (`hdrs.update(SECURITY_HEADERS)`/`headers.update(SECURITY_HEADERS)`) instead of first, so a colliding key can never win regardless of what any current or future call site passes. Not exploited by any existing call site (only `set-cookie` is ever passed, which doesn't collide), but the ordering was backwards for a header set whose whole point is to be a hard-to-bypass baseline. New `api/tests/test_responses.py` directly proves the fix (a call passing a colliding `content-security-policy`/`x-frame-options` in `headers=` still gets the real security values back); `test_qr.py` got a new test asserting `SECURITY_HEADERS` actually appear on QR responses (previously zero coverage for the one call site the original commit specifically called out as needing a bypass fix).
  - **[Confirmed] `gui-pages`'s `build_response` had no guard around the file read** — file(s): gui-pages/routing.py, gui-pages/tests/test_routing.py — done when: wrapped `read_file(filename)` in a `try/except OSError`, returning `500` with `SECURITY_HEADERS` still attached instead of an unhandled exception propagating out of the WASI runtime with no headers at all. Guards against `ROUTES`/filesystem drift (a page renamed/removed on one side but not the other) — not a live bug today since they match by construction, but cheap insurance. New test injects a `read_file` that raises `FileNotFoundError` and confirms the 500 + full header set.
  - **[Confirmed] `redirect`'s password-prompt CSP was missing `base-uri`** — file(s): redirect/passwordgate.go — done when: added `base-uri 'self'` alongside the already-present `form-action`/`frame-ancestors` (none of the three are covered by `default-src 'none'`'s fallback, since only fetch-directives fall back to `default-src` — the code clearly intended to lock down all three but missed one). Not exploitable today (no injection point into `prompt.html` — `html/template` auto-escapes `Slug`/`Error`), but now consistent with `gui-pages/routing.py`'s sibling CSP, which already had it.
  - Verified live end-to-end after all 4 fixes: `curl` confirmed `base-uri 'self'` now appears in the password-prompt page's CSP and `api`'s JSON responses still carry every header correctly; full browser regression (login → create link → view detail page → admin users, zero console errors) re-run to confirm nothing broke. `detect.mjs --json gui/` unchanged (same 2 known false positives). `uv run pytest` — 135 (api, +4 new) and 15 (gui-pages, +1 new) — plus `go tool componentize-go build` (succeeds; `go build ./...`/`go vet ./...` failing on `package main` remains expected per this file's own documented note) and `go test ./linkgate/...` all pass.

## CSP hardening — drop 'unsafe-inline'

Planned 2026-07-31 — full rationale, the nonce-vs-externalization decision, and the rejected alternatives are in `docs/plans/csp-drop-unsafe-inline.md`. Re-confirms and supersedes the "Future work" entry above for this item. Measured reality vs. that entry's estimate: the inline code is **925 lines** (719 `<script>` + 206 `<style>`), not "~700"; there are **7** static `style="…"` attributes (6 in HTML + 1 inside an `app.js` `innerHTML` template) that no nonce can ever cover; and there are **zero** inline event handlers, zero `eval`/`new Function`/`document.write`, and every inline block is a classic end-of-body script that moves to an external file with no code changes. Approach chosen: **pure externalization, no nonces** — `build_response(uri, read_file)` stays an unmodified pass-through with its injected `read_file`, and the 8 new assets are served by the `gui` static component via **8 new exact routes** (that component goes 3 → 11 trigger routes; the app goes 6 → 14). Tasks land as a sequence, not one change: every step before the last is invisible to the CSP and independently shippable, and the policy tightens atomically at the end.

with `document.documentElement.dataset.theme = "dark"` set by hand in devtools on all 5 pages, live `getComputedStyle` measurement against each element's real rendered background clears 4.5:1 for every text element in the plan's Verification list and 3:1 for the focus ring, with the primary button fill measuring at least 3.3:1 against its card background (expected 6.76:1 — a bare 3.00:1 is a fail here, not a pass) and its Deep-Navy label at least 4.5:1 on that fill (expected 7.87:1); `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).colorScheme` is `"dark"`; every `<article>`'s computed `boxShadow` is `none`; `--pico-font-size` still resolves to `100%` and `--pico-spacing` to `0.75rem`; any value that misses is re-derived at the same hue and the table in the plan is corrected to the measured number. — **note:** measured values matched the plan's table almost exactly (buttonVsCard 6.76:1, buttonLabelVsFill 7.87:1, cardVsCanvas 1.165:1, h1/h2 14.35:1, avatar 7.87:1, colorScheme "dark", boxShadow "none", font-size/spacing unchanged) — but hit a real bug first: the dark block's CSSOM rule was silently dropping out of the stylesheet entirely (confirmed via `document.styleSheets[...].cssRules`, not just getComputedStyle), because a prose comment contained a literal `--pico-form-element-*/--pico-card-*` — the `*` immediately followed by `/` is a real `*/` token that closes the CSS comment early mid-sentence at the top level (between rules, not inside a declaration list), so the parser then consumed everything through the block's own closing `}` as one invalid selector and discarded the whole rule. Root-caused via a long bisection (isolating the exact 3-block combination that reproduced it, then trimming down to the offending substring) rather than assumed. Fixed by rewording the comment (comma-separated instead of `*/`-joined) and fixing one identical pre-existing instance in the light block's comment (harmless there only because it sits inside a declaration list, not at the top level, but same latent bug class). Also had to restart `spin up` after each `theme.css` edit — `spin_static_fs` caches served file content per process and does not pick up on-disk changes until restart, unlike what earlier rounds assumed.

## KV explorer

Fermyon's prebuilt `spin-kv-explorer` (v0.10.0, third-party, unmodified) as a **local-development-only** aid for inspecting and repairing `links`/`analytics` KV data. Plan: `docs/plans/kv-explorer.md`. Four fixed constraints from the user: local only (never reachable in a deployed configuration), `links` + `analytics` only with `users` withheld, its full CRUD accepted and documented plainly, its CDN dependencies and inline code accepted and scoped rather than forked. The committed `spin.toml` never mentions it — a committed fragment plus a runner script generate a gitignored `spin-dev.toml` on every local run, and a test keeps dev-only components out of the real manifest.

## Bulk link management

Bulk creation from a pasted list or an uploaded file, and bulk Delete/Enable/Disable via row selection, on the dashboard. Plan: `docs/plans/bulk-link-management.md`. **This supersedes the 2026-07-24 "Bulk link management on the dashboard" Future-work entry above**, which said to re-plan before starting. Six fixed constraints from the user: two columns only (slug + destination, blank slug means auto-generate); password and start/end scheduling are batch-level controls applied to every link in the submission, not file columns; all-or-nothing validation (one bad row creates nothing and every bad row is reported); Delete and Enable/Disable only, with CSV export deferred to Future work; select-all covers the currently-filtered rows and the selection clears on filter change, sort change or a completed action; and the uploaded file is read client-side so no multipart parsing reaches a Wasm component. Two facts drive the design: the `all_links`/`owner_links:` indexes are read-modify-written per call with no CAS available, so bulk create and bulk delete each need **one** endpoint that reads each index once and writes it once (a request loop is incorrect, not just slow); and link-password hashing is a pure-Python 100,000-iteration PBKDF2 inside Wasm, so the batch-level password is hashed once per submission rather than once per row. All new logic is Python in `api/` — nothing here touches the Go hot path.

## Banned-word slug check — NOT BEING IMPLEMENTED (decided 2026-08-02)

> **Decided against and reverted.** Tasks 1-3 were built and passing (a 31-entry
> list, both predicates, wiring in `api/links.py` and `api/bulk.py`, 192 → 215
> tests) when the user reviewed the proposed word list and decided not to ship
> the feature at all. The implementation was reverted; `api` is back at 192
> tests and no trace of it remains in the code.
>
> The reasoning that made this defensible: the check only ever guarded
> carelessness, not abuse. Users are authenticated internal marketing staff, a
> determined person defeats a word list trivially, embedded evasion like
> `xxassxx` passes segment matching by design, and every future change to the
> list needs a deploy. Set against a real false-positive risk on legitimate
> campaign slugs, the value did not justify carrying a profanity list in the
> repo. Weighing the list itself is what surfaced that.
>
> The lines below are kept as a record of what the work would have been, not
> as open tasks. **Their `- [ ]` markers were deliberately removed** on
> 2026-08-04: a prose disclaimer stops a human reader but not a
> `grep '^- \[ \]'` scan, which kept resurfacing six abandoned tasks as
> outstanding work. Do not restore the checkboxes. **Do not pick them up without re-deciding the
> feature first.** `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md` retains the full analysis
> — including the segment-versus-substring reasoning, which is genuinely
> reusable if slug validation is ever revisited for another purpose.

A static, case-insensitive banned-word check on link slugs. Plan: `docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md`. Four fixed constraints from the user: the list is a module-level constant in `api/` code behind a predicate function (no KV, no admin UI, no CRUD endpoints, no new permission — kept behind a function so a future move to KV is a small, localized change); custom slugs only, with destination-URL filtering left entirely to the existing "Multi-domain short-link hosting + admin-managed destination domain allow/deny-list" Future-work entry; matching is **whole-segment** for custom slugs (split on `-` and `_`, so `black-friday-<word>` is rejected while `classic-glasses` and `assets-2026` are not — this is what avoids the Scunthorpe problem); and auto-generated slugs are checked too and regenerated on a hit. **Two matching rules, one word list, deliberately:** generated slugs use a **substring** rule, because a 7-character base62 string has no separators for segment matching to fire on and there is no false-positive cost to a random string nobody has seen. This is a carelessness guard, not a content-moderation system, and it cannot stop a determined insider. Existing links are entirely unaffected — slugs are immutable (no rename endpoint exists) and `redirect/main.go` never validates slug shape. Nothing here touches the Go hot path. Baseline before this work: `cd api && uv run pytest` → 192 passed.

- Add api/slugwords.py with the banned-word list and its two predicates (must land before every other task in this section) — file(s): api/slugwords.py (new), api/tests/test_slugwords.py (new) — done when: `BANNED_SLUG_WORDS` is a module-level `frozenset` of 20–40 lowercase, alphabetized entries seeded per docs/plans/banned-word-slugs.md ("The list itself" — unambiguous terms only, 3-character minimum, contents flagged in the PR for the user to review, not chosen unilaterally); `banned_slug_segment(slug) -> str | None` splits on `-`/`_` and returns the first whole segment that matches case-insensitively, as the caller typed it; `contains_banned_word(candidate) -> bool` does a case-insensitive substring match for generated slugs; both read the module global at call time so tests can monkeypatch it; the module has zero `spin_sdk` imports and takes no `store`; `cd api && uv run pytest` passes with new tests covering `classic-glasses` and `assets-2026` returning None, `black-friday-<word>` and `BADWORD` matching, `badwordly`/`xbadword` not matching as segments but matching under `contains_banned_word`, and four invariant tests over the real constant (all lowercase, all `^[a-z0-9]+$`, all ≥3 chars, non-empty).

## Multi-domain display

Short-link domains as a **viewer preference**, chosen in the persistent nav and persisted in `localStorage`, driving every URL the UI hands the user. Plan: `docs/plans/multi-domain-display.md`. **This supersedes the first half of the 2026-07-18 "Multi-domain short-link hosting + admin-managed destination domain allow/deny-list" Future-work entry above**, which said to re-confirm scope before starting; the second half (the destination-URL allow/deny-list) is untouched and has been restated as its own Future-work entry. Six fixed constraints from the user: no per-link domain field; no enforcement anywhere and **`redirect/main.go` is not touched by any task in this section**; slugs stay globally unique; the domain list is a Spin variable, not KV and not an admin page; `assigned_domains` per user is a convenience guardrail (not a security control, and deliberately not in `auth.KNOWN_PERMISSIONS`); and the selector follows the existing theme control's precedent exactly. The load-bearing fact: **`redirect` resolves purely by slug and never reads the `Host` header, so every link already works on every domain pointed at the deployment** — storing a per-link domain without enforcing it would be metadata that lies. The one genuinely new security surface is `GET /api/links/{slug}/qr`, which must allowlist-validate the client's chosen base URL against the configured list rather than trusting it: an endpoint that encodes an arbitrary client-supplied base URL into a QR code is a QR-poisoning vector, and the artifact is printed and outlives any later fix. Baseline before this work: `cd api && uv run pytest` -> 192 passed, `cd gui-pages && uv run pytest` -> 57 passed, `cd redirect && go test ./linkgate/...` -> ok.

## KV backup and restore

Operator-invoked backup and restore of the `links`, `users` and `analytics` stores, downloaded to and uploaded from the browser. Plan: `docs/plans/kv-backup-restore.md`. Six fixed constraints from the user: **no S3 or cloud storage of any kind** (the plan adds no `allowed_outbound_hosts`, preserving the no-outbound property `CLAUDE.md` cites as the reason there is no rate limiting); the file carries **no credential material at all** — user records are included but `password_hash` is stripped, and session keys and `_meta:bootstrapped` are excluded, which is also why the file is not encrypted; restore **replaces** the stores it covers rather than merging; users are restored **last** and the operator is warned they will be logged out; recovery works because omitting `_meta:bootstrapped` lets `ensure_bootstrap_admin` re-seed the admin from `SPIN_VARIABLE_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD` on the next start, who then resets everyone via the existing flow; and a restored account with no hash **can never authenticate** and is flagged in the users table so it is visible who still needs a reset. The first task is a spike that blocks the rest: whether `store.get_keys()` works at runtime decides if this is a true full-fidelity backup or a logical export that can only see what the app's own indexes know about — and the plan is explicit that it must not be called something it is not.

## Link tags and owner reassignment

Free-form, lowercase, per-link tags with client-derived autocomplete, plus owner reassignment for orphaned links. Plan: `docs/plans/link-tags-and-ownership.md`. Four fixed constraints from the user: a new `links.tag` permission following the granular model rather than an `admin`-role check, with tagging your own links needing no extra permission; owner reassignment gated on the existing `users.manage`, single- and multi-link, motivated by an employee leaving and their links being orphaned; tags free-form with autocomplete and no admin-curated vocabulary; and **bulk-by-tag is filter-then-use-the-existing-bulk-bar, with no server-side "delete all 300 links tagged X" action** — seeing-before-hitting over raw power. The load-bearing design decision, made during planning: **no `tag:` KV index and no `_meta:tags` registry**, because the dashboard already holds every visible link in `allLinks`, so tag filtering and autocomplete are client-side over data already in memory — which means no new KV key type, no racy two-index retag, and no new backup obligation. The highest-risk operation is reassignment (three writes, no transaction): records first, then the new owner's index, then the old owners', **never `all_links`**, so an interruption leaves a duplicate rather than a disappearance and re-running converges. `redirect` is untouched — Go's `encoding/json` ignores unknown object keys by default (confirmed via `go doc encoding/json Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields`), so `tags` costs the hot path nothing. No new page, no new route, no nav item. Baseline before this work: `cd api && uv run pytest` -> 289 passed, `cd gui-pages && uv run pytest` -> 64 passed, `cd redirect && go test ./linkgate/...` -> ok.

Fixes a reproduced defect — deleting a user leaves their links owned by a username that can be recreated, and the new account inherits them — plus a session-revival vector found during planning. ## Destination URL policy

An admin-managed allow/deny list constraining which hosts a link's `target_url` may point at, enforced at authoring time in `api/` and never in the `redirect` hot path. Plan: `docs/plans/destination-url-policy.md`. **The retroactive question is answered "report, never mutate"**: `GET /api/admin/url-policy/violations` lists existing links the current policy would refuse, changes nothing, and points the operator at the dashboard's existing bulk Disable/Delete. Rules live in a single `_meta:url_policy` key in the `links` store; an absent key means everything is allowed, so no deployment needs a migration. Precedence, complete: **a deny rule always wins; otherwise an allow rule (or a `default_action` of `allow`) lets it through; otherwise it is blocked.** A rule matches the host and **every subdomain of it** — a rule for `example.com` covers `evil.example.com` but not `notexample.com`. Baseline before this work: api 396, gui-pages 64, Go ok.

## KV store consolidation

Plan: `docs/plans/kv-store-consolidation.md`. Collapses the three named KV stores (`links`, `users`, `analytics`) onto Spin's single auto-provisioned `"default"` store using key prefixes, exposed to the rest of the code as a prefixing *view* (`api/kvprefix.py`) so no business-logic module and no existing test learns that prefixes exist. Unblocks — and reaches — an actual Akamai Functions deploy, which only allows the `"default"` label and supports no runtime configuration. Baselines before this section: api **474**, gui-pages **71**, Go ok.

## Click-count accuracy (sharded analytics counters)

Plan: `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`. Fixes the measured Akamai click under-counting — 0% loss at or below 2.7 clicks/second on one link, 25% at 9.4/s, 70% at 34/s, 75% at 65/s — by spreading `analytics:count:<slug>` over 16 shard keys, which leaves the redirect hot path at exactly 6 KV operations and needs no migration. **The second task is a hard gate:** it decides, with no code and no deploy, whether contention is per-key (sharding works) or app-wide (sharding is worthless); nothing below it may be built until it has passed.

- [x] Probe whether click-count loss is per-key or app-wide (BLOCKS every sharding task below) — file(s): (none — live measurement on the deployed app) — done when: three conditions have each been run with 100 requests and recorded in docs/plans/click-count-accuracy-scratch.md — (a) one fresh slug at 34/s, expected ~70% loss as the control, (b) sixteen fresh slugs round-robined at 34/s aggregate, (c) sixteen fresh slugs round-robined at 65/s aggregate; if (b) loses as much as (a), sharding does not work on this host: stop, implement nothing below, and re-plan against the "If the probe fails" section of docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md — **DONE 2026-08-06, PASSED.** Run as originally specified (16 slugs, 38.5 req/s aggregate) it showed 32.5% loss and read as a failure; that run was confounded — 38.5 req/s × 2 writes = 77 writes/s against Akamai's 50 write RPS cap, so it measured M2, not M1. Re-run below the cap: **1 slug @ 9.4 req/s (18.8 writes/s) lost 25%, while 16 slugs @ 9.2 req/s (18.5 writes/s, same app-wide write load) lost 0%**; 16 slugs @ 19.7 req/s (39.4 writes/s) also lost 0%. Identical write rate, one hot key vs sixteen — per-key contention is real and sharding addresses it.
- [x] Make dev/click-load.sh refuse to silently measure the wrong mechanism — file(s): dev/click-load.sh — done when: in addition to the original spec, the script prints the implied app write rate (`rate-per-second` × 2, since every recorded click is two KV writes) and prints a loud warning when that value reaches 50, naming Akamai's 50 write RPS cap and stating that any loss measured above it is throttling rather than counter contention — **note:** the script did not exist at all, so this was written once to the combined spec (the plan's line 507 original + line 524 supersession), not edited. Two additions beyond the spec, both in service of the same "cannot silently measure the wrong mechanism" goal: (1) it reports the **achieved** rate and its implied write rate alongside the requested ones, and repeats the cap warning post-run if the achieved rate crossed it — the requested rate is a target, the achieved rate is what any conclusion actually rests on; (2) pacing sleeps until an **absolute** target time (`start + n × interval`) rather than for a fixed interval, because request latency and per-iteration subprocess cost otherwise accumulate as drift — measured 7.4 req/s against a requested 9.4 before drift correction, 9.7 after. That 21% undershoot would have silently invalidated the later "100 requests at 9.4/s" verification task's comparison against its pre-change 75/100 baseline. Written for macOS's system bash 3.2 (parallel indexed arrays, no `declare -A`), matching `dev/kv-explorer-up.sh`'s documented `set -u` omission; `perl -MTime::HiRes` supplies the sub-second clock and sleep that macOS `date(1)`/`sleep(1)` cannot together. Verified live against a local `spin up --build`: round-robin exact (10/10 across two slugs), all 302s, `EXIT=0`; a nonexistent slug counted as `non-302 responses: 3 (codes: 404)`; connect-refused runs exit 1; the cap warning fires at exactly `rate 25` (50.0 writes/s) and stays silent at 9.4; arg validation (missing args, non-http scheme, zero rate, non-integer count) all exit 2 under `/bin/bash` 3.2.57; and `GET /api/links/loadtest1/analytics` confirmed **23 recorded clicks against 23 issued**, so the load genuinely drives the counter.
- [x] Add CountShards, CountShardKey and ShardFor to linkgate, with distribution tests — file(s): redirect/linkgate/keys.go, redirect/linkgate/analytics.go, redirect/linkgate/keys_test.go, redirect/linkgate/analytics_test.go — done when: `cd redirect && go test ./linkgate/...` passes with new tests asserting CountShardKey("abc", 3) == "analytics:count:abc:3", ShardFor(x, 0) and ShardFor(x, 1) return 0, ShardFor over 100000 draws puts each of the 16 shards within 10% of uniform, ShardFor over timestamp-shaped input 1 ms apart also puts each of the 16 shards within 10% of uniform, and the old CountKey function and TestCountKey are gone — **note:** implemented exactly to the plan's code blocks. `CountKey`/`TestCountKey` deleted; `TestCountShardKey` replaces it and additionally pins that no shard key can equal the legacy unsharded key (the no-migration claim rests on that). `gofmt -l linkgate/` and `go vet ./linkgate/...` both clean; all `./linkgate/...` tests pass. **The timestamp-distribution test was mutation-verified and it is the load-bearing one:** swapping `mix64` for `EventSlot`'s single multiply-then-reduce puts **all 100,000 draws into shard 0** — total collapse, not mild skew. Distribution tests use a fixed PCG seed so they cannot flake. That mutation also produced the finding recorded against the "real cause of the recent-events slot collisions" Future-work item below — the cause is now known.
- [x] Write the sharded count key from the redirect hot path — file(s): redirect/main.go — done when: recordClickCount reads and writes linkgate.CountShardKey(slug, linkgate.ShardFor(clickEntropy(now), linkgate.CountShards)), clickEntropy XORs math/rand/v2's rand.Uint64() with now.UnixNano(), the function's comment block no longer says the loss "needs a different counter shape", `go tool componentize-go build` from redirect/ succeeds, and an X-SS-Debug-traced redirect against a local `spin up` still reports kv_ops=6 — **note:** implemented to the plan's code blocks; the comment block was rewritten to name **both** mechanisms (per-key contention, which sharding fixes, and the app-wide 50-write-RPS cap, which it cannot touch) rather than the old single "needs a different counter shape" framing. `gofmt` clean, `go tool componentize-go build` succeeded. Live against a local `spin up --build`: traced redirect returned `server-timing: kv;dur=3.395;desc="6 ops"` and logged `kv_ops=6` — **unchanged**. Then 41 clicks (1 traced + 40 paced at 9.6/s) landed as `analytics:count:shardtest:<n>` across **14 of the 16 shards, summing to exactly 41** read straight out of `.spin/sqlite_key_value.db`. **Expected intermediate state:** the detail page under-reports until the next task teaches `api/analytics.py` to sum shards — the writer is sharded, the reader is not yet. **Incidental correction:** CLAUDE.md's KV-explorer bullet says local KV appears to be non-persistent with no `.db` file anywhere; this Spin (4.0.2) logs `Storing default key-value data to ".spin/sqlite_key_value.db"` on startup and the file is real and queryable — which is how the shard distribution above was verified. Worth fixing in CLAUDE.md when the documentation task below runs.
- [x] Sum the shards plus the legacy key on the analytics read path — file(s): api/analytics.py, api/tests/test_analytics.py — done when: `cd api && uv run pytest` passes with new tests showing counts in shards 0, 7 and 15 summing into one total and one merged days map, a legacy `count:<slug>` value summing in alongside shard values, and an unparseable shard blob being skipped without blanking the total — and test_analytics_reports_count_and_events still passes with its assertions unmodified — **note:** `COUNT_SHARDS = 16` and the pure `_merge_counts` helper added; `handle_analytics` now reads 17 keys (legacy + 16 shards) and the response shape is byte-for-byte unchanged, so `gui/links/detail.js` needed no edit. `_merge_counts` skips a blob that is absent, empty, non-JSON **or not a dict**, and type-checks `total`/`days` entries as `int` (excluding `bool`) before summing — a malformed shard costs only its own clicks. **`uv run pytest` — 512 passed** (508 baseline + 4 new). `test_analytics_reports_count_and_events` passes with assertions untouched and now carries a comment naming it the migration regression test. A fourth test beyond the three specified asserts every shard in `range(COUNT_SHARDS)` is actually read — a reader that stopped early would silently lose the tail shards, which is the same silent-loss failure the constant's own comment warns about.

  | rate | writes/s | runs | recorded / 100 | criterion 98-100 |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | 4.0 (sequential) | 8.0 | 1 | 100 | pass, but under-rate |
  | 9.5 | 19.0 | 3 | 97, 100, 98 (mean 98.3) | **marginal** — 2 of 3 in band |
  | 19.9 | 39.8 | 2 | 95, 90 (mean 92.5) | **FAILS** |

  Against the pre-change 75/100 at 9.4/s this is a large improvement, and both op-count criteria pass outright: a traced redirect reports `desc="6 ops"` (**kv_ops=6**, unchanged) and a traced `GET /api/links/{slug}/analytics` reports **52 ops** — 1 `open` + 1 `exists` + **50 `get`**, exactly matching the local post-change trace and exactly **16 more gets** than the locally-measured pre-change 34. (The pre-change trace had to be taken locally by swapping in `analytics.py` from `9394f4c`: the previously-deployed build's `log_debug_token` is unknown, so it cannot be traced. Op counts are code-determined, not host-determined, so this substitution is sound.)

  **Losses are permanent, not lag** — re-reading `shardverifyC` after a delay still gave 97.

  **The plan's model of why 16 shards suffice is wrong, and this is the finding that matters.** It reasoned from per-shard *rate*: ~1.6 clicks/s per shard at the app-wide ceiling, inside the band measured lossless at 1.2/s per key. But rate is not what causes a lost increment — **two clicks landing on the same shard while a read-modify-write is in flight** is. In-flight requests ≈ rate x KV latency, and KV latency here was 250-400 ms, so 9.5 req/s puts ~2.4-3.8 requests in flight and 19.9 req/s puts ~5-8. Collision probability over S shards grows roughly as k²/2S, which is quadratic in concurrency — and the measured loss (1.7% then 7.5%) tracks that shape, not the flat "inside the lossless band" the plan predicted. Sharding removed most of the loss; it did not remove it, and it will get worse as latency or traffic rises.

  **The lever is `CountShards`, and it is already governed by a RAISE ONLY, NEVER LOWER rule with a cross-language guard, so raising it is safe and needs no migration.** By the k²/2S relation, 16 -> 64 should cut residual loss ~4x (~1.9% at 19.9 req/s, inside the band). The cost is on the read path only: the analytics endpoint would go from 50 to 98 `get`s per page view, ~+48 KV ops at ~7 ms each on Akamai. The redirect hot path stays at 6 ops regardless of shard count. **Not done — it is a real trade-off (detail-page latency against counter accuracy) and belongs to the user, not to this task.**

## Click-count accuracy — what the live probe changed (2026-08-06)

Kept as the record of *why* the task lines above read as they do. The lines themselves are already corrected — there is no superseded copy to reconcile.

The gating probe in the section above **was run on the live app on 2026-08-06 and it passed** — sharding works, the design holds, and it is not builder work. But it corrected three things, and **four lines in the section above are wrong as written.** Read this section before actioning any of them. Revised plan: `docs/plans/click-count-accuracy.md`.
**1. The probe as originally specified was confounded and returned a false negative.** Run at 16 slugs / 34 req/s aggregate it showed 32.5% loss and read as a clean failure. It is not: every click is two KV writes, so 38.5 req/s attempts ~77 writes/s against Akamai's **50 write RPS cap**, and that run measured the cap rather than key contention. Re-run under the cap the signal is unambiguous — 1 slug at 9.4 req/s (18.8 writes/s) lost **25%**; 16 slugs at 9.2 req/s (18.5 writes/s, *identical app-wide write load*) lost **0%**; 16 slugs at 19.7 req/s (39.4 writes/s) lost **0%**. Those first two rows are the pair that decides it. **Every future measurement must hold `request_rate × 2 < 50 writes/second`, i.e. under ~25 requests/second aggregate, or it measures the wrong mechanism.**
**2. There are two independent mechanisms, and the original single-slug loss curve blended them.** M1, per-key contention on one hot counter — what sharding fixes. M2, app-wide write throttling above ~50 writes/s ≈ **~25 clicks/second across the whole application** — which sharding cannot touch and only fewer writes per click can. The curve's 34/s and 65/s rows are contaminated by M2 and are unusable for reasoning about sharding.
**3. The "~43 clicks/second" ceiling was arithmetic on the blended curve and is unreachable** — M2 binds first at ~25 clicks/s. The honest benefit is better than a number the app cannot reach: at the app-wide ceiling even a single link taking *all* the traffic sees only ~1.6 clicks/second per shard, against 0% loss measured at 1.2/s per key, so **16-way sharding removes the per-link penalty entirely below the app-wide ceiling, collapsing two constraints into one.** A single link above ~25 clicks/second is still lossy and sharding will not save it.
**Retraction:** the "~25 redirects/second" write-RPS ceiling was previously called academic in this file. **It is not** — it is the real measured app-wide ceiling and after this work it is the only binding constraint.
**Dropped, do not action:** the `OPTIONAL ... choose the recent-events slot at random` line above. `EventSlot` stays; see the dated entry under "Considered and rejected".

## Build-version response header (2026-08-07)

Added mid-session at the user's request, after deploy propagation twice made a measurement ambiguous.

- [x] Emit an operator-supplied build identifier on every response — file(s): spin.toml, redirect/main.go, api/app.py, gui-pages/app.py — done when: `redirect`, `api` and `gui-pages` all set `X-SS-Version` from a new `app_version` Spin variable (default `"unknown"`), an unauthenticated `curl -sI` on any of the three returns it, and all three suites still pass — **DONE.** Verified live on a local `spin up --build` with `SPIN_VARIABLE_APP_VERSION=local-64shard-test`: all three components returned `x-ss-version: local-64shard-test`. Suites unchanged (Go `linkgate` pass, api 513, gui-pages 71 — the new `[component.gui-pages.variables]` sub-table correctly does **not** trip `test_manifest_components.py`, which compares the component set via `tomllib` rather than grepping). Attached in each component's `app.py`/`setSecurityHeaders` rather than the shared `SECURITY_HEADERS` dicts, because it comes from a Spin variable and `api/responses.py`/`gui-pages/routing.py` must keep zero `spin_sdk` imports to stay host-testable. **Unconditional, unlike `Server-Timing`** — including on `api`'s exception path, since a build identifier that vanishes when a handler raises is missing exactly when it is most wanted. The value is opaque and operator-chosen, so how much it reveals is the operator's call.

**Why it exists.** `spin aka app deploy` gives up waiting after 60 seconds and reports `failed to wait for deployment to go live` on deploys that in fact succeed, and the app keeps serving the previous build for some minutes afterwards. Before this header the only way to tell which build was live was to probe for a behavioural difference — which is circular when the behaviour under test *is* the change. That circularity produced a wrong reading once this session: an early sample of the `asyncio.gather` change showed a serial signature and looked like a clean negative result, when it was simply the old build still answering. `spin aka app history` is not a substitute: it records the version row *before* the build is actually serving.

## Impeccable critique (10th pass, 22/40) + the three P1 fixes (2026-08-08)

First critique since the nav redesign pass (9th, 28/40) and **the first ever to cover the URL policy page, the consistency report, the backup page, the tags GUI, the bulk-action bar, CSV export and the owner filter** — 39 UI-touching commits that had never been reviewed. Snapshot: `.impeccable/critique/2026-08-08T05-42-30Z__gui.md`. Trend 26 → 30 → 27 → 28 → **22**.

**Read the drop correctly: it is not a regression.** The four prior passes scored a smaller app. The score fell because the measured surface grew ~40% and the new part didn't inherit the system the old part earned its scores with. Previously-critiqued pages still hold up — deterministic evidence was strong across the board (zero contrast failures in either theme on all five pages, lowest 4.58:1; zero console errors; zero page-level overflow at 1400/768/480/390 in both themes; zero focus-indicator gaps).

**The mechanical detector found nothing.** 2 findings, both false positives (a JS-assigned QR `src` a static scan can't see, and vendored Pico CSS). Every real finding came from design review or direct browser measurement. Worth remembering next time someone treats a clean detector run as a clean design.

**The overlay could not run, and that is the app behaving correctly** — CSP `script-src 'self'` blocked both inline and external injection. No workaround was attempted and CSP was not disabled.

- [x] Derive link state instead of echoing the stored `status` field — file(s): gui/app.js, gui/dashboard.js, gui/links/detail.js, gui/theme.css — done when: a link whose window has not opened no longer renders a green "active" badge — **DONE.** `resolveLinkState()` + `statusBadge()` live in `app.js` (three call sites — table, CSV, detail page — must never disagree) and mirror `linkgate.IsWithinWindow`: inclusive start, exclusive end, non-active stored status winning over the window. **The bug was confirmed live before the fix and after:** `bf2026` showed green "Active" while `GET /r/bf2026` returned 404; it now reads "Scheduled" in slate, verified in-browser. **No new design token** — `scheduled` reuses `.not-yet-live`'s slate, `expired` reuses `.expired`'s danger red, so the badge and the Starts/Expires cell cannot disagree. This also closes the mobile half: the state now lives in the Status column, which survives the ≤600px collapse that hides Starts, so the qualifier is no longer absent from the accessibility tree on a phone. CSV gained a **`State` column alongside the existing raw `Status`** rather than replacing it — a derived value silently replacing a stored one in a data export would be its own small lie.
- [x] Make `admin/url-policy.html` say when it holds unsaved work — file(s): gui/admin/url-policy.js, gui/admin/url-policy.html, gui/theme.css — done when: staged edits are visibly distinct from saved ones and leaving with them warns — **DONE.** A `savedPolicy` copy alongside `stagedPolicy` makes "is there unsaved work" answerable at all; `renderDirtyState()` is the single place every affordance is re-derived, so a future control can't add a staged mutation and forget to mark the page dirty. Four layers, verified in-browser: staged rows carry a **"Not saved"** badge (saved ones don't); the save button becomes **"Save 2 pending changes"** and switches from outline to filled; a `.form-note` advisory appears; and `beforeunload` blocks navigation **only while dirty** (`defaultPrevented: true` dirty, `false` clean — a guard that always fires trains people to dismiss it). The default-action summary now reads **"Will apply on save: …"** while dirty instead of asserting the new behaviour in present tense the instant the select changed. A successful save also **auto-runs the violations check**, since "what did this rule just break?" is the operator's immediate next question and it was behind a button they had to remember.

Verified in-browser: for `?slug=doesnotexist` all three sections are hidden, the QR `<img>` renders 0×0 rather than a broken-image box, and copy is a page-local override ("That short link doesn't exist — it may have been deleted.") because the shared `not_found` message says "try refreshing the page", which can never help here. `loadAnalytics()` is now **gated on `loadLinkInfo()` succeeding** rather than fired in parallel — it was overwriting the error, and its early return was the reason the empty-state rows never appeared (they only exist inside its success path). The no-slug case previously did `document.body.textContent = "…"`, destroying nav, styling and every route out; it now keeps the shell — verified landmarks `HEADER,NAV,MAIN` and the stylesheet still applied.

Measured: it drops Signal Blue to **4.03:1**, under the 4.5:1 AA floor, and pulls the outline-secondary Remove button down with it. Dropped; the "Not saved" badge carries the meaning in words, matching the `.expiring-soon`/`.expired` precedent where the text suffix carries the distinction rather than a second hue.
