The violations table now renders **8 slug chips in `SFMono-Regular` at the 999px radius plus 8 real status badges** (was: plain sans-serif `<a>` and bare text). Consistency findings render a slug as a linked chip and label their other fields (was: raw `key: value · key: value`). **Three date formats collapsed to one** `formatTimestamp`, and the two local `formatDateTime` duplicates are gone. `#rules-table` got a page-scoped stylesheet (with its `spin.toml` route — the asset-without-a-route gotcha CLAUDE.md warns about, verified serving 200) carrying the sticky action column and mobile collapse the other two tables already had: **its Remove button moved from x=542, entirely off-screen at 390px, to fully on-screen.** `#export-csv` now reports "Exported 14 links." — which also answers "what did I just export?", since the export follows the current filter and nothing said how many rows that was. `backup.html`'s standing advisory moved from `.form-error` red to `.form-note` slate, so a real `#restore-error` is no longer visually identical to permanent furniture (measured: advisory `rgb(82,96,120)` vs error `rgb(179,38,30)`).

**The search-box pill fix is worth reading before touching any Pico override — it is a NEW variant of the specificity trap this repo already records three times.** Pico renders `input[type=search]` as an 80px pill, violating the Pill-Is-For-Links Rule directly (the widest pill on the dashboard sat above twelve slug pills meaning something else). The obvious fix, `border-radius: var(--pico-border-radius)`, **changed nothing — measured live, still 80px.** Pico does not set `border-radius` on that element; it redefines **`--pico-border-radius: 5rem` on the element itself**, so the override read the very variable it was overriding. Reset the variable, not the property that reads it. Now 4px, with the chip still 999px.

**A real regression was introduced and caught by measuring rather than by looking.** Fixing the rules table exposed that `renderViolations()` injects a **bare `<table>` with no `<figure>` wrapper**, unlike every other table in the app — so once violations actually rendered, the table broke the *page* horizontally at 390px (`documentElement` scrollWidth 520 against a 375 client) instead of scrolling inside itself. Pre-existing, but invisible until this pass made the table non-empty. Wrapped; re-measured at **375/375 page overflow with the table scrolling inside its own figure (327/496)**.

**Verification:** 390px re-measured on dashboard, users and url-policy in **both themes** — zero page overflow, zero nav overflow. Detector re-run: same 2 pre-existing false positives, no new findings. Suites: api 520, gui-pages 71, Go linkgate ok. **Test-data gap worth knowing:** the seeded `contractor` account was meant to be disabled and the PATCH never applied (`status` is absent on every user record), so the disabled-user status badge has still never been exercised live — in this pass or in the critique that described it.

## Clicks column, timestamp resolution, and the critique's minors (2026-08-10)

Picked up once the user lifted the budget constraint and confirmed **recent-events stays** (so the timestamp fix is worth doing rather than throwaway) and **bulk becomes explicitly desktop-only** rather than silently hidden.

- [x] Give event timestamps millisecond resolution — file(s): api/responses.py, api/analytics.py, gui/app.js, gui/links/detail.js, api/tests/test_responses.py — done when: distinct clicks in one second render as distinct rows — **DONE.** The record always carried ms (`redirect` writes `UnixMilli`); `_parse_event` was rounding it away. New `to_iso8601_utc_ms` rather than a flag on `to_iso8601_utc`, because the two have different obligations — link windows round-trip through `parse_iso8601_utc` and must keep their exact shape, while an event timestamp is display-only. `formatTimestamp` gained `{ precise: true }`, used by the events table alone. Three tests pin the format, the zero-padding, and that `parse_iso8601_utc` round-trips the new form (a claim the docstring makes, so it should be tested rather than asserted).
- [x] Add a Clicks column to the links table — file(s): api/analytics.py, api/app.py, gui/dashboard.{html,js,css}, gui/app.js, api/tests/test_click_totals.py — done when: click totals are visible from the list surface — **DONE, and the read cost was the whole design.** The naive shape is `COUNT_SHARDS + 1` reads per link — **65 × N, i.e. 13,000 reads at 200 links against a 1,000/second app-wide cap**, which is why this was deferred as a product call rather than treated as a small addition. Instead `handle_click_totals` enumerates the analytics namespace **once** and reads only the count keys that exist: a link with clicks in five shards costs five reads, not sixty-five, so cost tracks real traffic rather than links × shard count — and **raising `CountShards` again no longer multiplies this endpoint.** Seven tests, including two that pin the cost claim directly (only-existing-keys, and never reading another user's analytics). **Rejected and recorded so it is not re-proposed:** a denormalized `analytics:total:<slug>` would make this O(N) reads but adds a *third* KV write per click — writes are the binding constraint, so that trade is backwards.
  - Routed at **`/api/analytics/click-totals`, deliberately not `/api/links/clicks`** — "clicks" is a legal custom slug, so that path would be shadowed by a real link the moment anyone created one.
  - Totals load **after** the table renders and paint in place rather than re-rendering. A full re-render clears the selection by design, so re-rendering a second after load would silently drop any checkbox ticked in the meantime. Until they arrive each row shows an em-dash, **not `0`** — a real zero and "not loaded" are different facts.
  - Sorting is numeric, not `localeCompare`, which would order 10 before 9. Verified live in both directions.
  - **Replaced the table's positional cell lookups with `data-cell` names.** The old `children[3]/[6]/[7]` had already shifted once when the select column landed, and this column would have shifted them again — silently writing the start date into the clicks cell.
- [x] State that bulk actions are desktop-only — file(s): gui/dashboard.{html,css} — done when: the page says so at the width where selection is unavailable — **DONE.** `#bulk-desktop-only` renders only below 600px, where the select column is hidden. Previously the control simply vanished and the page claimed nothing, which reads as a bug rather than a decision.
- [x] The critique's minors — file(s): gui/favicon.svg (new), spin.toml, all page HTML, gui/theme.css, gui/admin/backup.js — done when: each is closed or explicitly declined — **DONE.** Favicon reuses the nav brand glyph on Deep Navy (a pinned tab should read as the same product as the header) with `<link rel="icon">` on all seven pages; **`prompt.html` is deliberately excluded** — its CSP is the strictest in the app (`default-src 'none'`), a favicon is fetched under `img-src`, and widening the one policy guarding the page where a visitor types a credential is not worth a tab icon. Disabled controls now take `cursor: not-allowed` (Pico leaves them at `pointer`, so the only disabled control in the app read as clickable while inert). The clean consistency report now says **"All 12 checks passed"** and lists them behind a `<details>`, since "no inconsistencies" is only reassuring if you can see what was looked for.

**The mobile refit is the part worth reading, because adding the column broke a measured invariant.** At 390px only ~249px of content width exists before the sticky actions column. Adding Clicks put four content columns into three columns' space: **Expires' right edge landed at 373px against an actions column starting at 273px — straight underneath it**, the exact overlap that block exists to prevent. Expires lost the tie-break rather than Clicks, and the reason is a consequence of the P1 status fix: **the Status badge now derives expiry itself**, so it answers that question one column earlier, while Clicks answers one nothing else on the row does.

**A second correction, recorded because the obvious reading is wrong:** tightening the Status cap did **not** create clearance. The freed 8px went straight to the actions column (87 → 95) — an auto-layout table reallocates spare width rather than leaving a gap, so clearance is 0 either way. What actually prevents the overlap is that the columns now **sum** to the container: the figure measures **327/327 and does not scroll**, so no cell can sit under the sticky column at all. A future column that pushes the total past the container brings the overlap straight back — **check `scrollWidth` against `clientWidth`, not the gap between two cells.**

Verified at 390px in both themes: zero page overflow, figure no longer scrolls, Clicks populated. Detector: same 2 pre-existing false positives. Suites: api **530**, gui-pages 71.

## EventSlot hashing fix (2026-08-07)

Unblocked by the cause being found: the "Replacing `linkgate.EventSlot` with random slot selection" entry under "Considered and rejected" was dropped **specifically** because deleting `EventSlot` would have orphaned the then-open investigation into the collisions. That investigation closed on 2026-08-07 with the cause proven, so the stated reason for dropping it no longer holds. This is the hashing fix, not the random-selection variant that was rejected — `EventSlot` keeps its signature and stays a deterministic function of the timestamp.

- [x] Make `EventSlot` delegate to `ShardFor` — file(s): redirect/linkgate/analytics.go, redirect/linkgate/analytics_test.go — done when: `EventSlot` no longer contains a bare multiply-then-reduce, `gofmt`/`go vet`/`go test ./linkgate/...` are all clean, and the new tests fail against the old implementation — **DONE.** The whole change is `return ShardFor(uint64(now.UnixNano()), numSlots)`; `ShardFor`'s `numShards <= 1 → 0` guard subsumes `EventSlot`'s old `numSlots <= 0` guard exactly, so the boundary tests were untouched and still pass. Reusing `ShardFor` rather than writing new mixing is deliberate — it is already mutation-verified by the counter's timestamp-distribution test. **Three new tests, all mutation-verified against the restored old implementation** (6 cadence subtests + parity + the original bug report, every one failing).

- [x] Correct the derivation in CLAUDE.md — file(s): CLAUDE.md — done when: the section reflects what the Go code actually does — **DONE, and it found two errors in the previous write-up.** The earlier numbers were computed in Python, whose integers are arbitrary-precision; **Go's `uint64` multiply wraps at 2^64.** The `numSlots / gcd(stride, numSlots)` formula only commutes with that wraparound when `numSlots` divides 2^64 — i.e. is a **power of two**, where the collapse is total and the derivation exact (every spacing tested reaches **1 slot of 16**). At `numSlots = 30` the wraparound perturbs it, and **the tabulated "1 s → 3 of 30" was actually 11 of 30** over 20 clicks. Replaced with a sharper, run-length-independent result: 2^64 is divisible by 2 and every realistic spacing in nanoseconds is even, so **slot parity was pinned by the base timestamp's low bit forever — half the ring was permanently unreachable for the life of a link.** Verified at 5,000 clicks across four spacings and both base parities. Also noted that the live observation (8 requests 300 ms apart → 3 events) sits *above* the idealized 1, because real spacing has jitter — so that number agreeing was never the proof; the parity result and the power-of-two case are.

- [x] Clear the stale "unfixed" references — file(s): CLAUDE.md — done when: no section still describes this as an open defect — **DONE.** Two found beyond the main section: the Analytics intro's "separate, unfixed problem — `EventSlot` is unchanged", and the Security-tradeoffs click-count bullet, **which had also gone stale in a second way and still said the counter was sharded over 16 keys rather than 64.**

**Not done, and deliberately: no live re-measurement of the recent-events retention rate.** The fix is pinned by mutation-verified unit tests over the exact spacings that were failing, and the remaining loss is ordinary balls-in-bins overwriting, which no deploy can improve. A deployed verification would also be confounded by the app-wide write cap — a throttled events write is indistinguishable from a slot collision when read back — so it would need to run under ~25 clicks/second to mean anything. Worth doing if someone is deploying anyway; not worth a deploy cycle of its own.

## Parallelize sequential KV reads (identified 2026-08-07, COMPLETE 2026-08-07)

Opened by the `asyncio.gather` finding in the click-count work: the host genuinely overlaps concurrent KV reads (measured 19–58× at 100 operations), and `api/analytics.py` is currently the **only** place that exploits it. Several other paths still issue one KV round trip at a time.

**Measured baseline, live deployment, 2026-08-07 — `GET /api/links` (the dashboard):** `kv_ops=19, kv_us=436698, dur_us=442920` with **14 links**. That is ~23 ms per sequential round trip: ~115 ms fixed plus **~23 ms per link**, and `GET /api/links` has no pagination. Projected: ~1.3 s at 50 links, ~2.4 s at 100, ~4.7 s at 200. Bulk create allows 50 links per submission, so this degrades quickly in normal use.

- [x] Parallelize `handle_list`'s per-link record reads — file(s): api/links.py, api/tests/test_links.py — done when: the `for slug in slugs` loop issuing `await get_link(...)` one at a time is replaced by a single gathered fetch, `cd api && uv run pytest` passes with the existing list tests unmodified plus one asserting a link whose record is missing is still skipped rather than erroring, and a traced `GET /api/links` against a deployed build shows `kv_us >> dur_us` with `dur_us` no longer scaling per link — **DONE 2026-08-07, both criteria met on the deployed build** (`ac650c9-gatherreads`). Overlap is now proven rather than inferred: `kv` (the SUM of per-operation durations) exceeds `handler` (wall time), which is arithmetically impossible under serial execution. At 14 links, **kv_sum 433–1039 ms inside 135–278 ms of wall — 2.7–4.8×**, against the pre-change baseline's 0.99× (436.7 ms inside 442.9 ms). And wall time no longer scales per link: seeding the store to **50 links** left the median essentially unchanged — **~173 ms at 50 links vs ~178 ms at 14** — while op count rose 19 → 55. The old shape projected ~1,265 ms at 50 links (~115 ms fixed + ~23 ms/link), so this is ~7× at that size and grows from there. **Effective parallelism rose with fan-out rather than saturating** — 2.7–4.8× at 17 gets, 9.2–22.7× at 53 — the same scaling seen when the analytics endpoint went 50 → 98 gets.
- [x] Parallelize `backup.py`'s export read loop — file(s): api/backup.py — done when: the `for key in keys: await store.get(key)` loop at ~line 231 is gathered, `uv run pytest` still passes, and a traced export shows the same op count with materially lower wall time — **DONE 2026-08-07, and this one turned out to be a correctness fix, not just a speed-up.** Traced on the deployed build over a store with 926 analytics keys: **999 ops, kv_sum 48,135 ms, wall 957 ms — 50.3× overlap.** Same op count, ~50× less wall time. See the retraction below: the sequential form was plausibly *unable to complete* an export of this store inside Akamai's 30-second handler limit.
- [x] Consider the same for `consistency.py`'s walk — file(s): api/consistency.py — done when: its read loops are either gathered or a note records why not — **DONE 2026-08-07 — gathered, but the two stores are deliberately asymmetric and that asymmetry is the point.** The **links** store is fetched wholesale, including keys the loop classifies as `unrecognized` and discards: an allowlist there would have to restate the loop's branch conditions, and a condition that drifted out of it would silently hand the loop `None` and report a healthy key as `unreadable_value`. The **users** store gets an explicit two-shape allowlist (`_meta:usernames` and `session:*`) instead, because a `user:` record's value holds a PBKDF2 hash and **no check reads one** — fetching wholesale would pull every account hash in the store into the handler for zero benefit. Deployed trace: 69 ops, 6.8× overlap, 280 ms wall, all 12 checks present, `ok: true`, no credential material in the report. **The pre-existing `test_handle_consistency_never_leaks_password_hash` would NOT have caught a wholesale fetch** — it inspects the report body, and a `collect` that read every user value and discarded it still passes. `test_collect_never_even_reads_a_user_record_value` now asserts `get()` is never called on a `user:` key at all, and is mutation-checked against exactly the wholesale simplification a future reader would reach for.

**Shared helper: `api/kvbatch.py`'s `gather_reads`.** Bounded (100 concurrent), order-preserving, reads only. The bound is not decoration: export reads every key in the store, so an unbounded fan-out over a large store trades a latency problem for a read-cap one, and export is the path closest to the 30-second handler limit. **100 is empirical, not derived** — it is the largest fan-out actually measured working against Akamai (the 64-shard analytics endpoint's 98 gets, whose parallelism was still rising rather than saturating). Re-measure before raising it; the read cap is app-wide, so one handler monopolising it degrades every concurrent request. Order preservation is load-bearing for all three callers: `handle_list` returns links in index order, and `backup.py`/`consistency.py` both zip results back against their key lists.

**RETRACTION — "export is read-bound and safer (5,000 reads at 1,000 RPS ≈ 5 s)" was wrong, and CLAUDE.md's Akamai section repeats it.** That arithmetic assumes the export is *throughput*-bound against the 1,000 RPS read cap. A sequential `for key in keys: await store.get(key)` is **latency**-bound instead: one read at a time at ~20–48 ms each is ~20–50 reads/second, not 1,000 — off by a factor of ~20–50. The measured trace above sums to **48 seconds of KV time for 999 operations**, i.e. at or beyond the **30-second handler duration limit**, on a store holding only 14 links. Two caveats keep this an inference rather than a measurement: per-operation latency is inflated by queueing under 100-way concurrency, so the true sequential figure is likely nearer ~20 s at the documented ~20 ms/op; and no pre-change export of this store was traced, because the previously-deployed build's `log_debug_token` is unknown. Either way the old estimate was optimistic by more than an order of magnitude, and the honest statement is that export was **within striking distance of timing out and is no longer close to it.** The `MAX_BACKUP_ENTRIES = 5_000` cap was never the binding constraint it was assumed to be.

**Note on what still is not fixed: `GET /api/links` has no pagination.** Gathering converts ~23 ms/link into roughly a constant, but the handler still issues one read per link, so a large deployment fires one bounded burst per dashboard load against an app-wide read cap. Pagination is the actual answer if link counts ever get large; this change buys a lot of headroom, not unlimited headroom.

**Do NOT parallelize writes.** Reads are latency-bound against a 1,000 RPS cap with large headroom; **writes are capped at 50 RPS**, so `backup.py`'s restore loop (~line 292) and the bulk handlers are cap-bound rather than latency-bound. Gathering them buys nothing and risks throttling. This distinction is the whole reason the analytics change was safe.

## Deploy of the Clicks column, and what tracing it found (2026-08-10)

Deployed `051cfa7` as `app_version=051cfa7-clicks` (Akamai Version 14) and traced the new
endpoint, which is why this section exists: `/api/analytics/click-totals` was designed around
a read-cost argument that had never been checked against a real store.

**The design's own argument holds, and the endpoint is cheap.** 9 KV operations per call
(1 `open`, 1 `exists` for the session, 1 `list_keys`, 6 `get`s), 176–296 ms handler time over
6 interleaved samples — against `/api/links`'s 19 ops and 142–281 ms in the same window.
The feared shape (`COUNT_SHARDS + 1` reads per link, 65 × N) never materialises: only shards
that exist are read, so 14 links cost 6 reads, not 910. **Correctness cross-checked live** —
the busiest slug reports 524 from `click-totals` and 524 from `GET /api/links/{slug}/analytics`,
which sums all 65 keys by a completely separate code path.

**But the enumeration, not the reads, is now the endpoint's dominant cost, and that was not
in the original argument.** `list_keys` measured **69–162 ms (mean ~99 ms)** and is
`slow=list_keys:analytics:...` — the single slowest operation — in **every** trace. It is
~4× a single `get` (~24 ms), it is **~44% of the endpoint's wall time**, and it is
**un-overlappable**: `gather_reads` cannot issue a single read until the key list exists, so
the endpoint's effective parallelism is only **~1.2×** against `/api/links`'s 3.2–4.6×.

**The cost tracks the whole physical store, not the namespace being enumerated — measured,
not inferred.** `scoped_list_keys` calls `raw_list_keys(store.raw)` and filters afterwards, so
every namespace pays the full-store walk. `GET /api/admin/consistency` enumerates `links` and
`users` — **3 user keys and ~18 link keys** — and each of its two `list_keys` calls still cost
**~62 ms**, essentially the same as the 941-key analytics namespace. A 3-key namespace and a
941-key namespace costing the same is the proof.

**Why this matters for scaling:** the store is **962 physical keys, 941 of them analytics**
(measured via a traced export: 200, 63,983 bytes, **1.01 s wall** — matching the recorded
957 ms baseline, so no regression). Analytics keys grow at up to 94 per link (64 count shards
+ 30 event slots), currently ~52/link. **Every dashboard load now pays a full-store walk that
grows as analytics grows**, and analytics is the fastest-growing and only unbounded namespace.
**The growth *rate* is NOT measured** — two data points at one store size cannot establish it —
so this is a flagged risk, not a projection. Measure `list_keys` against a materially larger
store before assuming it is linear or that it is fine.

**The existing "Cache the physical KV key enumeration for the lifetime of one request" entry
under Future work is the fix, and this measurement is its trigger.** It would collapse
consistency's two walks into one immediately; it does nothing for `click-totals`, which makes
only one. For that endpoint the lever is a narrower enumeration (a prefix-scoped `get_keys`,
if the host supports one) — worth checking before anything is designed.

- [x] Deploy `051cfa7` to Akamai — done when: `X-SS-Version` reports the deployed label — **DONE.** The CLI hit its documented 60-second readiness timeout and reported `failed to wait for deployment to go live`; the deploy had in fact succeeded, exactly as CLAUDE.md says. Confirmed by polling `X-SS-Version` until it flipped, and no request was measured before it did.
- [x] Verify the Clicks column on the deployed build — file(s): (none — verification step) — done when: it renders real totals with no console errors — **DONE.** Live values (524 / 2 / 0), **zero console errors** — which also clears the new favicon against `gui-pages`' no-`'unsafe-inline'` CSP. At 390px every documented invariant still holds: figure **327/327 and does not scroll**, no page overflow, select column collapsed to 0 with `#bulk-desktop-only` visible, and `td[data-cell="clicks"]` resolving — confirming the named-cell refactor that replaced the positional `children[3]/[6]/[7]` lookups.

**Not re-measured, deliberately: recent-events retention.** The `EventSlot` fix was already
measured live on `9fdbf78-p1p2-fixes` (8 clicks 300 ms apart → 8 distinct events, against 3
under the old code) and `051cfa7` does not touch it. Repeating it would only add ~38
permanent analytics keys to the store — which, per the finding above, is now a cost.

## Measure the `list_keys` growth rate (2026-08-10)

The trigger named at the end of the section above. `/api/analytics/click-totals` runs on every
dashboard load and its enumeration is its dominant, un-overlappable cost; the store grows at up
to 94 analytics keys per link and analytics is the only unbounded namespace. Two data points at
one store size could not establish a growth rate, so the risk was flagged rather than projected.

**Method.** Seed junk *links* (never clicked, so they add no analytics keys and are fully
reversible via bulk delete) and re-trace `click-totals` at each size. That endpoint is the right
probe precisely because its `get` count is fixed by real click data — 6-7 reads — while its
`list_keys` walks the whole physical store, so seeding isolates the enumeration. Every figure is
reported **normalized against a `get` from the same request**, because Akamai KV latency swings
~3x between windows and a raw-millisecond comparison across stages would attribute a regime swing
to store size.

- [x] Establish a baseline at the current store size — file(s): (none — measurement) — done when: N>=12 traced `click-totals` samples at 962 keys give a median `list_keys` and a median `list_keys / mean_get` ratio — **DONE: 64.2 ms, 2.59x a single `get`.** This already corrects the previously-recorded figure: **the warm median is 64 ms, not the ~99 ms mean recorded on 2026-08-10.** The first sample taken after an idle period measured **174.6 ms** and every subsequent one sat at 60–70 ms, so the earlier mean was pulled up by cold samples. **Discard the first traced sample after idle** — it is a different measurement.
- [x] Measure at successively larger store sizes — file(s): (none — measurement) — done when: at least three store sizes spanning a wide range have been measured the same way, and the shape (linear / sublinear / flat) is stated with the evidence — **DONE, four sizes spanning 10.4x. It is LINEAR at ~68.7 µs per physical key with essentially zero fixed cost (R² = 0.997).**
- [x] Restore the store to its pre-measurement size — file(s): (none — cleanup) — done when: every seeded link is bulk-deleted, a fresh trace shows the key count and `list_keys` back at baseline, and the dashboard shows the original 14 links — **DONE.** 9,000 seeded links bulk-deleted in 180 requests (~8 min); `GET /api/links` reports **14 links**, a backup reports **964 keys** against the 962 baseline (+2 analytics, unrelated to seeding — the seeded links were never clicked), and `GET /api/admin/consistency` returns `ok: true` with **zero findings across all 12 checks**, so 180 bulk deletes left no index drift.
- [x] Record the finding — file(s): TASKS.md, CLAUDE.md — done when: CLAUDE.md's "Parallel KV reads" enumeration paragraph states the measured growth shape instead of "the growth rate is NOT measured", and the confirmed absence of a prefix-scoped enumeration is recorded where the fix was proposed — **DONE.**

**Result — measured on the deployed build `051cfa7-clicks`, 2026-08-10. Each row is the median of 10 traced samples.**

| physical keys | `list_keys` | ratio to one `get` | mean `get` | `click-totals` wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 962 (baseline) | **64.2 ms** | 2.59x | 25.6 ms | 193 ms |
| 1,962 | **144.9 ms** | 5.45x | 26.3 ms | 274 ms |
| 4,962 | **315.4 ms** | 12.33x | 25.4 ms | 450 ms |
| 9,962 | **689.9 ms** | 26.23x | 26.8 ms | 852 ms |
| 964 (after cleanup) | **69.2 ms** | 2.54x | 28.6 ms | 213 ms |

`list_keys_ms = 68.7 µs/key x keys - 2.8 ms`, **R² = 0.997**.

**Two controls make this a measurement rather than a correlation.** First, **`get` never moved** — 25.4 to 28.6 ms at every single store size — so the latency regime held for the whole run and the raw millisecond comparison is valid, not just the normalized ratio. That matters because CLAUDE.md records 3x regime swings between windows minutes apart, which is exactly what would otherwise masquerade as a growth curve. Second, **the cost came back down**: the final row is the same store, re-measured after cleanup, back at baseline. The effect rose 10x and returned.

**What it means, and the number worth remembering: every physical key in the store costs ~69 µs on every single dashboard load.** Extrapolating the fit (linear, so extrapolation is defensible here in a way it was not before):

| store size | enumeration cost per dashboard load |
|---|---|
| ~14,100 keys (~150 links at the 94-keys/link ceiling) | **~1.0 s** |
| 20,000 keys | ~1.4 s |
| ~94,000 keys (~1,000 links) | **~6.5 s** |
| ~434,000 keys | **~30 s — Akamai's handler duration limit** |

The handler limit is far away; **the usable limit is not.** At 962 keys the enumeration is 33% of `click-totals`' wall time; at 9,962 it is 81%.

**The lever proposed for this is CONFIRMED UNAVAILABLE.** The previous section said "the lever is a narrower enumeration (a prefix-scoped `get_keys`, if the host supports one) — worth checking before anything is designed." It was checked: **`spin:key-value/key-value@3.0.0`'s `get-keys()` takes no arguments at all** — no prefix, no cursor (`Store.get_keys(self)`, and the Go SDK's `(*Store).GetKeys()` is the same shape). There is nothing to scope. Any fix has to avoid the enumeration rather than narrow it.

**An unexpected convergence, and the reason this measurement changes a priority.** 941 of the 962 keys are analytics, and **30 of the up-to-94 keys per link are `events:` ring-buffer slots** — a feature already documented as a best-effort sample that the dashboard never reads. The existing Future-work entry *"Reduce the redirect's KV writes per click from two to one"* proposes dropping that write to double the app-wide click ceiling. It would **also cut analytics key growth by roughly a third**, and therefore slow this enumeration's growth by the same fraction. That entry's own trigger (sustained traffic near ~25 clicks/second) has not fired, but it now has a **second, independent justification** that its write-up does not mention. Consider the two together rather than separately.

**Not separated, deliberately: key count versus total bytes.** Seeding added ~200-byte link records with ~20-character key names, against analytics keys with ~30-character names. `get-keys` returns key names only, so value size is unlikely to matter, but this experiment cannot prove it — it varied both together. Treat "~69 µs per key" as the honest per-key figure for keys of roughly this app's shape, not as a claim about which property drives it.

**Method note for anyone repeating this.** Seed junk *links*, never clicks: a link that is never resolved creates no analytics keys, so the seeding is fully reversible through bulk delete, whereas clicks would leave permanent analytics keys behind. And probe with `click-totals` specifically — its `get` count is pinned by real click data (6-7 reads) and does not grow with seeded links, so the only thing moving between stages is the enumeration. Seeding ran at ~1,000 links/minute (50 per bulk request); deleting is slower at ~1,100/minute.

## Orphaned analytics purge

The consequence of the measurement above. `links.handle_delete` and the bulk delete path never
remove analytics keys — a deliberate decision, argued in `docs/plans/kv-consistency-check.md`'s
rejected alternative #1 on the grounds that "orphan analytics are harmless in a way orphan links
are not". **That clause is now false and the measurement is what falsified it:** an enumeration
costs ~68.7 µs per physical key, `GET /api/analytics/click-totals` makes one on every dashboard
load, and **907 of the store's 943 analytics keys (96%) belong to 28 slugs with no link record** —
62.3 ms of every dashboard load spent walking data nothing can ever read, against 14 live links of
which only 2 have any analytics at all. The audience is marketing staff who create heavily and
delete heavily, so live links plateau while orphans grow without bound.

Plan: `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`. Shape: a cheap report (`GET
/api/admin/analytics/orphans`, 2 KV operations regardless of orphan count) plus a chunked,
client-driven purge (`POST /api/admin/analytics/purge`, ≤50 slugs and ≤250 deletes per request),
both gated on `users.manage`, both on the existing maintenance page. **No new KV key type, no
change to `redirect`, no change to what a click writes, and deliberately not a 13th consistency
check** — see "Considered and rejected" for all seven rejected alternatives, including the
arithmetic showing why inline purging cannot fit bulk delete's 30-second envelope.

Two properties worth carrying into review. **The report may be misled by index drift; the purge
cannot be** — the report derives liveness from `all_links` (cheap), the purge from
`exists("slug:<S>")` on the record itself, so an `unindexed_link` is skipped rather than deleted.
And **the purge deletes enumerated keys, never constructed ones**, which is what makes it pick up
the legacy unsharded `count:<slug>`, keys left by an older larger `analytics_event_slots`, and any
future raise of `CountShards`, for free.

## Row-level Disable/Enable (2026-08-10)

Picked up after the user described the intended audience: **marketing staff who are not
technical, who will create a lot of links and delete many of them as they make mistakes and
correct.** That reframes an already-shipped control as a defect. A single-link status control
existed — a `.edit-disabled` checkbox in the row edit form — but reaching it meant clicking Edit
and scrolling past Destination, Starts, Expires, two password fields, Tags and Owner. **Delete,
which is irreversible and kills a URL that may already be printed or in a QR code, was one click
away in the actions column.** The safe correction was harder to reach than the destructive one.

- [x] Add a row-level Disable/Enable button — file(s): gui/dashboard.js — done when: a link's status can be changed from the row without opening the edit form, and the redirect behaviour actually follows — **DONE.** `statusToggleHtml` renders it **between Edit and Delete**, so the reversible action sits in the user's path before the irreversible one. Label states the outcome (`Disable` / `Enable`) rather than the current state, which is well-defined because only `active` and `disabled` are ever stored — `scheduled`/`expired` are derived from the window by `resolveLinkState()`. **No confirmation dialog, deliberately:** it is instantly reversible by the same button, and the existing bulk Enable/Disable already run without one (only bulk delete confirms). Adding friction would re-create the imbalance this fixes.
- [x] Retire the edit-form checkbox — file(s): gui/dashboard.js — done when: exactly one control owns `status` — **DONE, and the two together were a live bug rather than a redundancy.** `editRowHtml` is built once by `renderLinksTable()`, so a checkbox rendered *before* a button toggle still held the old value and **would silently revert the status on Save.** `handleEditFormSubmit` no longer sends `status` at all; `handle_update` gates every field on `if "field" in payload`, so omitting it leaves the stored status untouched. Verified directly: editing a disabled link's destination and tags saved both and left it disabled (still 404s), which is exactly what would have regressed.
- [x] Verify live, including the redirect — file(s): (none — verification) — done when: the full round trip works in a real browser with no console errors — **DONE.** Disable → badge, button label, `aria-label` and `data-status` all flip in place and `/r/{slug}` returns **404**; Enable → returns **302** to the corrected destination. Sibling rows untouched. **Zero console errors or warnings**, which also clears the new button against `gui-pages`' no-`'unsafe-inline'` CSP. Suites: api 530, gui-pages 71.

**Repaints in place rather than calling `loadLinks()`.** A full re-render clears the bulk
selection by design, so refreshing here would silently drop any checkbox ticked beforehand — the
same reason click totals paint in place. **Starts/Expires repaint too, not just the badge**: both
cells' "starts soon"/"expires soon" notes are predicated on the link being active, so updating
only the badge would leave an expiry warning on a link that no longer resolves at all. The status
cell gained `data-cell="status"`, continuing the named-cell refactor that replaced positional
`children[n]` lookups.

**Layout impact, measured rather than assumed, because this adds a 5th button to the sticky
actions column.** At **390px the documented invariant still holds exactly: the figure measures
327/327 and does not scroll**, no page overflow, actions column unchanged at 95px — because below
600px the group wraps into a stack capped at `max-width: 100px`, so a 5th button adds height, not
width. All five buttons measure **44px tall**, meeting DESIGN.md's tap-target floor.

**On desktop it does widen the table, and the honest version is narrower than it first looked.**
At a 1280px viewport the figure went 1176/1176 to 1210/1176 — fits to scrolls. But that was
measured against artificially short seeded URLs. With a realistic UTM-bearing marketing URL the
table **already scrolled before this change** (1192 > 1176), so the button widens an existing
scroll (1192 → 1251) rather than creating one, and the sticky actions column is precisely the
mechanism for that. Worth re-checking if the Destination column's 352px cap is ever revisited.

**A dev-workflow gotcha found the hard way and now recorded in CLAUDE.md's Commands section:**
editing a file under `gui/` does **not** take effect on a running `spin up` — `spin_static_fs`
serves a snapshot taken at startup. A fix that was correct on disk kept reproducing the old
error, and `curl localhost:3000/dashboard.js` served the stale file while the on-disk file was
right. Restart `spin up`, and diff the served asset against the file when a GUI fix appears not
to work.

- [x] Deploy the row-level Disable/Enable control — file(s): (none — deploy) — done when: `X-SS-Version` reports the new label and the toggle works against the deployed app — **DONE 2026-08-10, deployed as `app_version=872c2ce-disable-btn`.** The CLI hit its documented 60-second readiness timeout and reported `failed to wait for deployment to go live`; the deploy had succeeded, and polling `X-SS-Version` showed it live **~100 s** after the CLI gave up. No request was measured before it flipped. **All five variables re-supplied and each verified rather than assumed:** login succeeds (`admin_bootstrap_password`), `/api/auth/me` reports the real `fwf.app` domain with no `localhost` leak (`public_base_urls` — the documented silent-revert trap), and the served `dashboard.js` contains `status-btn` and no `edit-disabled`. End-to-end on the deployed app: active **302** → PATCH disabled → **404** → PATCH active → **302**, with `target_url` unchanged through the status-only PATCH. Test link deleted afterwards; it left ~2 analytics keys behind, which is the very ratchet `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md` exists to fix.

## Recent-events table was throwing in production (found 2026-08-11)

Found by the builder while verifying the orphan purge, and **unrelated to that
work** — it shipped in `051cfa7` on 2026-08-10 and was live on Akamai in both
`051cfa7-clicks` and `872c2ce-disable-btn`.

- [x] Fix `formatTimestamp`'s `precise` branch — file(s): gui/app.js — done when: the recent-events table renders on a link that has events — **DONE.** `Intl.DateTimeFormat` was constructed with `dateStyle: "medium"` *and* `hour`/`minute`/`second`/`fractionalSecondDigits`. **ECMA-402 forbids combining `dateStyle`/`timeStyle` with any individual component option**, so the constructor threw `TypeError: Invalid option`. Fixed by spelling the date parts out (`year`/`month`/`day`), which reproduces `dateStyle: "medium"` exactly.

**The builder's diagnosis named the wrong cause and the distinction matters.** It reported `second: "2-digit"` + `fractionalSecondDigits: 3` as the invalid combination. That pair is perfectly legal — verified directly: `{hour, minute, second, fractionalSecondDigits}` formats fine, and it is the presence of `dateStyle` alongside *any* of them that throws. Acting on the reported cause would have meant deleting `fractionalSecondDigits`, silently reverting the millisecond precision that `051cfa7` existed to add, while appearing to fix the bug.

**Why it survived a deploy verification.** The throw is inside `links/detail.js`'s recent-events render loop, so **a link with no events renders fine** and only links that actually have events show an empty table. The `051cfa7` deploy check exercised the dashboard's Clicks column and a freshly-created link; neither path enters the loop. **A smoke test on a fresh link cannot see this class of bug — exercise a link with real traffic.**

**The irony worth keeping:** `051cfa7` added millisecond resolution specifically to answer a critique finding that identical-looking timestamps "read as broken". It shipped a change that made the table not render at all, and the feature has therefore never actually worked in production until now.

Verified live: 5 clicks 300 ms apart render 5 rows at `01:42:56.544` / `.206` / `55.852` / `.504` / `.164` — distinct milliseconds visible, which is the whole point of the change. Zero console errors.

## Deploy of the orphan purge + events fix (2026-08-11)

Deployed `55dc06d` as `app_version=55dc06d-orphan-purge`. The CLI again hit its documented
60-second readiness timeout; the build went live **~110 s** later, confirmed by polling
`X-SS-Version`. All five variables re-supplied and verified: login succeeds, `/api/auth/me`
reports the real `fwf.app` domain with no `localhost` leak, and both changed assets are served
(`app.js` carries the events fix, `admin/backup.js` carries the purge UI).

**This also puts the recent-events fix live**, so that table works in production for the first
time since `051cfa7` shipped it broken.

**First orphan report against the real store — it confirms the hand-analysis that motivated the
whole feature, from a completely separate code path:**

| | |
|---|---|
| analytics keys scanned | 947 |
| live slugs | 14 |
| **orphan slugs** | **29** |
| **orphan keys** | **911 (96% of the namespace)** |
| live keys | 36 |
| unrecognized | 0 |

Earlier hand-decoding of a backup gave 907/943; the small drift is the test links created and
deleted in between. Two independent methods agreeing is the point. At the measured ~68.7 µs/key,
purging would take **~63 ms off every dashboard load**. The largest orphans are the
`shardverify*`/`s64verify*` load-test slugs left by the 2026-08-07 sharding measurements.

- [x] Deploy `55dc06d` — done when: `X-SS-Version` reports the label and both changes are live — **DONE.**
- [x] Run the purge against the deployed store and re-measure `list_keys` — file(s): (none — measurement) — done when: the purge has removed the 911 orphan keys, a fresh `click-totals` trace gives a new `list_keys` median, and the drop is compared against the ~68.7 µs/key model's prediction (911 × 68.7 µs ≈ 63 ms, i.e. ~66 ms → ~3 ms). **This is a destructive action on the deployed store and is deliberately left for an explicit go-ahead** — the data is unreadable by definition, but it is not recoverable once deleted.

**PURGE RUN AGAINST THE DEPLOYED STORE, 2026-08-11 — and it falsified part of the model.**

Run with explicit user go-ahead. **4 chunked rounds, biggest-slug-first, 234 + 227 + 233 + 217 =
911 keys deleted**, every round inside the 250-key budget. Analytics namespace went **947 → 36
keys**; the orphan report now returns `orphan_slugs: 0`. **Live data verifiably intact:** the
busiest slug still reports **524**, matching both the figure recorded at the `051cfa7` deploy and
an independent cross-check through `GET /api/links/{slug}/analytics`, which sums the shards by a
completely separate code path.

| | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| physical keys | 968 | 57 | −911 |
| `list_keys` median | **74.9 ms** | **23.9 ms** | **−51.0 ms** |
| ratio to one `get` | 2.57× | 0.85× | −1.72× |
| `click-totals` wall | 223.5 ms | 167.9 ms | −55.6 ms |

Both rows were measured in the **same latency window** (`get` 28.5 vs 28.9 ms), so this comparison
is sound in raw milliseconds and not only in ratio.

**The model predicted the drop but not the floor, and the floor is the new finding.** It
predicted 62.6 ms of saving against 51.0 ms measured (~19% over), because it predicted the
post-purge cost would fall to **~1 ms** when it actually bottomed out at **23.9 ms**. The
2026-08-10 fit was taken over four store sizes that were *all ≥ 962 keys*, where a ~20 ms fixed
cost is 2–30% of the total and is absorbed into noise as a ~0 intercept. At 57 keys it is
essentially the whole measurement.

**A `list_keys` costs about one KV round trip plus ~68.7 µs per key.** The floor measures **0.85×
a single `get`** — i.e. the enumeration is at minimum one operation, which is what it must be.
**Enumeration can never be made free, only proportional-to-nothing**, so ~24 ms is the hard
ceiling on any future win from shrinking the store. Refitting all six points regime-normalised
gives `lk/get = 2.53e-3 × keys + 0.31`, R² = 0.9989 — **the slope is confirmed unchanged**, so
every forward-looking growth projection in this file still stands; only the low end was wrong.

**The honest caveat:** even the refit under-predicts the 57-key point by 45%, because least
squares over a range dominated by large values cannot fit the low end well. Treat "~1 KV
operation" as the floor, not the refit's 0.31 intercept.

## Inline analytics purge on single-link delete

Reopens **rejected alternative #3** of `docs/plans/analytics-orphan-purge.md`, which is amended
in place to point here. Its bulk-delete half stands (4,750 writes is 95–123 s against a 30 s
handler limit, re-derived); its single-link half does not. That rejection priced the **saturated**
95-key link, but analytics keys accumulate by coupon-collector — `64(1-(63/64)^C) +
30(1-(29/30)^C)` — so the dominant case for this audience, a mistyped link deleted after ~3
clicks, holds **~6 keys: ~24 ms of enumeration plus ~138 ms of writes**, three orders of magnitude
below the "~2–2.5 seconds" the rejection quoted. Its one-line dismissal of the conditional variant
was also inverted: the enumeration measured **23.9 ms** against **~2,185 ms** for 95 writes, so it
is not "most of the cost" — it is what makes an inline purge cheap, by turning 95 speculative
writes into a handful of real ones.

**The gap being closed is organisational, not arithmetic.** The shipped tool is operator-driven,
and the audience creating the orphans is not the audience that runs it: a marketing user deleting
a mistake has no reason to ever open the Store maintenance page, so today every such delete
ratchets the store up until an administrator remembers.

Plan: `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`. Shape: `links.handle_delete` takes an
injected `purge_analytics` callable (`links.py` cannot import `analyticsorphans` — `analytics.py`
already imports `links`), invoked **after** the record and both index writes, wrapped so a KV
failure can never turn a successful deletion into a 500. `MAX_INLINE_PURGE_KEYS = 128` is a rail
that cannot fire at shipped configuration, not a policy. **Bulk delete is untouched, `redirect` is
untouched, no new KV key type, no new route, no new Spin variable, and the manual operator tool
and its confirmation posture are unchanged.**

**`consistency.py`'s "orphans are normal state" argument was checked, not assumed, and it
survives.** `docs/plans/kv-consistency-check.md`'s rejected alternative #1 names its own revisit
trigger as "deletion being changed to purge analytics" — but four sources of orphans survive this
change: bulk delete, every orphan created before this ships, a `failed` inline purge, and a
`deferred` one. Orphans remain expected state between purges, so a 13th check would still pin
`ok: false` on a structurally flawless store. Only `api/app.py`'s consistency-route comment needs
a clause updated, from "`links.handle_delete` never removes them" to "bulk delete never removes
them".

**Two figures in the plan are MODELLED, not measured, and are flagged as such.** Per-link key
counts come from the coupon-collector formula; one production data point cuts against them — the
2026-08-11 report found **36 live analytics keys across 14 live links** while the busiest live
slug reports **524 clicks**, which the model would put near saturation on its own. The likely
reconciliation is that click history spans configuration changes (pre-sharding clicks went into
one key; 16-shard-era clicks spread over 16, not 64), so a link's key count reflects clicks since
the last config change rather than lifetime clicks. A verification task measures a real one.

**Open questions closed 2026-08-11 — and the first was settled by measurement, not opinion.**
See `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`'s "Decisions taken" section.

**The key-count model is validated.** The plan flagged that the production store showed 36 live
analytics keys across 14 links while the busiest slug reports 524 clicks — which coupon-collector
would put near saturation (~94 keys) on its own. Decoding a live backup resolves it: **`cYrI0dR`
holds ZERO shard keys**; all 524 clicks sit in the single legacy unsharded `count:<slug>` key, so
its history predates sharding entirely and the model never governed it. **`jwh`, the only link
whose whole history is post-sharding, holds 5 keys against a predicted 6 at 3 clicks.** The model
holds on the only link that can test it. Corollary worth keeping: **legacy high-traffic links are
cheap to purge** (31 keys, not 94) because their clicks never fanned out across shards.

The other two: **no policy cap** on inline purge (accepted worst case ~2.2 s at ~86% of the
app-wide write cap, matching the already-shipped purge endpoint's 5.75 s per chunk), and the
**delete confirmation copy is unchanged** (deleting a link already made its analytics unreachable,
so nothing observable changes for the user).

**A correction to something this file asserted, promoted here because it changes what the work is
for.** The "feedback property" — inline purging keeps the store small, keeping enumeration cheap —
is real but **weak**, and earlier wording overstated it. Post-purge production is 57 keys of which
**36 (63%) are live analytics**, and in a mature deployment live analytics *is* the store. At 100
live busy links that is ~9,400 keys and **~650 ms of enumeration per dashboard load with zero
orphans present**. **Inline purge removes the unbounded term, not the baseline** — it buys time.
Pagination, caching `click-totals`, or cutting the `events:` write are still eventually required.

## Links pagination — deferred, and what actually binds (2026-08-11)

Asked to plan pagination for `GET /api/links`, with an explicit invitation to answer the prior
question honestly first. **The answer is defer: pagination is third in line, and for the problem
people usually mean by it, it is the wrong tool.** Plan, with the full design so that firing a
trigger means execution rather than re-planning: `docs/plans/links-pagination.md`.

**The arithmetic that decides it.** Reads per dashboard load, analytics key counts MODELLED from
the coupon-collector formula `64(1-(63/64)^C)` + `30(1-(29/30)^C)` (validated at exactly one live
point — `jwh`, 5 keys at 3 clicks against a predicted 6), enumeration cost using the **measured**
`~24 ms + 68.7 µs/key`:

| shape | physical keys | enumeration | `click-totals` gets | `/api/links` reads | `/api/links` share |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| today (14 links, 2 clicked) | 57 | 24 ms | ~6 | 17 | 74% |
| 100 links @ 50 clicks | ~6,000 | ~440 ms | ~3,500 | 103 | **2.9%** |
| 500 links @ 50 clicks | ~30,200 | ~2,100 ms | ~17,400 | 503 | **2.8%** |
| 1,000 links @ 10 clicks | ~19,000 | ~1,330 ms | ~9,300 | 1,003 | 9.7% |

**`GET /api/analytics/click-totals` runs on the same dashboard load and costs ~35× more reads, on
two independent unbounded axes** — a full-store enumeration (measured, linear, un-overlappable)
and one `get` per *existing* count-shard key of every visible slug (`api/analytics.py:147-149`).
Its docstring frames the second as the win: *"cost becomes proportional to real traffic rather
than to links × shard count."* Proportional-to-real-traffic **is** the unbounded term, and the
2026-08-10 seeding run cannot speak to it — it seeded links that were deliberately never clicked.

**A new inference worth confirming: a single handler's read throughput appears to top out at
~1,000 reads/second, exactly Akamai's published per-app cap.** Computing ops ÷ wall from the four
recorded gathered traces — `/api/links` 55 ops → 318/s, consistency 69 → 246/s, analytics 100 →
407/s, **export 999 → 1,044/s** — throughput rises monotonically with fan-out and stops dead on
the published number. If that is the cap rather than coincidence, **wall time for any fan-out
above ~1,000 reads is `reads ÷ 1,000` seconds and no parallelism improves it**, which turns the
table above into hard floors: ~3.5 s at 100 links, ~17.4 s at 500. The competing explanation is
queueing under 100-way concurrency (100 in flight ÷ ~96 ms/op also gives ~1,044/s); both give the
same practical rule. UNCONFIRMED either way — task 3 below.

**Two problems are both called "pagination", and they have different answers.** Server read cost
is not the binding constraint and pagination recovers under 3% of it. Client render and memory
cost is real, unmeasured, and its answer is **windowed rendering** — no API change, no cascade,
no correctness regression, because `allLinks` stays complete. That entry is under Future work.

**Priority of the already-planned inline analytics purge is UNCHANGED — ship it next.** It is
planned, unbuilt and cheap, and it removes the unbounded orphan term. But every figure above
assumes **zero orphans present**, so it does not move them: post-purge production is 57 keys of
which 36 (63%) are live analytics, and in a mature deployment live analytics *is* the store.

- [ ] Measure GET /api/analytics/click-totals' shard-read fan-out against a clicked store — file(s): (none — measurement) — done when: on the deployed build at least 3 link-count/click-count combinations have been traced with X-SS-Debug recording get count, list_keys and wall time, the per-link get growth is compared against the coupon-collector prediction 64x(1-(63/64)^C), the reads-per-dashboard-load figure is stated, and every seeded link is deleted and its analytics removed via POST /api/admin/analytics/purge afterwards with a follow-up orphan report showing orphan_slugs 0
- [ ] Confirm or refute the ~1,000 reads/second single-handler throughput ceiling (depends on the trace above) — file(s): CLAUDE.md — done when: ops divided by wall time is computed for a traced handler with a fan-out above 2,000 reads and compared against the existing four points (55 ops 318/s, 69 ops 246/s, 100 ops 407/s, 999 ops 1044/s), and CLAUDE.md's "Parallel KV reads" section either states the confirmed ceiling with the rule that wall time for a large fan-out is reads divided by 1000 seconds, or records the refutation and what the real scaling is
- [ ] Record the pagination deferral, its trigger and the ranking (depends on all three measurements) — file(s): CLAUDE.md, TASKS.md — done when: CLAUDE.md's "Parallel KV reads" closing paragraph no longer implies pagination is the next fix, states instead that click-totals binds first on two independent axes with the measured reads-per-load ratio, distinguishes server read cost from client render cost and names windowed rendering as the answer to the second, and TASKS.md's "Future work (not scheduled)" carries a links-pagination entry naming both triggers from docs/plans/links-pagination.md

**Measurement hygiene for tasks 1-2, learned the hard way and worth repeating here.** Clicks
leave permanent analytics keys, so the cleanup in task 2 is not optional — leaving them behind
corrupts the next `list_keys` measurement anyone takes. Hold click seeding under ~20 requests/s
(`dev/click-load.sh` warns at 50) or the run measures the app-wide write cap instead. And discard
the first traced sample after any idle period: it measures ~175 ms against a 60-70 ms warm median.

**Blocker cleared before it was raised: the deployed build's `log_debug_token` IS known.** The plan
records task 2 as blocked behind a redeploy on the belief the token could not be recovered. It
can — it lives in the operator's deploy-secrets file outside the repo, `55dc06d-orphan-purge` was
deployed with it, and it has been used to trace this deployment repeatedly today (including the
purge before/after measurement in the section above). **No redeploy is needed.** This blocker was
genuine for *earlier* builds (see the two notes above about unknown tokens on previously-deployed
builds) but is not for the current one; a planning agent cannot see that file, which is why it
was flagged.

**Verified independently, and it inverts the priority — `handle_click_totals` has a second
unbounded axis that the 2026-08-10 seeding run structurally could not detect.** It reads every
existing `count:` key for every visible slug, so reads scale with **shards touched**, which grows
with traffic toward the 64-shard ceiling:

| clicks/link | shards hit | reads @ 100 links | vs. the naive 65×N it was designed to avoid |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 3.0 | 295 | 5% |
| 50 | 34.9 | 3,488 | 54% |
| 200 | 61.3 | 6,126 | **94%** |
| 500+ | 64.0 | 6,398 | 98% |

`api/analytics.py`'s own docstring calls the win *"proportional to real traffic rather than to
links × shard count"*. That is true and it is **not a bound**: proportional-to-real-traffic is
itself unbounded, so the protection holds for quiet links and **evaporates for exactly the busy
links a marketing team cares about**. **The 2026-08-10 measurement could not have found this** —
it seeded 9,000 links that were deliberately never clicked, so they produced no count-shard keys
and the endpoint's `get` count stayed at 6 for the whole experiment. That isolation was correct
for measuring the enumeration and is precisely why this axis went unmeasured. **Any future
measurement of this endpoint must seed clicks, not just links.**

## MEASURED: the Clicks column does not scale, and it outranks everything queued (2026-08-11)

Run after the user pointed out that the `fwf.app` deployment is a disposable test site and that
measurements should reshape its data freely rather than tiptoe around it. **That correction is
what made this measurable** — the previous run's caution (seed links, never click them) is exactly
what hid the effect.

**Method.** 20 links seeded, then clicked in stages, tracing `click-totals` at each. The `get`
count in the log line **is** Σ shards-touched, so this measures the axis directly rather than
inferring it. Clicks paced at ~17 req/s (~34 writes/s), under the 50 write/s cap, so counter loss
is not a factor.

| stage | clicks/link | `get` measured | coupon-collector model | err | wall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | **7** | 7 | 0% | 175 ms |
| B | 5 | **106** | 104 | +2% | 197 ms |
| C | 25 | **417** | 424 | −2% | 412 ms |
| D | 100 | **930** | 1022 | −9% | 792 ms |

**The model holds across a 130× range of read counts.** Stage A is the headline for method:
**20 new links moved `get` not at all**, because unclicked links create no count keys — which is
precisely why the 2026-08-10 seeding run could not see this axis.

**Two things this establishes.**

1. **Reads scale with traffic, without bound, toward 64 per link.** `handle_click_totals` reads
   every existing `count:` key for every visible slug. `api/analytics.py`'s docstring calls this
   "proportional to real traffic rather than to links × shard count" — true, and **not a bound.**
2. **Wall time scales too, once reads pass `gather_reads`' 100-concurrent bound.** 175 → 792 ms
   across the stages. Below 100 reads gathering hides the cost; above it, the fan-out serialises
   into waves and the user feels it. `GET /api/links` never showed this because it stayed under
   the bound.

**Extrapolated, and this is the part that reorders the backlog** — reads issued by ONE dashboard
load, against Akamai's **1,000 reads/second app-wide cap that redirects also draw from**:

| links | clicks/link | reads | share of the app-wide cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 | 50 | 3,488 | **349%** |
| 100 | 200 | 6,126 | **613%** |
| 200 | 200 | 12,251 | **1,225%** |

**A single dashboard load at 100 modestly-successful links would need roughly six seconds of the
entire application's read budget.** Every concurrent redirect competes with it. This is a design
limit, not a tuning problem, and it binds far sooner than pagination (2.9% of reads) or the
orphan ratchet (which inline purge addresses).

- [x] Measure `handle_click_totals`' traffic-driven read axis — file(s): (none — measurement) — done when: the coupon-collector model is confirmed or refuted against real clicks — **DONE, confirmed.**
- [ ] Decide what to do about the Clicks column's read cost — file(s): api/analytics.py, docs/plans/ — done when: an approach is chosen with its trade-offs recorded. The denormalised `analytics:total:<slug>` rejected in that docstring ("adds a THIRD KV write to every click") deserves re-costing **against these numbers** rather than against the ones available when it was rejected: it would make the endpoint O(N) reads with no traffic term at all. The write cap is 50/s and the read cap 1,000/s, so the trade is 1 extra write per click against thousands of reads per dashboard load — the opposite conclusion to the one reached before, and it should be re-argued rather than assumed either way.

**Cleanup:** all 20 seeded links deleted and their 1,597 analytics keys purged in 7 chunks; the
store is back to exactly its pre-measurement state (36 analytics keys, 14 links, 0 orphans).

**One honest gap:** stage D came in 9% under model. Click loss is unlikely at 34 writes/s, so the
likelier cause is shard-selection non-uniformity — but the seeded links were deleted before their
recorded totals were compared against the 2,000 clicks issued, so this was not run down. Check
recorded totals *before* cleanup next time.

## The Clicks column's read cost — re-costing the denormalised total (2026-08-12)

Answers the open "Decide what to do about the Clicks column's read cost" task in the section
above. Full re-costing: `docs/plans/denormalised-click-total.md`.

**Verdict: the original rejection stands, and its stated reason is wrong.** `api/analytics.py`'s
docstring rejects `analytics:total:<slug>` because "writes are the binding constraint". Measured
against the new numbers, that is now the *weaker* half of the argument — a 33% cut in a
25-clicks/second sustained ceiling this deployment has never approached is a smaller real cost
than 613% of the app-wide read budget per dashboard load, and the third write costs **no TTFB at
all**, because `sendRedirectThenRecord` (`redirect/main.go:380-398`) hands the 302 to the host
before any analytics runs. The read-side win is real and large: `1 + N` reads with no traffic term
and no enumeration, a 60× reduction at 100 links × 200 clicks.

**What actually kills it is accuracy.** `analytics:total:<slug>` is one key per slug,
read-modify-written per click, with no compare-and-swap — byte for byte the pre-sharding
`analytics:count:<slug>` shape MEASURED live 2026-08-06 at **0% loss below ~2.7 clicks/s and 25%
at 9.4 clicks/s on one slug**. The sharded sum stays exact, so the dashboard's uncaveated Clicks
column would silently under-report a busy campaign link while the caveated detail page reports it
correctly. **`wasi:keyvalue/atomics`' `increment` cannot rescue it — Akamai documents that
interface as unsupported** (fetched 2026-08-12), and the bindings shipping in both SDKs makes that
a trap rather than an option. **Dropping the `events:` write buys back the whole write budget and
does nothing at all for the accuracy problem**, which is why it is rejected as a *trade* while
staying live as a Future-work item on its own merits — the user's 2026-08-10 decision that recent
events stays is not overturned here.

**The operating ceiling, for monitoring.** One dashboard load costs
`1 + N × 64 × (1 − (63/64)^C)` reads for N visible links averaging C clicks. It crosses 1,000
reads — one full second of the app's entire read budget, shared with every concurrent redirect —
at roughly **200 links × 5 clicks, 48 × 25, 29 × 50, 20 × 100, or 16 × 200**. Production today is
at ~7 reads and ~175 ms (14 links, only 2 ever clicked, and the busiest slug's 524 clicks sit
entirely in the *legacy unsharded* key, contributing 1 read rather than 64). **The trigger is not
link count; it is how many links have been clicked more than a handful of times**, and 16 campaign
links at 200 clicks each is an ordinary year for this audience.

**Two things this schedules, and one spike.** A measured multiplier is removed for free —
`loadClickTotals()` runs inside `loadLinks()` (`gui/dashboard.js:379`), which fires from **9**
call sites, so a user who bulk-creates then tags then disables pays four full-store enumerations
and four full fan-outs for data that provably cannot have changed (only a click changes a click
total). And `wasi:keyvalue/batch`'s `get_many` — confirmed *supported* on Akamai by the same
sentence that killed atomics — could collapse the fan-out into one host call with **no new key
type, no backfill, no `redirect` change, no write-budget change, no accuracy change and no feature
loss**. Whether Akamai bills a `get-many` of K keys as 1 read or K is the single unconfirmed fact
that decides whether it is a complete fix or only a latency fix.

**Priority of the two planned-but-unbuilt items is UNCHANGED.** `docs/plans/inline-analytics-purge-on-delete.md`
ships next: it addresses the **enumeration** term, and nothing recommended here touches that term
(the batch spike collapses the fan-out and leaves `list_keys` exactly as it is). Pagination stays
third, and its "do not pick this up before `click-totals` is bounded" constraint is untouched,
because this does not bound `click-totals`. The `## Links pagination` section's task 2 ("measure
the shard-read fan-out against a clicked store") is **satisfied** by the 2026-08-11 measurement.

**Independently verified 2026-08-12, including two corrections to the brief that produced this plan.**

**The Akamai support claim is confirmed verbatim** (`techdocs.akamai.com/akamai-functions/docs/use-the-key-value-store`): *"the `wasi:keyvalue/store` and `wasi:keyvalue/batch` interfaces are supported"* and *"the `wasi:keyvalue/atomic` interface is not supported because it requires a consistency guarantee not provided by our global store."*

**So `wasi:keyvalue/atomics`' `increment` is a documented dead end, and worse, a trap — this retracts an earlier suggestion in this session that it was a promising spike.** The bindings ship in *both* SDKs (`wasi_keyvalue_atomics_0_2_0_draft2.py`), so code using it would compile cleanly and could plausibly work under local `spin up` before failing on Akamai. Anyone reaching for an atomic counter to fix the read-modify-write contention should stop here: the property that makes it attractive is exactly the one Akamai says its global store cannot provide.

**A concrete blocker for the `get_many` spike, found while verifying and not in the plan.** `get_many`'s signature is `get_many(bucket: wasi_keyvalue_store_0_2_0_draft2.Bucket, keys)`, but this app opens every store through `spin_key_value_key_value_3_0_0.Store` (`spin_sdk/key_value.py`: `Store = kv.Store`). **These are different WIT resource types, so the app's existing store handle cannot be passed to the batch interface at all.** The spike's first question is therefore not "does Akamai bill a `get_many` of K keys as 1 read or K" but **"can this component reach `wasi:keyvalue/batch` in the first place"** — which requires opening the store via `wasi:keyvalue/store.open()`, and raises two further questions: whether the `spin:up/http-trigger@4.0.0` world imports `wasi:keyvalue` at all, and whether a store opened that way still respects `spin.toml`'s `key_value_stores` allowlist (a security boundary, not a detail). **Answer those before costing anything else** — if the interface is unreachable from this world, the whole option is moot regardless of billing.

**Two corrections to the brief that commissioned this plan, both mine:**
- I listed a `consistency.py` obligation for any new KV key type. **It does not apply here** — `CONSISTENCY_STORES = ("links", "users")` (`api/consistency.py:29`), so the analytics namespace is never scanned. Verified.
- I **omitted** a real fourth obligation: `parse_analytics_key`/`classify_analytics_keys` would classify a `total:<slug>` key as `unrecognized`, making it a **permanently unpurgeable orphan** for every deleted link and breaking the unbuilt `purge_slug_analytics`. Any new analytics key shape must teach those functions about itself.

**Independently verified 2026-08-12 before commit, not taken on the builder's report.** Re-ran all
three suites (api **572**, gui-pages 71, Go green and untouched) and re-did the live run from a
clean `spin up --build` with a **sibling control link**, which is the check that actually matters:

| | before delete | after delete |
|---|---|---|
| `victim` (12 clicks) | 22 analytics keys | **0** |
| `sibling` (8 clicks) | 15 analytics keys | **15 — intact** |

`DELETE /api/links/victim` returned `analytics_purge: {"status": "complete", "found_keys": 22,
"deleted_keys": 22}`, the orphan report went to zero, and `sibling` still resolved 302 with its
count still incrementing. A zero-click delete returned `found_keys: 0` cleanly. **Bulk delete
still orphans (12 keys) and the operator tool still cleans them up** — correct behaviour here, not
a regression.

**Three design points checked in the code rather than assumed:** write ordering is record →
both indexes → analytics (so an interruption leaves recoverable orphans, never a live link with
vanished history); the purge is wrapped so a KV failure returns `status: "failed"` instead of
turning a successful deletion into a 500; and deletes are a sequential `for` loop with no
`gather_reads` anywhere near them.

**`MAX_INLINE_PURGE_KEYS = 128` is confirmed a rail, not a policy.** The per-slug ceiling at
shipped configuration is `64 + 30 + 1 = 95`, so the deferral branch **cannot fire**; `CountShards`
would have to exceed 97 before it became reachable. That is exactly what the closed decision asked
for.

**The builder's disclosed deviation is ACCEPTED.** `handle_orphan_purge` was left calling
`classify_analytics_keys` directly rather than being rewired through `purge_slug_analytics`. The
two have genuinely different semantics — the endpoint batches across up to 50 slugs against a
shared 250-key budget, biggest-first; the inline path is one slug against a 128-key rail. The
expensive, subtle part (key classification) **is** shared: all three call sites go through
`classify_analytics_keys`. Only a two-line delete loop is duplicated, and the task's done-when
asked for unchanged behaviour with existing tests passing, which holds.

asymmetry.** This is not the documented latency-regime swing, because both figures come from one
request: reads here are ~4× *faster* than CLAUDE.md's recorded 20–26 ms while writes are ~3×
*slower*. The repo's per-operation table (get 21.2 ms, set 26.1 ms) has them near-parity; they are
not, at least in this window. **Every write-path estimate in this repo derived from ~23 ms/write is
therefore optimistic by ~3×.**

**Consequences, in order of how much they matter:**

1. **The inline purge's worst case is ~7.1 s, not the plan's modelled 2.2 s.** Still comfortably
   inside Akamai's 30-second handler limit, so **the decision to ship it stands** — but the margin
   is 4× rather than 14×, and it is now measured rather than assumed.
2. **The bulk-delete rejection is reinforced by ~3×.** 50 links × 95 keys at 75 ms is **~356
   seconds**, not the 95–123 s that was already judged impossible. That door is now firmly shut.
3. **A user-visible latency the plan under-estimated: a real delete took 1.9 s.** The GUI comment
   claiming "~300 ms typical" was modelled and is corrected in `gui/dashboard.js`. The delete
   button is disabled for the duration, but nothing else tells the user why the page paused —
   see the open question below.

**The cleanest confirmation that the feature works: this measurement needed no cleanup.** Every
previous analytics measurement in this file ended with a manual purge; this one left the store at
exactly its pre-test state (36 keys, 0 orphans, 14 links) because the deletes cleaned up after
themselves. The sibling control also proves scoping: `dsibling` kept all 8 clicks while `dvictim`
was purged.

**Caveat on durability, stated because this file has been burned by absolutes before.** `list_keys`
measured 74–91 ms here against **23.9 ms at a comparable store size on 2026-08-11** — so it moved
3× while `get` moved 3× the other way. Op-type ratios are themselves unstable across windows, not
just absolute values. Treat the 11× read/write asymmetry as measured-in-this-window, and re-measure
before leaning on it for any new design.

Decide whether a multi-second delete needs user feedback beyond the disabled button — file(s): gui/dashboard.js — done when: either a progress affordance exists or the decision to leave it is recorded with its reasoning. **Note this reopens nothing:** the closed decision was that `analytics_purge`'s *result* is not rendered, which is different from whether the *wait* is communicated. At 1.9 s measured (and ~7 s at the ceiling) on the app's most common corrective action, for non-technical users, a silent pause may read as a hang.
